#4198. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

#4197. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel Won’t Get News For “Some Time”

After The Elder Scrolls fans started getting a little too sure that Sentinel news was coming today, Bethesda has stepped in to set the record straight on what to expect.

Last week, Xbox and Bethesda dropped a bombshell on The Elder Scrolls fans by finally giving us a concrete, non-interview update on the long-awaited next game. The new trailer followed in the reveal’s footsteps by being entirely CGI and incredibly short, but at least gave us something to chew on with a reveal of the subtitle Sentinel and confirmation of a return to Hammerfell.

That excitement dwindled a little bit when it was reported that Sentinel was still more than two years away from releasing, which some fans outright refused to believe. Even after the original reporter doubled down, some were convinced that the trailer was teasing big news for today, something that got so out of hand that Bethesda even stepped in.

Ever since the teaser trailer for Sentinel was released last week, there have been theories floating around that something would be shared today, November 11, which is Skyrim’s anniversary. Some thought the trailer’s visuals hinted at it, while others speculated that Bethesda was counting down to it through anniversary posts.

The Elder Scrolls 6 looked poised for a cross-platform launch, but with Xbox embracing exclusives again, things aren't so certain.

Things really came to a head when Redditor Sorry-Instruction330 shared a post from kiwitalkz that teased an incoming announcement that many tied to The Elder Scrolls 6. That thread got so much traction that Bethesda itself stepped in to share a statement debunking the 11/11 rumours and really setting the tone for when we’ll get an update.

The statement confirms that Bethesda isn’t making “any big announcements” today and that while it’s “excited you’re excited”, nothing new will be shared on Sentinel “for some time”. So basically, if you’re expecting anything other than a Skyrim celebration post to mark 15 years, then you’re going to be sorely disappointed.

From the sound of it, Sentinel might not even launch on this generation of consoles, or at least be a cross-gen game.

If you somehow still didn’t believe that a reliable reporter with plenty of Bethesda scoops like Jason Schreier was mistaken, then Bethesda outright saying it’s going to be a long time should really clue you in. This game is not on the horizon by any means, even if we can finally stop just calling it The Elder Scrolls 6.

Warhammer Survivors never quite matches Vampire Survivors, but there's something so satisfying about carving through hordes of pixelated tyranids.

#4196. Bandai Namco Shuts Down Reflector Entertainment, Expects €21 Million in Losses

Lauren has experience in the gaming and esports space, writing news, guides, features, reviews, lists, conducting interviews, and more. Before joining the team at DualShockers, Lauren was a Features Writer at Adventure Gamers, a Guides Writer at Gameranx, as well as contributing as a News Writer at PCInvasion and Daily

Bandai Namco has announced that it is shutting down one of its studios, Reflector Entertainment. Perhaps one of the lesser-known studios under Bandai Namco’s wing, Reflector Entertainment has yet to show its potential.

The latest and only project by Reflector Entertainment is Unknown 9: Awakening, which rolled out in October 2024. It’s an action-adventure where you step into the shoes of Haroona, who is able to enter a mysterious dimension that overlaps our own, and she can channel numerous powers on her quest.

Tripwire Interactive has been hit with layoffs for a second time this year, but it has been confirmed that work continues on Killing Floor 3 and Maneater 2.

The game is just one of many parts of the IP’s narrative universe, as there are also stories told across podcasts, comics, novels, and web series.

Bandai Namco acquired Reflector Entertainment in 2020, and even though the studio is based in Canada, Reflector joined the family over at Bandai Namco Europe. At the time of the acquisition, the studio was already working on Unknown 9: Awakening. After Unknown 9: Awakening’s weak reception among fans and critics, Reflector Entertainment announced that 18% of its staff were being laid off, just one month after the game’s launch.

Unknown 9: Awakening sits at a Top Critic Average of 62 on OpenCritic, along with just 17% of critics recommending the game. Of course, that’s less than ideal, especially with the backing of Bandai Namco, who are known for delivering some of the biggest franchises, including Dark Souls, Code Vein, Dragon Ball video games, and so much more.

The reason given for the liquidation of Reflector Entertainment was that it came as part of a continuous review into The Group’s business portfolio, and “after comprehensively considering future business plans, necessary additional investment, and the possibility of profitability and business continuation, the Company has decided to discontinue Reflector’s business, dissolve and liquidate it.”

The statement clarifies that a concrete liquidation schedule “is undecided as of now. The Company will advance the necessary procedures according to local laws and regulations, and once said procedures are completed, the liquidation will be complete.”

The matter comes with huge losses for Bandai Namco, as they expect to “post an extraordinary loss of approximately 21 million euros (approx. 3.5 billion yen) on its consolidated financial statements for the third quarter (nine months) of the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027, and thereafter.” The final figure and timing remain under review, but the impact will be eye-watering, nevertheless.

After Unknown 9: Awakening’s weak reception among fans and critics, Reflector Entertainment announced that 18% of its staff were being laid off, just one month after the game’s launch.

It’s unknown how many employees are impacted by the closure of Reflector Entertainment, and at the time of writing, Reflector Entertainment has yet to comment on its liquidation.

Sadly, Reflector Entertainment joins a long list of studios to be shut down or hit with layoffs this year. As a result of the XBOX layoffs, for example, two separate agreements to sell off the creators behind Hellblade, Ninja Theory, fell through. As a result, the studio is facing a proposed closure.

Consultation with Arkane Lyon, the team behind Dishonored and the upcoming Marvel’s Blade game, remains underway and is expected to continue through the end of the year.

Despite Ghost of Yotei's resounding success, an eighth of the team has been laid off.

#4195. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

#4192. The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin may be your next anime gacha obsession, with a hint of Ghibli, and this latest trailer may be what sells you on it

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

You can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#4191. Grand Theft Auto VI Will Run At 30 FPS On All Consoles, But PS5 Pro Will Feature 'Improved Clarity' And Ray-Traced Shadows

Grand Theft Auto VI launches next week on Thursday, November 19, and you can preload the game on your PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S starting today, Rockstar Games has announced. The studio has also revealed what kind of visuals players can expect on their respective consoles, making clear that regardless of where you play, GTA VI targets 30 FPS gameplay.

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life – while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants," Rockstar writes in a blog post.

Rockstar Games also breaks down the different graphical settings available on PlayStation and Xbox consoles. On PS5 Pro, GTA VI will feature "improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro." On PS5 and PS5 Pro, the game will include "high-fidelity haptic feedback" fully integrated into DualSense controllers and adjustable via accessibility settings, improved spatial rendering so all in-game sounds take full advantage of Tempest 3D audio, and improved load times, "making Grand Theft Auto VI play best on PlayStation 5 consoles."

On Xbox consoles, Rockstar doesn't dive into performance; instead, it focuses on Xbox Cloud Gaming on Xbox Series X/S and Xbox One consoles, noting this feature will use Xbox Series S graphics settings.

GTA VI will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox.

GTA VI launches November 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

#4190. The Abxylute M6 Is An Ideal Bluetooth Mobile Controller For Those On The Go

Gaming on the go feels so much better with the abxylute M6, and you won't have to clean your screen every few minutes.

We’ve come a long way since Snake was the pinnacle of mobile gaming. Today’s phones are portable computers capable of running console-quality titles, both natively and through cloud streaming, but often these can be frustrating to play with touch controls which sorely impact the overall experience. With its M6 model, live now on Kickstarter, abxylute aims to deliver the comfort of playing with a controller alongside the convenience of portability.

On first impressions, the abxylute M6 is a sleek piece of kit, reminiscent of hardware like the Xperia Play. Your MagSafe or equivalent-enabled phone attaches via a powerful magnet, which then slides upwards to reveal the controller underneath. The magnetic island itself can be slid left or right to fit the magnetic area of your phone, and even removed and carried separately if you find it adds just a bit too much bulk in your pocket.

This marks a change from the usual telescopic mobile controllers which place the buttons to the sides of your phone, making for a very wide device, instead keeping the footprint to around the same size as a regular DualSense or Xbox controller. My M6 came with an extra attachable grip for even more comfortable holding, something I would very much come to depend on during testing.

The M6 comes with three pairing modes depending on what you are playing: PS Mode for Remote Play and PlayStation emulators, Xinput Mode for anything Xbox or PC, and NS Mode that turns the M6 into a useful extra Pro Controller for Nintendo emulation. Connecting the M6 to my phone was an easy process - I first selected the mode, held the Pair button until the LED began flashing, then selected the controller in my phone’s Bluetooth settings. My phone treated all three modes as separate controllers, but once connected for the first time, all three paired almost instantly each time I wanted to use the M6. When it was time to stop, I simply slid the top down to sever the connection after a few seconds.

Other features include vibration that isn’t too overpowering, a programmable macro button that can do pretty much anything you ask of it, and turbo mode on just about any button. With abxylute’s dedicated mobile app, you can map the controls to touchscreen games, and even import your local games and emulators for easy access. It goes without saying that it supports a wide range of games that already have native controller support.

If you like to use controllers, even while mobile gaming, you've come to the right place. Here are the best mobile games with controller support.

Overall I was impressed by the build quality of the M6. The face and shoulder buttons had a clickiness to them that I like, while the linear triggers were satisfyingly springy. The M6 uses 20° capacitive joysticks, and while they felt highly responsive, they also felt a little too loose for my liking at first. I was using a Pixel 8 Pro, and while this phone doesn’t have a magnetic component, the M6 came with an adhesive-backed magnetic ring I could attach to my phone. I also use a case with a magnetic ring built in, and the M6 had no issues holding either firmly in place.

All-in-all, I liked what the M6 had to offer in terms of ergonomics and quality, and appreciated that I could have the screen and controls centrally in my field of view at the same time.

Now, how does it perform when it’s actually being used? I firstly tested the following native Android games - Asphalt Legends, GRID Autosport, Fortnite, Final Fantasy Tactics: The War of the Lions, and Warframe - for a good spread of control schemes. These all worked flawlessly out of the box on the Xinput pairing mode, with no customisation needed, as they recognised the Xbox controller and adapted accordingly.

I used PlayStation Remote Play next, opting for a game that requires extreme precision at all times: PGA Tour. Golf games are a passion of mine, but I was a bit hesitant. I expected a double-kick of Bluetooth and streaming latency to impact my experience, but outside of the standard remote play delay, I couldn’t fault the controller one bit. I wanted to, when I shanked my first shot on the Old Course of St. Andrews straight into the drink, but in reality I was just rusty. Once I’d found my groove again, the birdies flocked back to roost. For a different kind of stress test I fired up my current game, Yakuza 3, also via PS Remote Play. This requires constant mashing of buttons and stick movement, and for the large part the controller performed really well.

Co-op gaming online has never been better than with the creation of Steam's Remote Play feature.

Generally speaking, the M6 performed almost perfectly across all the games I tested, with one slight gripe - stick sensitivity. They were a little too loose for my liking - in GRID, this meant the car swaying all over the track, making precision cornering harder than it perhaps should have been. For Fortnite, Warframe, and Yakuza, the sensitivity meant that the camera was constantly moving, and I found it hard to target enemies as a result. In the former two games the camera sensitivity can be altered in the settings, which helped, but in Yakuza this wasn’t an option. Your mileage may vary here, and players more used to stick-based action games will likely manage just fine.

What I did notice with the action games was that the holding position needed to constantly use the shoulder buttons, reaching over the triggers, meant that the controller naturally tipped backwards. Because it was already top-heavy, this meant that I needed to apply more force with my ring and little fingers to hold it in place. For short gaming sessions this wouldn’t be an issue, but for longer stints this would leave my wrists feeling fatigued, and I’d need to take breaks. The included grip is essential here, giving that added leverage to hold the controller in place without tipping, and it was more manageable when I could rest my arms against a table or my lap. I’d like to see a version of the grip that has slightly larger ‘handles’, so that your hold acts more as a counterweight without the strain.

The final game I tested was League of Legends: Wild Rift. I’m a long-time player of the PC game, but always hesitant with Wild Rift because I disliked the touch controls. The abxylute app guided me through a tutorial on mapping, and once I’d figured out the control scheme I wanted to use, it was actually a game-changing experience. I could move about as fluidly as if I was using a mouse, and abilities activated instantly. I was a much more effective player, securing kills and controlling the map compared to when I used touch controls, and it made for the best time I had with the M6 overall. I can see myself committing to playing more Wild Rift now I know I have this tool available.

As part of testing, I also gave the M6 to my nephew Toby, as he’s a serial mobile gamer and far closer to the target demographic than I am. He tested Roblox natively and Forza Horizon 6 through Xbox Remote Play on his Samsung phone, and while he had similar gripes with the ergonomics, the M6 ultimately got his seal of approval. He liked the feel of the buttons and the build quality, and was surprised by the apparent lack of noticeable latency. He felt it was a controller best suited for shorter stints, something I think encapsulates the mobile gamer of today perfectly.

The abxylute M6 is an excellent piece of kit for what it aims to do, and while it has some minor drawbacks, these don’t get in the way of actually playing games. It’s something you can keep in a jacket pocket or a small bag when you’re on the move, and enjoy a short session largely without hassle or having to deal with touch controls and grubby screens afterwards. I’d have no qualms getting Toby one of these for Christmas, and it’s seriously making me consider mobile gaming as a viable option for the many bus trips I take rather than the numerous dedicated handhelds I already own.

#4189. Interview: Old School RuneScape's creative director on keeping the old school spirit alive - Part One

The popularity of Old School RuneScape can't be understated, in some ways even outweighing the popularity of the mainline RuneScape itself. So, it should be no surprise we found it difficult to pin down the Old School RuneScape development team for an interview back in summer!

But, fortunately, a few months on, we've managed to put some of our most burning questions to none other than Old School RuneScape's creative director, Kieren Charles!

So, I'm creative director of Old School, and that basically means I'm overseeing what it is we do and what our core fundamental strategy is behind our content, the way we try to do things, our philosophy, and the way we work with our players, and I'm overseeing everything the team does at the core of it. I've been a part of Old School for 11 and a half years since I joined as a member of QA.

The whole team was about 10 or 11 people back then, and so it kind of often feels quite surreal to be in the sort of role I am now, with a game that I've grown up with since I was a kid.

So, Hardcore Worlds came out last Wednesday, and we're absolutely thrilled with the impact that it’s had and how smoothly the launch has gone. Just seeing all of our content creators jump in. There have been so many amazing moments so far already. And thrilled with just ultimately how that's been received, and the team had to work really hard to get that over the line. So, so proud of what they were able to do.

So there are multiple factors and things to talk about with this question, honestly. And so some things we backport, and often that's stuff that, with hindsight, we still think is amazing. If we think it could be improved or it doesn't quite fit Old School from a design philosophy perspective, then it's going to need changes or tweaks, and we will absolutely do that.

Chosen Commander, which we're bringing out in early next year, is a backport of the first-ever Quest finale RuneScape ever did back in back in 2009 or so. People love that story and the character of Zanic, this cave goblin that you sort of befriend and take on a tour around Lumbridge and everything. There's no reason to mess with it. But what we do need to mess with is why you do it, the rewards, what you unlock as a matter of progression through that story, and make sure that fits the bill.

We did Blood Moon Rises in summer this year, which is our grandmaster conclusion to the Vampyre story, where you finally come face to face and fight Drakan. We did that entirely our own way. And we did that because we ultimately just had a vision of something. We thought this was this is going to be absolutely amazing, let's do it this way. This fits Old School RuneScape better and the way we want to tell the story.

And Chosen Commander was from 2009. So, it's very much already in the spirit of Old School, while the vampire finale that RuneScape did previously was much, much further in the future, much separate from the 2007 kind of era.

That is one of the core requirements of how we think about updating this game. If you're hurting that familiarity, and that's an intangible thing really you can't really pin down.

I wish I had this epic Bible I could just hand the team and say, 'this is the guide', right? But it's really not that simple. It's an intuition for, like, what's going to hurt when that changes; would players be hurt by it? Would nostalgia be hurt? Would familiarity be hurt? And then what's the spirit of the game design principles?

Design principles might shift when running an MMO for 20 years, but for Old School, we believe that those are the things that need to be retained. Old School won't ever be full of like daily stuff that you need to do every day. Temporary content that's like super FOMO oriented; we just don't do that kind of thing.

We have a real respect for the achievements and stuff the players have attained. Things we released in 2005 that predate Old School, like getting your fire cape. That is still to this day, 21 years later, a significant achievement and milestone on many player accounts.

That may have been the very end milestone back in 2005, but it's not the end milestone now; however, it's still a significant step, and that content will always be valuable. So every time we're adding something like Chosen Commander or Fractured Archive, that we just launched, we're building them in mind that they're going to be relevant for 20 years; forever, in theory

There's a significant overlap in how people use mobile. Like, you can imagine sort of three groups, right? You've got players who only play on an actual computer. You've got people who only play on mobile. And then you got a bunch of people who play on both. A humongous chunk sits in that category where you utilise both. And the reality is some things feel better on your PC, some things feel better can feel better on a phone.

I mentioned the raid we just launched [Fractured Archive], which is super challenging. People do do it on mobile, but it's extremely difficult to be doing that on a touchscreen where you just don't have the same level of control as keyboard and mouse control. But people can do it on mobile.

On the flip side, you have really chill content like, for example, you want to train your combat; you can go and kill the gemstone crab, and you just need to press it every five minutes while playing on mobile.

And the point is you don't even have to pay attention to it in some activities. And mobile's so great for being able to do those sort of things on-the-go. So in terms of how we think about it, it's not necessarily something we need to think about all the time. The great thing is we have the entire game on mobile, and so everything we add to the game is for both platforms.

That said, we do want the mobile experience to be better and we think there's so many things we can do to to make it to make it improved. Um, and that comes down to those core interactions. I think we could make dialogue a little bit easier to interact with; it could be a little bit easier. It's those sort of things where mobile needs attention, more than adding a new raid or a new quest.

Old School is founded on what the player wants, right? Like ultimately, it's the very nature of how we work. And so, it's scary. I do feel like we're I I see ourselves as more like we're looking after this game and making sure it's set up for a strong future and whatever happens.

And I want the version of the game that's available now to always be the best version we've ever had. And so ideally everything we do is making the game as a whole package better than it used to be. And that sounds so simple, but obviously that's easier said than done.

And we've all had experiences of games we love changing in ways that we dislike. And that was the origin of Old School: changes were happening in RuneScape, the combat system being much more deeply modernised and so on. And ultimately you had a whole bunch of people who had that sudden feeling of 'I wish we had back what we used to have from that 2007 version'.

People reference 2006-2007 as like the original sort of golden era of RuneScape; people were picking it up on a browser because it was playable on a school library computer. So people have that appetite for that era, which we need to look after. Like I've inherited it myself, and so many people on the team grew up playing this game; so we kind of just get it in a similar way.

But we don't do anything without players telling us they want it. We can't add the new raid to the game or Menaphos next year without players saying yes on a vote.

That's a difficult process to go through, and we have to basically sell players on it. Why do we want to do this? What problems is it going to solve? Why should you be excited? And then players hopefully vote yes. But if people vote no, we can't do it. That would break our principles of how we work. So in some ways it takes a little bit of the pressure off. If we get it wrong, we find out tomorrow; we don't find out when we've launched it.

And I'd much rather find out at a poll and be disappointed that we're not moving forward than launch something that feels like it's damaged the game in players' eyes. And so with RuneScape and Old School, to me, they coexist nicely. There's some overlap. People want different things. Some people want the modern combat system, which is much more ability-driven. Some people want the laid-back Old School one where a lot of stuff is click and wait. And the best thing is you get to offer two RuneScapes to the world and now a third with Dragonwilds! This interview ended up being so long that we've actually split it into multiple parts! So, watch this space, and once part two of our interview with Old School RuneScape's creative director Kieren Charles is up, we'll link it through here!

In the meantime, if you want to see what other mobile MMORPGs are making waves, why not check out our list of the best mobile games like World of Warcraft to see some of our choice picks?

#4188. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

More specifically, preloading on Xbox Series X/S will begin Tuesday, November 10, at 12 a.m. GMT (4 p.m. PT/7 p.m. ET on November 9), and on PS5 at midnight local time in your time zone. Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Music makes many games what they truly are, setting the tone and doubling down on a moment's emotions, whether somber, pulse-pounding, or chilling. Without their OSTs, many games would feel like a shell of themselves, solid without the soul. Many games have used the need for music to get musicians on the map or back into the public spotlight, creating a beautiful loop.

The EU's proposed Digital Fairness Act targets loot boxes, pay-to-win mechanics, unclear in-game prices, and subscription traps.

Final Fantasy is a series absolutely defined by its music, with truly legendary composers and artists stemming from every title. Sadly, Final Fantasy 14’s Twitter announced earlier today that Eikichi Iwai, bassist for the band made for the game THE PRIMALS, has passed away. After recently performing at the most recent Japanese Fan Fest, his passing is a sudden low blow that has staggered fans across the globe.

THE PRIMALS are the standout musicians of Final Fantasy 14, far from the only incredibly talented maestros making the music happen, but definitely the flashiest. Often brought out to live events for both their own original tracks and covers of some of 14's other greatest hits, THE PRIMALS helped forge some of the greatest tracks to grace Final Fantasy 14, and Iwai-san's absence will be deeply felt in future events.

While the rest of the musicians behind FF 14 and his bandmates on THE PRIMALS will feel the most potent loss, fans across the globe are aching as well, already holding in-game mourning vigils throughout Eorzea. Sitting by fires and playing different pieces of music Iwai worked on, fans are lamenting his passing the best way they know how, by celebrating all he gave to them.

THE PRIMALS are the standout musicians of Final Fantasy 14, far from the only incredibly talented maestros making the music happen, but definitely the flashiest.

THE PRIMALS have backed some of the most pivotal moments in Final Fantasy 14’s history, bouncing from raid layers to incredibly crucial story moments to general world traversal. As a band, they’re incredibly flexible and talented, with a good part of that grit coming from Iwai’s incredible bass play. The future of the band is currently uncertain, especially with how sudden Iwai’s loss truly was.

Eikichi Iwai passed at age 57, a titan of his craft and an incredible musician across his pursuits, charming millions who played Final Fantasy 14 and all who followed his long history with the band Chirinuruwowaka, of which he was a founding member. Never one to slow down or stop making music, with his recent showing at the latest Japanese FF14 Fan Fest being cited as one of THE PRIMALS best ever showings.

After suffering a loss like Iwai’s, it’s important to remember just how lucky we are to enjoy such incredibly skilled artists in their primes. Final Fantasy 14 has its issues, but music has never been one of them, carrying many crucial emotional scenes with next-level tracks again and again.

Close in the Distance, A Long Fall, and Rise, all written by Masayoshi Soken, show a mastery of tone and emotion across an incredible range, perfectly putting players in the mindset of the current moment. THE PRIMALS’ own coverage of tracks like Footfalls and Dawntrail gives each song life, fueled by THE PRIMALS’ incredible energy.

I genuinely believe you could find someone who cites almost every song in Final Fantasy 14 as one of their favorites, and that’s amazing. The incredible display of artistry throughout the title is a large reason why it has lasted as long as it has with the massive fanbase it has cultivated.

With live service games and MMOs like Final Fantasy 14, it can be all too easy and lucrative to fall into the trappings of consumerism, focusing on the product rather than the art. FF really doesn’t have that issue. FF14 has always felt like a title guided by the artists who create it, and after the loss of such a powerful artist, it’s up to the rest of us to keep on that path. Rest in peace, Eikichi Iwai.

#4185. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

#4184. House House Discloses AI Use For 'Under 0.1%' Of Big Walk's Code Following IGF Voting Controversy

Big Walk developer House House has found itself at the center of a controversy over the upcoming Independent Games Festival on March 3, 2027, after a group of its jurors said they would not vote for any game that has used generative AI in any capacity. The jurors' statement does not name House House or Big Walk, but the studio eventually updated its FAQ to explain how it used generative AI for coding after IGF discussions. After vaguely posting on social media, those associated with IGF made clear that a sticking point in the voting process was Big Walk.

Former games journalist and game developer Austin Walker posted the IGF jurors' statement on Bluesky, explaining that voting has been difficult this year due to the "significant increase in the number of submitted games developed with generative AI tools."

"This has set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools, and at this point there is no universal consensus on what (if anything) is to be done," the statement reads. "The IGF has affirmed that we may cast our votes according to our own tastes and values. But we, as a contingent of IGF jurors, feel that this trend and the games embracing it deserve stronger pushback than a vote in silence."

The statement continues, explaining that not all jurors are on board with the blanket statement, citing reasons including "their ability to safely sign without professional blowback." It continues, "Above all: Our goal is to state solidarity with those who despair over the future of their art, their craft, and their industry – including those who have experimented with these tools, but who now believe they are not in our best interest."

The statement continues with the jurors' beliefs regarding gen-AI, including its negative effects, that any gen-AI used in any process of game development is not okay, noting specifically that "AI-generated code is not an exception to these harms," and more.

"For those reasons, this year we are declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity," the statement says. "We urge the IGF to adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work." The statement then includes the names of the IGF jurors who signed it.

Big Walk isn't specifically mentioned within that statement. However, Kyle LeClair, a four-time IGF judge and a juror for the upcoming IGF, tells Aftermath that "it got to the point where the most-discussed game this year almost entirely involved its AI usage, overshadowing pretty much everything else." LeClair says it felt like a boiling point, adding, "Anyhow, strong props to the jurors for taking this stance and putting out this letter as well, even if some people believe that using AI for coding purposes is a more gray area, we're at a point where the amount of AI slop clogging up the indie game scene means having to take hard stances such as this in order to discourage such an amount of recklessness."

Again, no mention of Big Walk. However, game developer Bruno Diaz took to BlueSky to confirm the speculation: that most-discussed game was Big Walk. "Okay, because the cat is out of the f---ing bag, I might as well combat misinformation a bit: 1. The reason IGF judges are aware of the LLM use in the development of Big Walk is through a disclosure shared by House House. 2. This disclosure was required by IGF rules. 3. While some have characterized the LLM usage as just fixing one individual blocking bug, this is a bit inaccurate; the description given by House House mentioned there being several instances, though they did also say it was mostly 'consultative' use and not code gen or agents."

Diaz notes that they believe that distinction is without a difference, adding that "to my knowledge, it is not the case that Big Walk is non-compliant with the former [Steam's AI disclosure requirements]."

"Yes, there was a large discussion about this in internal IGF forums," Diaz said. "Yes, a lot of people said things that I personally think were disingenuous, extremely disappointing, or just (frankly) dumb. No, I have no intention of talking about it in further detail or exposing anyone. [...] Ultimately, it is extremely difficult for a group of over 100 people to keep a secret so I expected this to come out eventually. Shrug emoji. If you think something is reputationally damaging, consider not doing it."

With discussion surrounding Big Walk happening during the IGF discussions, House House updated its FAQ to address, "Was AI used to make Big Walk?" Here's what the FAQ reads, in full:

"In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs. In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

The primary use case for House House’s use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code. If you’re technically-minded, and curious, here’s an example. We needed to cull shadow casters by distance from the camera, but Unity URP only allows culling shadow casters by distance in camera forwards, so shadow casters behind the player were being rendered at an infinite distance. This made our game run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. We researched the problem extensively, and we looked at the URP code ourselves, but we couldn’t find a way. Then, we were able to speak directly to an engineer at Unity, who asked around and ultimately concluded that what we wanted wasn’t possible. Finally, we posed the question to an LLM chatbot. After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP.

We originally wrote a version of the above disclosure as it was a suggested part of our IGF submission. We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest.

This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.

Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

As you can see, House House did not disclose its use of AI-generated code because "Steam as a platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage." It says it is posting the disclosure now as "it has become a matter of public interest."

House House recently made headlines for choosing not to put Big Walk on Xbox in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS boycott against Microsoft Games. Earlier this year, it gained widespread critical acclaim for its unique emphasis on cooperative puzzle-solving – you can read more about that in Game Informer's Big Walk review.

#4182. 10 Most Creative Traversal Abilities in Metroidvanias

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Movement abilities in Metroidvanias are a fundamental part of their appeal, determining both the pace of exploration and our ability to interact with the surrounding world.

The genre is built on understanding spaces, their composition, and how to traverse them, making movement a crucial variable regardless of the game's perspective, mechanics, or philosophy.

As a result, the possibilities a game enables for movement along the Cartesian plane largely determine how satisfying, tense, or rewarding a campaign will be, depending on its intended purpose.

Therefore, in order to pay homage to those video games that make the best possible use of the philosophy of moving from one place to another, here are the ten most creative traversal abilities in Metroidvanias.

One of the main problems games in this genre face when creating spectacular movement abilities lies in their limitations, as they have to be balanced so that they aren't too powerful.

For this reason, Silk Soar from Hollow Knight: Silksong is a masterpiece of design. Among all the powers in Metroidvanias that let you fly upwards, it's part of the few that properly contextualize the limits of its capabilities.

Not only do you acquire it in the game's last third, unexpectedly opening paths out of nowhere, but its use is also tied to your needle, requiring the presence of a ceiling to be used, so you can't just break the map's traversal in its entirety.

In terms of creativity, it's on the spectrum's simpler side, yet it solves a major verticality imbalance by granting you a great deal of ease in exploration without making you overpowered, which is a tremendous feat.

Going in the opposite direction from the previous entry, Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo is a constant display of reinterpreting Metroidvanias' most common forms of movement, with Walk the Dog being the crown jewel.

The game plays with yo-yo tricks to establish its mechanics, adapting them with thematic coherence to make you feel that, more than just having powers within a video game, you're learning new maneuvers to show off.

In this particular instance, it's as simple as being able to move orthogonally across the map at a greater speed, but this is maximized thanks to the bounce pads distributed throughout all areas that change your direction and make the ability the key to numerous puzzles.

Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo is brimming with ideas magnificently adapted to its setting, making it by far one of the most inventive Metroidvanias to come out this decade.

Well Dweller breaks one of the genre's cardinal rules by not including a double jump at any point in its story, though it compensates with a Slingshot mechanic that is simply mesmerizing.

The title allows you to throw your weapon and embed it in any surface to use it as a springboard and jump higher than usual, encouraging inquisitive and creative exploration in a truly compelling way.

Most of the game's movement is based on the biomes you find yourself in, whether in the form of bubbles, air currents, or elevators, and it works precisely because this direct yet versatile ability adapts to any situation.

Of course, it leaves you without any means of defense, but, like Kratos's Leviathan Axe, Well Dweller's matchstick flies back to you when you need it, which also leads to spectacular and almost cinematic moments when transitioning from platforming to combat.

If you're looking for games that subvert your expectations, try these eight Metroidvanias that totally reinvent themselves halfway through.

In terms of inventiveness, Animal Well is a couple of notches above the rest of the genre, with all its progression tools being as unique as they're rewarding.

Since the title is more puzzle-based than platforming-focused, most of its abilities are proportional to said distribution, but the Disc is a versatile component that you can use both to solve environmental puzzles and to traverse in seemingly impossible ways.

Throwing the frisbee and timing its trajectory to hop on and soar through the air never gets old, both because of how mechanically satisfying it is and because of all the paths mastering this skill opens up.

Animal Well is a sandbox where most of its castles are built through iteration and experimentation, but fortunately, you have the Disc on your side to make the journey faster, smoother, and more enjoyable.

Despite my reservations about Constance due to its short length and limited side content, its movement mechanics are some of the smoothest I've ever seen in the genre, with Paint Dive being the standout.

It functions as both a dash and a dematerialization of the character, allowing her to blend into the environment and pass through obstacles and hazards as a graceful mass of purple paint that seamlessly integrates with the surroundings.

In its abstract form, it's simply a directional boost, yet its execution is elevated by the environments, which force you to use the ability in increasingly diverse ways, ensuring it's more than just a regular push.

Given that platforming is Constance's forte, Paint Dive plays a prominent role throughout the entire campaign, making it a proportionally more important element of the game than many of the other abilities on this list.

From classic Resident Evil to Dark Souls, these are eight Non-Metroidvanias that heavily influenced the genre.

Returning to what I mentioned about Silk Soar and the problems of having very powerful abilities, the Crystal Arrows in Aeterna Noctis take the conversation to another level by granting you the power to teleport to wherever you aim them.

Certainly, they're used in many of the most excruciatingly difficult platforming sections the genre has ever seen, but also in one of the deepest movement systems.

Being able to chain together consecutive teleportations while fighting and traversing Aeterna's world quickly becomes a delight, especially once you get used to them and feel you've mastered their immeasurable offensive and defensive potential.

While Aeterna Noctis' structure doesn't fully capitalize on the Crystal Arrows, they remain magnificent and satisfying, surprisingly without ever breaking the game's sequence.

Castlevania: Symphony of the Night dares to take its most unusual ability and only make it necessary for a limited number of sections, yet the Mist Form remains an unforgettable memory for anyone who plays the game.

Becoming an incorporeal entity to pass through bars is the kind of power fantasy that only a character like Alucard can materialize, with the added significance of having achieved something so astonishing thirty years ago.

Although there aren't many mandatory instances where you must use it, the ability is a major surprise when you unlock it, primarily when it becomes an incredibly powerful toxic weapon that allows you to both move freely and eliminate all enemies in your path.

Years have passed, and I don't think I've ever been so impacted by unlocking a new ability, which only speaks to Castlevania: Symphony of the Night's timeless greatness.

Of all the innovations that Ori and the Blind Forest brought to the genre during the formative years when its heirs were still establishing themselves, Bash is undoubtedly the most prominent.

The ability to bounce off both enemies and projectiles to move omnidirectionally and reach new heights and locations is absurdly incredible from the very first minute to the last.

The mechanic was significantly improved in the sequel, yet its stellar and unprecedented appearance in the franchise's first title is a core memory of the genre, particularly due to its use in combat to stylize every fight sequence.

I must admit Ori and the Blind Forest isn't among my favorite Metroidvanias, though that doesn't stop me from acknowledging that, in terms of uniqueness, there's no other ability that truly compares to Bash.

If you're already tired of 2D side-scrolling games, I recommend you read about these ten best first-person Metroidvanias, ranked.

By 1994 standards, the existence of a video game of Super Metroid's caliber seems absolutely insane, as years have passed and the game remains so fresh and enjoyable that it's astonishing how ahead of its time it was.

People usually praise the Shinespark or the Morph Ball, which are masterful abilities by any measure, but I have to admit that what truly amazed me was the Grapple Beam and how wonderfully it utilizes Zebes' layout.

You spend much of the journey wondering what those strange cross-shaped blocks are for, and when you discover that they allow you to aim a beam that lets you swing freely, spin, and propel yourself at top speed, you can't help but be blown away.

Whether you played it back then or today, Super Metroid surprises you with its mastery at every turn, and there are so many ways I could have included it on this list that all I can do is stand up and applaud.

I'm going to lean towards modernity to define the top spot on this list and praise the work of MIO: Memories in Orbit, a contemporary masterpiece of the genre whose scale is truly breathtaking.

There are many reasons to say this, but unlocking the Striders, tendrils into legs and arms that can grab any surface to walk on walls, was the moment in its campaign when I realized I wasn't just playing a good Metroidvania.

Even though their use is limited by a stamina bar, thinking about the titanic effort it must have taken to craft each room of its vast map based on the eventual access to this omnipotent movement tool makes me dizzy.

Not only does it have fluid and pristine animation with perfect sound design, but it also blends seamlessly with exploration and platforming mechanics to make everything related to movement a true gift for players.

I've had many surprising moments with movement mechanics in the genre, yet the Striders in MIO: Memories in Orbit are unique while also being functional, powerful, and visually appealing, which is an elevated balance that's extremely difficult to achieve.

From the best bosses to essential lore explanations, these are eight Metroidvanias that hide their best content behind the most unexpected paths.

#4181. Our first look at Diablo 4's Warlock and the game's next season arrive in today's livestream - watch it here

Diablo 4’s next, long-awaited Developer Update finally airs today. This meaty livestream was first announced nearly a month ago, when Blizzard initially revealed that the game’s next class is the Warlock.

#4180. Pikmin 4 Is Still Great, But Dandori Academy Is Underwhelming

Pikmin 4 was released for the original Switch in 2023, and it ranks among my favorite games on the platform; I happily award it the honor of being the best Pikmin game. It looks and plays great, and Oatchi the dog makes the sometimes annoying process of managing a collection of little plant creatures willing to do your bidding much smoother.

The over-titled Pikmin 4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy releases November 12, and much like other comparable Nintendo games that have been ported and improved for Switch 2 (like Kirby and Mario Party), the base game is as good as it was initially and looks even better. If you skipped Pikmin 4 on Switch for whatever reason (probably because it was day one of the Barbenheimer epidemic), I encourage you to play it now. You have about a week to beat it before… something else comes out. Who’s to say.

The “big” addition here for the Switch 2 version of the game, alongside improved performance and visuals and the ability to give Oatchi verbal commands, is Dandori Academy. The Academy is an expanded time trial mode that awards medals for practicing specific levels, which you can then play and upload your high scores on specific days. For example, I can play the Advanced B level, Rockaway Cellars, as much as I want, but it only really counts if I play it on November 12. And you only get one try (though you can unlock retry tickets).

In theory, I like the unique approach to high-score battling, and the limited timeframe adds fun intensity, but this isn't what I am looking for from Pikmin. I recognize and acknowledge the design decision to place timers on your interactions in Pikmin, but it’s never been my favorite part. I like building my adorable little army and exploring, discovering, and retrieving as many unexpected items as possible. But I mostly get annoyed at the ticking clock, especially when I am watching my crew meander toward my spaceship holding a Game Boy Advance SP (or whatever they manage to find on the never-acknowledged, but potentially post-apocalyptic Earth you are exploring).

I also like having a list of missions to complete, and in Dandori Academy, there isn’t much acknowledgment of your success in practice. You can earn a platinum medal while practicing Rockaway Cellar, but it’s mainly to let you know that this is what you could earn when you play on the right day.

The main takeaway is that Pikmin 4 is still excellent, and I was grateful to transfer my save file from the Switch version (and I was tempted to start a new game + save), but Dandori Academy is not a strong incentive to return if you already played the game. It is a nice bonus and an interesting concept that reimagines the familiar time trial mode featured in plenty of video games, but the original campaign is still the main attraction.

#4179. Diablo 4's next season is short, but it lets you become The Butcher, and it has Doom: The Dark Ages skins you probably can't afford

Blizzard has unveiled the next Diablo 4 season, which kicks off next week to hold us over until the launch of the game's big expansion in April.

The big Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a new activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

The Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a new item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the new season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

#4178. GTA 6 Lead Says The Series Still Has “So Much To Do” In America

Rockstar Games co-studio head Rob Nelson says future Grand Theft Auto games could take place outside of America, but that the setting still has “so much to do”.

When Grand Theft Auto 6 launches in just over a week, it’s poised to be one of the most detailed and expansive open-world games of all time. Just like how GTA 5 built on San Andreas with its much bigger take on Los Santos, GTA 6 is transforming Vice City into Leonida, a whole state that’s now one big tribute to Florida instead of just Miami.

Even though Rockstar is primarily based in Scotland and the first two games in the series were set in an alternate version of London, every single GTA since has been set somewhere in America. Fans have wondered for some time whether Rockstar would ever consider going somewhere new, and we finally have an, admittedly vague, answer.

Earlier today, The Guardian published an interview with Rockstar North co-studio head and GTA 6 lead Rob Nelson about the game’s impending release. A big focus of the interview is how much work goes into creating Rockstar’s worlds and making them as believable as possible, with Nelson notably reminiscing about staying out in a Miami nightclub until 4am.

62 items, and you don't need to visit the stores in-person to get them.

After pointing out that Rockstar and GTA are famous for depicting American cities and the US, The Guardian asked Nelson about the possibility of the series having a game set outside of America. In response, Nelson said, “Never say never”, finally giving long-standing GTA Tokyo believers a little bit of hope in the process.

Funnily enough, former Rockstar developer Obbe Vermeij recently suggested that the studio was “definitely” considering letting a Japanese studio develop a GTA game.

That being said, you probably shouldn’t count on Grand Theft Auto returning to London any time soon, as Nelson noted that the team still has “so much to do in America”, even with the series being pushed to its limits with Leonida. Nelson thinks that everyone is an outsider to GTA’s version of America, which is something the team doesn’t seem in a rush to step away from.

Still, it’s about as close as we’ve ever gotten to hearing Rockstar say that Grand Theft Auto could exist outside of the US. I think everyone is expecting the eventual next game to give us a grand return to Liberty City, but here’s hoping that whatever follows that isn’t afraid to leave the States behind.

#4177. An Elder Scrolls Classic Is Finally Getting the Remaster It Deserves After 22 Years

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

As a nostalgic gamer, I have a soft spot for forgotten games that were left behind by time, especially when they're part of a franchise as beloved as The Elder Scrolls.

While most players have spent the past two decades exploring Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim, one rather unusual entry in the series has been sitting on a much less familiar platform: the Nokia N-Gage. Thankfully, that's about to change!

The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey, a first-person RPG originally released in 2004, is getting a second chance thanks to an independent project called Shadowkey Reforged.

Developed by Dan Whelan, the project brings the forgotten spin-off to Windows, Mac, and Android with a new engine, widescreen support, controller compatibility, and plenty of visual and gameplay improvements. Even better, it's launching today, November 11.

Morrowind is rightfully regarded as one of the greatest open-world RPGs of all time, but it's aged badly and would benefit from a full remake.

For anyone unfamiliar with it, Shadowkey was the third entry in The Elder Scrolls Travels, a series of portable spin-offs released between Morrowind and Oblivion. Unlike the mainline games, however, it was exclusive to Nokia's N-Gage, a rather ambitious handheld-phone hybrid that didn't exactly have the longest life on the market.

That exclusivity made Shadowkey one of the more inaccessible chapters in the franchise's history. And while you could technically track down the original hardware and a copy of the game, that's hardly the most convenient way to revisit a 22-year-old RPG.

That's where Shadowkey Reforged comes in! Rather than simply emulating the N-Gage, Whelan built a new engine capable of running the original game's data and scripts on modern devices. Players can choose between a Classic mode that preserves the original presentation and a Modern mode featuring upgraded artwork, improved lighting, and several gameplay additions. So yes, it is literally the best of both worlds.

For anyone unfamiliar with it, Shadowkey was the third entry in The Elder Scrolls Travels, a series of portable spin-offs released between Morrowind and Oblivion.

The latter isn't just a fresh coat of paint, by the way. Modern mode introduces features inspired by newer Elder Scrolls games, including stamina-based sprinting, stealth, and ragdoll physics. You can also toggle individual features to customize the experience instead of committing to one preset. And if you happen to have The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind installed, there's another neat little bonus: Shadowkey Reforged can use its soundtrack and sound effects, preserving a connection between two games released during the same era, in case you want an extra touch!

Skyblivion team says a former volunteer is threatening legal action, even after the devs removed their code and rebuilt the affected systems.

Interestingly, Whelan has also been transparent about using AI during development. According to the developer, AI tools helped with coding, building the engine, and debugging, while the updated artwork combines AI-generated images with Photoshop and manual sprite editing.

Shadowkey Reforged is available as a free, unofficial project, with versions for Windows, Mac, and Android. However, there's one important detail players should know before getting too excited: the download doesn't include the original game's files. This means you'll need to provide your own copy of Shadowkey to play it – you can check more info about that on the port’s website.

Still, it's great to see such an obscure piece of The Elder Scrolls history getting another shot at life. Bethesda hasn't announced an official remaster, but Whelan's project might be the closest many players will get to experiencing this forgotten adventure without digging up a Nokia N-Gage.

#4176. Diablo 4’s Warlock looks like an unhinged Necromancer with Sorcerer energy in first look at gameplay

Diablo 4's practitioner of forbidden arts, The Warlock, has been officially unveiled as the second class coming with Lord of Hatred.

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Update, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

Since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Update to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

The Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside new Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the big day.
