#4111. Zenless Zone Zero Version 2.8 is refreshing your team comps with a new mechanic, and the game is coming to Steam

Zenless Zone Zero will soon become the first HoYoverse game to make its way to Steam, though we wish we had more details.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a pretty exciting Zenless Zone Zero Special Program that not only delivered all the details on the next big update, it also came with the unexpected announcement that the action RPG is on its way to Steam.

Previously, all HoYoverse games with PC versions have always been directly available from the developer’s website, or through the Epic Games Store. In other words, Zenless Zone Zero will soon mark the massive company’s debut on Valve’s platform.

The main focus of the livestream, of course, has been Version 2.8, otherwise known as New Eridan Sunset. This upcoming release is scheduled for May 6, though the Steam version does not yet have a date.The new release sees the release of two new Agents, as well as the brand-new Wind attribute enemy.

The release also acts as the last chapter of Season 2, and it sees Ramiel becoming the main target of different factions in the Outer Ring. The two new arrivals, together with Proxies and Cissia will embark on a quest to learn the new identity of Ramiel.

The first new Agent is Promeia, the executioner of Krampus. She’s an S-Rank Ice Anomaly Agent who can consume Trial by Cold to trigger Abloom on enemies. This is done by converting Corrosive Chill.

By using her EX Special Attack, she can enter the Bound Absolution state, which allows her to automatically Perfect Dodge any attack that targets her. If you have another Anomaly or Support Agent on the team, Promeia can further boost the entire squad’s Abloom damage.

The second addition in 2.8 is Starlight - Billy, also an S-Rank Agent, though wielding Physical Rupture instead. This is the upgraded form of Billy, and he arrives on a combat motorcycle to bring his signature Starlight Knight to the fight. Through it, he can deliver big Physical burst damage.

The higher Billy’s health, the more Sheer damage he deals. In fact, all Physical damage he deals lands as Sheer damage. Further building on his tank-like role, his skills can also restore his own health.

Re-runs in Version 2.8 will be Lucia in the first half, and Orphie & Magus in the second. The other exciting addition coming with this update is the new Wind attribute enemy, and the accompanying Vortex mechanic.

When an enemy is inflicted with the Wind Attribute Anomaly, any other Anomaly attack type that gets applied will trigger Vortex, rather than Disorder. This deals AoE Anomaly damage of the type that matches the corresponding element.

Throughout the version’s runtime, you’ll be able to take part in the Marcel Bootopia-themed event, which gives you control of Eous and lets you explore a Bangboo resort island. The island has been closed due to an outbreak of Hollows, and you must rescue Bangboos and find treasures.

If you do, you’ll earn Booltergeist and its Bangboo core for your troubles. This is an A-Rank Bangboo that can float around and fire lasers in combat. Its damage is further boosted whenever certain teammates are present.

The Ultimate Verdict Trial is another event you can check out that lets you fight alongside newcomer Promeia, or take part in other mini-activities that all reward Polychrome. Finally, you can look forward to a new Hoshimi Miyabi outfit: Dignified Blossom, which will be available in the store.

Before you jump back in next month, it always helps to catch up on the latest Zenless Zone Zero codes to make sure you’re not missing out on any freebies.

#4110. Review: Metaphor: ReFantazio (Switch 2) - An Extraordinary JRPG That Could Use Another Optimisation Pass

A game with the name 'Metaphor' that tackles issues such as culture diversity, democracy, and classism isn't exactly subtle in its delivery, but is just as poignant in 2026 as it was when the game first released in 2024.

Atlus has brought its critically acclaimed turn-based role-playing to Switch 2, and in doing so, reminded everyone of two things: That Atlus are absolute masters at delivering striking stories, endearing characters, and engaging combat through the lens of an incredibly unique art style, and that optimisation for handheld consoles is not their strong suit.

Metaphor: ReFantazio is simultaneously the story of a young boy yearning to reconnect with his dear friend, the prince of the kingdom of Euchronia who had been struck with a curse that left him in a comatose state, a story of prejudice and social manipulation through the kingdom itself, started by the assassination of the king at the hands of Louis Guiabarn, a common-born army officer wanting to challenge the status quo through true meritocracy, AND the story of the parallels between fantasy and reality, using real-life situations as elements of idealistic fantasy within Metaphor's world, things that could never happen for the residents of Euchronia.

The way that Metaphor deftly handles so many threads of varying sizes and scopes is nothing short of extraordinary, especially when the themes of anxiety, willpower, and hope are so striking in the real world.

The individual characters in Metaphor are largely brilliantly written, with their own struggles and demons to battle, even if they aren't party members or sometimes even less important to the overarching plot. Characters like the bat-like Eugief, Heismay, battles prejudice for his race whilst trying to mourn the loss of a family member, but displays his own prejudice against the rabbit-like Papirus for their part in his grief. The stoic Brigitta, owner of the capital's magic igniter shop, casts an icy exterior, only to show her true colours through a puppy she can't resist but take in.

Even the game's main antagonist, Louis, is incredibly compelling, bringing an immediate presence to the screen through his striking design and charismatic dialogue, but as is par for the course, there is far more than meets the eye with Louis. There are a lot of plates to spin in Metaphor, but almost all of them are tantalising events to keep returning to.

It's difficult not to make comparisons between Studio Zero's Metaphor and the Persona series, as they share a lot of DNA: a calendar-based system that has you not only exploring dungeons for treasure and boss fights, but also balancing improvement of social stats, or virtues as they're known here, and bonds with party members and other important NPCs to learn more of their personal stories and gain benefits to the more traditional JRPG aspects of the game in the process.

But Metaphor stands alone in Atlus' repertoire by not only drawing from Persona, but the core Shin Megami Tensei franchise as well, while infusing its own flair in its combat mechanics through the Archetype system.

Archetypes in Metaphor are much closer to the Final Fantasy series' job system than they are to Persona, with each character gaining skills and masteries through use of interchangeable classes gained through the social parts of the game, and combat-earned AP gained to level them up. MAG, a currency gained through both combat and socialisation, can be used to transfer skills from one archetype to another, giving you plenty of ways to experiment with your own builds between the seven party members and the 30 different Archetypes alone.

Combat itself utilises the Turn Icon system resembling core Shin Megami Tensei games, with extra actions gained by striking a critical hit or weakness, or serious losses by missing an attack or hitting an absorbed element. You can also strike at an advantage by attacking enemies in the overworld in real-time, or take them out entirely if you're high enough above them in level (a feature I wish all future JRPGs would carry!), but if an enemy gets the jump on you, it can be devastating. All of these elements combine to make arguably the best combat Atlus has ever put out in a JRPG.

It's also impossible to discuss the game without mentioning its frankly stellar soundtrack. Composer Shoji Meguro's unique flavour is felt throughout the game, with one of the best battle themes to ever grace a JRPG, drawing from Buddhist sutra inspirations with priest Keisuke Honryo's unforgettable chanting.

All of this is to say that Metaphor: ReFantazio is an incredible JRPG, and one that will keep you coming back over and over for well over 80 hours. However, on Switch 2, the experience hasn't come across without a few hiccups along the way.

After releasing Persona 3 Reload on Switch 2 last year, which itself suffered greatly from frame rate issues and muddy visuals, and experiencing inconsistencies with Metaphor: ReFantazio itself in its original release, I was sceptical, to say the least, and that scepticism ended up having merit, as I'm not sure I've seen a game look quite so beautiful and hideous at the same time!

From an artistic standpoint, Metaphor is sumptuous, taking the 'more is more' approach from Persona and applying a much wider colour palette; the UI and menus are stunning, of that there's no doubt. But technically speaking, Metaphor is a bit of a mess.

There are options to run in performance, balanced, or graphics modes both handheld and docked, but regardless of which mode you pick, there were inconsistencies throughout. One moment in combat could look stunning AND run well, and the next cutscene you'd encounter the strangest case of anti-aliasing and fuzzy textures, despite there only being two characters in the room.

Frame rate issues also persist regardless of performance or graphics settings, never enough to overtake the other amazing qualities of the game, but always enough to notice and occasionally distract. Persona 3 Reload did eventually get a performance update that fixed a lot of issues; suffice it to say, I truly hope Metaphor gets one as well!

Additionally, while so much of Metaphor's main dungeons and set pieces are a sight to behold, Atlus's dungeon designs have often left something to be desired, and that's apparent in Metaphor's side dungeons. When on a side quest, it's fairly easy to get turned around in the sea of brown tunnels and foggy forest areas, simply on the back of them all looking identical! It's a stark difference to the Regalith Cathedral, Sandworm's Belly, or Skyrunner main dungeons, for sure.

Metaphor: ReFantazio is an extraordinary JRPG, juggling stories and systems alike with grace and effortlessness, but it is let down somewhat by poor optimisation on Switch 2.

Anyone looking for a huge, sprawling adventure with lovable characters, compelling parallels to the real world, and progression systems that will keep you coming back for more will be far from disappointed with this game, but there's no metaphor for a dodgy frame rate and visuals that can occasionally take you out of the fantasy.

#4108. The Sunday Papers

Sundays are for looking upon my DIY works and despairing. Strewn sawdust, spilled paint, and hunks of broken MDF litter my living room kingdom. When will it be over? When will I be free? When will I be able to reassemble my sofa, sit down with a cup of tea in hand, and admire my books, unpacked and arranged on perfectly fitted alcove bookshelves?

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

"Today?" I whisper hopefully in response to a paragraph of rhetorical questions. "Probably not," snaps back Reality. Especially if I don't get out of bed soon. Still, here in bed I can read the best writing about and not about games from the past week.

Inside our Gchat walls, there is a growing exhaustion with genAI stories. Every day another gaming boss talks about the inexorable march of the tech before putting out a trailer filled with blurry text and six-fingered characters. I don't doubt the tech is getting better, but it's not inevitable. As such, Rob Fahey's latest GI column is something of a balm:

There is currently a concerted and not-so-subtle campaign underway to try to manufacture consent for the use of AI in game development.

At its core, this is about presenting AI as a fait accompli. Every week or so we get a new report making dubious claims about almost every development studio already using AI. The message to developers is "you'll be left behind if you don't use it too"; to players, it's "this is already done and there's no turning back". Consume like good little consumers. Shut up and eat your slop.

A further tonic comes from Merritt K, who writes for Aftermath about the technological improvements rolling through Karaoke.

Doesn't it feel like everything — especially everything Big Tech touches — is getting worse? Generative AI, not merely content with robbing humans of our craft and jobs, has escaped containment into physical reality in the form of shitty event flyers and small business signage. Hugely profitable industries like video games and film are being torn apart by the financialization of the economy as shareholders seek ever-increasing short-term profits. Algorithmic pricing of rent and groceries threatens to further punish the working class for the crime of not being born rich.

But in the heart of despair, we must reach for that which is good and pure and — dare I say it — better than it used to be. Karaoke is one of those things. And it is better not because of the disruption of tech giants, but, as is often the case, thanks to the work of enterprising maniacs toiling in obscurity, purely out of the love of the game.

I've been playing Forbidden Solitaire this week, where FMV sequences starring Xalavier Nelson Jr as an obsessive fantasy-author-turned-video-game-developer are played for laughs. So it was with a minor sense of whiplash I read Ashley Bardhan's piece for This Week In Video Games. Bardhan speaks to horror developers inserting themselves into FMV games to confront and explore violence against women.

Cara Cadaver uses her own photos and videos to represent multiple victims of sexual violence and murder in her unflinching 2025 game Vile: Exhumed. She tells me over email, “Being a woman is inherently a horrifying and violent experience, any way you slice it. One of my inspirations for making games in general is pulling from real-life experience and telling stories that most every woman has lived in some way; that’s real horror.”

“Horror in general has been a major outlet for me while dealing with trauma, and so much of horror as a genre goes back to women,” Cadaver says. “Women’s stories belong in horror — and that has been the case as long as horror has existed.”

Over at RPS-but-it's-The-Fade, Brendan's run through what made Bioware games great (and also terrible).

Bioware established romance as a must for any blockbuster RPG worth its frost salts (and not just RPGs).

Kissing your friends on the mouth is everywhere in mainstream and indie games today. It's a verb now. Characters are "romanceable". I played Nivalis Nights last month and could not get away from the swarms of horny NPC citizens trying to jump my noodle serving bones. Baldur's Gate 3 launched with a bug that made your companions fuckable in just a few nights, and people didn't even notice. They thought: that's normal and right, I should shag everyone, gender and orientation be damned. See that mountain? You can fuck it. And that's (at least partially) thanks to Bioware.

GTA is an unignorable thing. It is one of those breakout cultural objects that has its own gravity, drawing in attention and comment from politicians, mainstream press, parents, schools, comedians, columnists, footballers, taxi drivers, and hairdressers. In all the weight of it, I hadn't yet really seen it as a game. Simon Parkin's Edge cover feature may not reveal many new details about the game but it has made me appreciate it as a game (and maybe even get a little bit excited for its eventual PC release.

Nelson, grave-faced but friendly, wearing all black, with grey-flecked stubble, settles into a leather-and-chrome Eames chair while we perch on a burnt-orange sofa facing a pair of expansive wall-mounted TVs. In the past, Rockstar has carefully stage-managed encounters such as this. For previews of previous GTAs, one team member played the game while a publicist read from a pre-prepared script, further evidence of the paranoia that can take hold when an artist is working on something the entire world is desperate to see.

Today, however, Nelson has no script and, apparently, no plan. For the next 90 minutes he simply plays the current build, following his nose, confident that the game's systems will hold together wherever he pushes them, that this world's glories will glint and shimmer no matter which angle he approaches from. It is an extraordinary demonstration not of paranoia but of trust – in the game, in the team that built it, perhaps even in us.

Nelson picks up the controller and lets Grand Theft Auto VI speak for itself.

I am guilty of forgetting and looking away, but the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has not ended, it is deepening. Writing for the LRB, Selma Dabbagh bluntly captures the ugly events of the past two years :

In January 2025 Donald Trump described Gaza as a ‘demolition site’. ‘You’re talking about probably a million and a half people,’ he said, ‘and we just clean out that whole thing.’ The number is closer to two million people – not a ‘whole thing’ but two million individual human beings – who have been driven into an area that’s less than a third of the densely inhabited land they lived on. Their cities and arable lands – palms, olives, coriander, citrus and pomegranate trees – have been obliterated.

I'd like there to be a big reason for this week's music recommendation, but really it's just a little victory lap. I managed to nab some tickets to see This Is The Kit, so give Bashed Out a listen, yeah?

#4107. Genshin Impact Luna 7 brings us the first playable Hexenzirkel as things take a turn in Sumeru

Genshin Impact's Luna 7 update will kick off a new Archon Quest chapter, and deliver some interesting new additions to the playable roster.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a new Genshin Impact Special Program, where the developer revealed everything there is to know about the game’s next major update. Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana, or as its friends call it, Luna 7, was unveiled as part of the showcase.

This next update has a lot going for it, and it will be in players’ hands everywhere on May 20.

Luna 7 will take us back to Sumeru for its new Archon Quest, where a new crisis that threatens to plunge the nation into chaos is brewing. Nahida is out of the picture, and someone who looks suspiciously like Il Dottore has emerged.

If you complete this chapter at launch, you’ll earn up to 560 Primogems, as well as Nicole's Ascension Materials. Nicole is the first of three playable characters arriving with this update. Something else you’ll unlock if you finish the chapter quickly is a new Weekly Boss that HoYo says has “unpredictable abilities.”

And if you haven’t played in a while, don’t worry, you can refer to the Guiding Notes feature to catch you up on what’s been going on in the world. This is part of a larger effort from the team to make story progression more seamless, and also includes improved quest autosave prompts.

Nicole Reeyn is highest-profile and most interesting, being the first playable member of the Hexenzirkel. The mage is a 5-Star Pyro Catalyst wielder intended as a support member of the team. She can boost the ATK of all party members, even those not currently on the field. She also generates a shield while doing so.

Her Elemental Burst allows her to summon an Arcane Projection that follows the active character, sending out Coordinated Attacks that match their Elemental Type. Outside of combat, Nicole can help you find treasures by calling upon a Seelie to guide you to them. Quite fitting, as you’ll be exploring in the inside of the Witch's Lodge in Nicole’s Meeting Point in Luna 7, so bring her along.

Lohen, the Vice Captain of the Knights of Favonius' Fifth Company, is the second new character. Also a 5-Star addition, he is instead a Cryo Polearm wielder designed for aggressive combat. His main use is dealing massive Cryo DMG, and he can do that by managing two resources unique to him: Joy, and Will to Win.

Through his Elemental Skill, he can enter the Masterstroke state, allowing him to build up (and consume) Joy to unleash enhanced skills. The more his teammates fight, the more Will to Win he biulds, which can later be used to boost his effectiveness further. For an even more powerful display of force, bring along a Hexerei character when he’s on your team.

Prune is the third and final addition. Prune is a 4-Star Anemo Catalyst wielder, and her kit is inspired by her Witch Hunter aspirations. Using a bell and a hammer, she can deal DMG of several elements at once, and trigger Swirl reactions.

Nicole, and Lohen will debut in Luna 7’s first half, while Prune will follow in the second. The first half will also see a Durin rerun, with Mavuika returning in the second half. You can look forward to a new limited-time event as part of Luna 7, with a focus on Klee's Little Hexenzirkel.

You’ll find a series of mini-games you can play alongside Prune, as well as Qiqi, Yaoyao, and Sayu. If you play, you could earn the Super Awesome Magic Key, an exclusive weapon skin. Miliastra Wonderland is doing its thing, too, with a new sports festival for you to take part in.

One new gameplay addition worth calling attention to is that Manekins can now perform actions in Teyvat. The Kamera, which you can use to capture moments with Manekins, is getting upgraded, too, with new editing tools and assets.

Before you pick the game back up, be sure to check out our recently-updated Genshin Impact codes page for some free stuff you may be missing.

#4106. It looks like footage of a Persona 1 remake has leaked, and if it's legit I really hope you don't hate the colour purple

I'm sure the artist formerly known as Prince would have loved it, at least

In this genAI world, every single leak that makes its way out into the world should be seen as more of a "leak" until proven otherwise. With that said, it does kind of seem like a remake of the first Persona game is on the way, with some footage supposedly leaking and showing it in action.

The leaked footage was shared yesterday to the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit, originally uploaded to the file-sharing site Gofile on Halloween, i.e. yesterday, i.e. October 31st. You will not at all be surprised to hear that, stylistically, it's incredibly in line with the vibe of contemporary Persona, a la the visual design established with Persona 5 that's been carried through to the Persona 3 and 4 remakes.

There's not a whole lot of footage to actually look at, just shy of two minutes all told. One bit shows the game's protagonist walking through a school at night before starting a battle. Again, the battle system looks like what you'd expect from Persona, being turn based and whatnot. The colour theme for this one is overwhelmingly purple, too, which at least lines up with the series' 25th anniversary artwork. What's perhaps slightly odd is that Persona 2's protagonist can be seen in battle; not sure if this is implying a combination of the two games, if two remakes are being made in tandem and it's a temporary use of assets, or if it's just an odd placeholder.

Persona 1 and 2 remakes wouldn't exactly be much of a surprise. Ashley interviewed series producer Kazuhisa Wada not too long ago, and he literally said "Persona 1 and 2 are something we’ll probably eventually do too." A knowing tease from Wada, perhaps? Who knows! Either way, the gameplay on display here looks believable, and Sega's leakier than a broken faucet (various Persona bits have leaked in the past too), so, something to keep an eye on at the very least, even if best taken with a pinch of salt.

#4105. Mystic Messenger's most loyal players are getting banned in droves for seemingly playing the game too much

With the 10th anniversary of Mystic Messenger nearly upon us, the dating sim has inexplicably begun issuing wide-spread bans for its most active players.

Mystic Messenger, arguably one of the best dating sims around, has been dormant for about seven years. Despite not receiving new content or any meaningful updates in all that time, the game remains popular with its core fans, many of whom just woke up to some shocking news about their accounts.

The free-to-play mobile dating sim has started banning players with seemingly too many Hourglasses - the game’s virtual currency - saved up in their accounts. So far, it looks like players with 1,000 or more have been targeted, but others with far fewer hoards have reported getting the axe, too.

The news exploded on the Mystic Messenger subreddit overnight, with over a dozen reports from players logging in to play normally, only to receive an in-game notice that their accounts had been banned.

The message players received is identical, and doesn’t mention the specific reason for the ban. “Your account has been banned because abusive behavior has been detected from your account,” it reads, ending with a support email address the affected user can contact if they believe they’d banned in error.

It didn’t take a while for players to realise that most, if not all of the bans are for players with thousands of Hourglasses in their accounts. The virtual currency can both be acquired in-game just by playing, as well as through direct real-money purchases.

For a nearly ten-year-old game that stopped receiving content three years into its life, it’s easy to see how a dedicated group of players would be able to acquire so many Hourglasses by simply playing regularly for so long.

When contacted by the affected players, Cheritz, the developer and publisher of the game, has instructed them to send receipts of how they acquired Hourglasses (assuming they were purchased) to verify whether or not they’d been fraudulently obtained.

Considering that Mystic Messenger has practically been abandoned by its developer, certain exploits have emerged over the years that allowed players to farm Hourglasses faster than intended, but those instances have always been dealt with then and there.

The blanket and sudden nature of this ban is what’s spooked players, especially those who’ve been logging in for years and never thought accruing in-game currency from playing the game too much would make them the target of a ban.

The running theory is that most of the bans are unintentional, and may be the result of a new automated security system that’s been implemented. It’s entirely possible, especially if its’s AI-based, that the new system simply couldn’t distinguish between those who have earned (or bought) their Hourglasses fairly, and those who used exploits.

The timing of the ban wave is also suspect. With the game’s 10th anniversary coming up in July, it could be that Cheriz is preparing to release a large update for Mystic Messenger, which may include new content. If most of the playerbase is already sitting on massive amounts of in-game currency, they may simply use that to fast-track their way to unlocking the new content, which would greatly affect the developer’s bottom line.

This is a problem that other live service games have run into in the past. Just recently, extraction shooter Arc Raiders added a cap to the amount of Cred players can hold in their accounts very quickly after its launch. That currency is used to buy cosmetic sets in the store, so the logic is easy to follow.

All of that has certainly put a damper on the enthusiasm of the game’s most active players, many of whom were excited to get together in person for the coming 10th anniversary, participate in community nights and so on to celebrate.

It’s also disheartening to see a fanbase so loyal; playing a game as regularly for so long without new content, to be treated so poorly. Even without knowing what the game is, it’s impressive that so many people have kept the flag of their favourite game flying for so long.

#4104. James Gunn fuels rumors that we're never seeing Peacemaker again after he liked a fan's comment

DCU fans fear we may never see John Cena's Peacemaker again

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With James Gunn and Peter Safran stepping down as DC Studios co-CEOs, the future of the DCU is truly up in the air. But to make matters worse, Gunn seems to have already nailed the coffin shut on one DCU hero.

Underneath Gunn's DC Studios exit statement on Instagram, one fan commented, "We're never going to see Peacemaker again." Though Gunn didn't outright confirm the statement, he liked the comment, which pretty much tells us that the fan is right.

Not long after Skydance acquired Warner Bros. earlier this year, the company has already started to make major changes to the conglomerate, starting with replacing Gunn and Safran with former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham, starting on December 1, 2026. Though Skydance, which owns Paramount, has yet to reveal what its intentions are with the DCU, reports suggest the company plans to "dismantle" Gunn's DCU Chapter One.

This would seemingly mean that DCU characters such as John Cena's Peacemaker, David Corenswet's Superman, Milly Alcock's Supergirl, and more would cease to exist and be replaced, just as the DCEU's characters were the last time around. Seeing Peacemaker on the chopping block wouldn't be too surprising, as he is a character who has been championed by Gunn from the start, first appearing in the director's 2021 movie The Suicide Squad, and later given his own HBO show.

But there may be light at the end of the tunnel for some characters, as Gunn's statement states that although he is "relieved" to be stepping down and going back to "pure filmmaking," that's not to say that he and Safran are "immediately done with DC or superheroes," adding that "the characters we set up will live on."

The good news is that titles already deep in development, such as Man of Tomorrow and The People v. Gorilla Grodd, are still happening. But another show seemingly in danger is Lanterns, which, despite becoming one of HBO's most successful new shows ever, has yet to be renewed. Showrunner Chris Mundy says a second season is a 50/50 coin toss right now, but Variety reports that Skydance doesn't think that the show is capturing the zeitgeist, which may be why it hasn't been officially greenlit.

For more, check out our guide on how to watch the DC movies in order, and keep up with upcoming DC movies and shows announced before Gunn's departure.

#4103. Feature: These Are Xbox's Best 25 Games From 2001-2026 According To Metacritic

As we continue our celebrations for Xbox's 25th anniversary this Sunday (November 15th), we thought it might be fun to look back at the past 25 years on Metacritic, and specifically the best-rated Xbox games from each year.

The website has a significant history of review roundups dating all the way back to 2001, and looking at the list, the early years in particular are jam-packed with historic Xbox games! Halo is in there multiple times, as is Gears of War and Grand Theft Auto, and then we start to see an indie explosion with the likes of Inside and Hades in later years.

So, here are Xbox's best 25 games from 2001-2026 according to Metacritic from each individual year. Just keep in mind that we've eliminated a couple of expansions, as we're only counting full game releases.

Of course, when it comes to 2026 specifically, there's every chance GTA 6 will end up taking the top spot within a couple of weeks' time, so just keep that in mind - Hades 2 has done amazingly well, but will most likely be surpassed.

And by the way, this list doesn't tell the full story - here's what it would look like if you took the individual years away:

Pretty different, right? It's no surprise that there were multiple years that fared better than others in terms of highly-rated releases, so the likes of The Orange Box, Red Dead Redemption 2, Portal 2, Halo 3 and others still make the lineup.

Anyway, Metacritic doesn't tell the full story by any means here, but it's a useful resource to look back and see how well the critics positioned these games at the time, and whether we reckon they're still justifying their high scores.

So, what do you reckon to these? We'd love to hear your thoughts down in the comments section below.

Guide The Best Original Xbox Games Of All Time

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

There is undoubtedly a time when review scores became more inline with the scores we see today. In other words, there is no way that Halo: Combat Evolved would score 97 under todays review score regime. Don't misunderstand me, Halo: CE is still a great game, but if reviewed today it would be marked down for its samey locations, limited enemy types etc. etc. (and I just picked that game, rather than picking on that game).

I wonder when that would have been? Any thoughts, @FraserG?

Does the passing of each generation further refine the scores that professional reviewers give, and I wonder what those same games would be given if reviewed today...?

I don't think there's any guarantee that gta6 gets a higher average review than 95, so Hades 2 may well end the year with top spot.

@Fiendish-Beaver I think about this a lot. Really, only Nintendo games can break the 95 barrier now.

When you look at gears e day that kind of content is probably a 93 if we go back 15 years

@Llamageddon Yeah, 95 is a tough score to beat. It could be tight for R* to contend with that.

@Fiendish-Beaver I agree with the Halo point. I think a lot of games back then got a lot of praise due to the graphical jumps between generations. I mean, 16bit > 32bit was ridiculously jaw-dropping. The same can be said about 64bit > 128bit. I think many games from the Xbox / PS2 / Gamecube era wowed more than impressed. We don't really see that today, do we? Generational jumps just seem so slight (when we compare games at the end of one gen to the beginning of the next). That said, Halo 4 is the best Halo for me, followed by 1, then 2, then ODST. Halo 3 can go kick rocks. That game sucked.

Hey, @Kaloudz. Nice to see you around. Hope you are well, matey.

I agree, it was probably the wow factor that saw games receive such high scores back when gaming was much younger, and I suspect that by early in the Xbox One / PS3 era (so probably 2015ish) we had experienced much of what there was to see, and so we moved from wow to technicality. We started to judge games more on performance and variety, their technical achievement and overall enjoyment. I'd say we don't judge games based on their graphical prowess because otherwise all these retro style games would be marked down severely, which obviously does not happen.

Gains in consoles are so incremental these days that I think a game that released from 2015 onwards is probably judged by much the same standards now as it was back then.

What would be interesting, would be for someone to take up reviewing games, and to review older games but by todays standards. So someone that had never played the first Gears of War, plays it through, and gives it a review score based not on the wow, but on its technical achievements, level design, enemy variety, and what have you. I imagine that we would see a very different set of scores if games were reviewed now from what they were given when they originally released, but it would be interesting to see just how these older games would fair...

@Fiendish-Beaver I agree it is harder to get to that 95ish score than it was. I think there's a few different things going on there.

Firstly as @Kaloudz said there was a big graphical jump between generations. But there was also much larger GAMEPLAY jumps back then too. Games and their mechanics were often breaking new paradigms whether that was Mario or Zelda in 3D for the first time or Gears and Halo pushing third and third person console shooters into the mainstream on console. It felt exciting. Now most games feel much more iterative, especially AAA games.

There were also typically fewer reviews for each game, and those reviews were generally from a smaller cross-section of gamers in similar demographics who were more likely to have similar tastes, that led to homogenisation of some scores. Now a game might be marked down by a new demographic, which is fair enough, aggregate scores don't tell the whole story, we all like different things.

Linked to that I know some people believe that Nintendo games get unfairly scored higher than they might for some reason, but I don't see it that way. I think there is often a universal joy to Nintendo games that resonates with far more players. More simply put: they haven't forgotten how to make their games joyful and fun on an almost primal level. That won't be for everyone - nothing is - but it is for a wider cross section of people, and reviewers, hence they are more likely to score higher as an aggregate.

Look at Ocarina of Time remake. Not only a hit with critics currently scoring 96 on Metacritic from 94 reviews but also currently a 9.6 from 10.5k user reviews, it's rare to see both critics and users in such harmony. Having swallowed it whole and finished it already, I would agree it's the easiest 10 in years imho. Bring on GTA6.

As for the list as you'd expect with a best of list it's wall to wall bangers. I'm surprised there's more games than I thought on that list I haven't played yet, but I really struggle to start 100+ hour games like Persona 5 or BG3. One day!

BG3 is such a good game, @themightyant. Take it from someone that has been playing games for over 50 years, BG3 is the best game ever made. I have played through it multiple times now, and have amassed over 1000 hours in the game, and there are probably still things that I have not seen...

@Fiendish-Beaver Oh i'll get to it. I have no doubt, and it's not through lack of interest either. I just struggle to start games that I know will take me 100+ hours... and this one probably 200+ hours. (FYI your 1000 hours isn't helping!!! lol)

I love self employment, flexibility of work hours, but when I REALLY get into a game I often make poor life choices, and work or life suffers with no one looking over my shoulder. That is fine for something like Ocarina of Time remake - book Thursday and Friday off and finish it across 4 days, it's not that long and doesn't really impact my life.

But for games like Elden Ring, BG3, CyberPunk etc. that I pretty much KNOW I will fall head over heels into and at least partially no-life for weeks I need to be very careful when I start them. Pretty much all my most want to play games fall into this group sadly. I have at least twenty 100+ hour games near the top of my backlog.

Yes, sorry, @themightyant. I do occasionally forget that people do not have the luxury of time that I enjoy these days. If I want to game 8 hours a day every day for a fortnight that is something I could easily do (I don't, but I could).

It is a big time commitment, of that there is no doubt, and I totally understand what you mean when you say you find it off-putting because that is precisely why I have not played Assassin's Creed: Valhalla, and why I may not end up playing Crimson Desert, both of which I own, but neither of which I have played. I'd like to play them, but in the case of Valhalla, I worry I will get bored towards the end, which is what happened with both Odyssey and Origins, both of which I never finished despite putting over 100 into each of them. In the case of Crimson Desert, it feels like they keep adding to the game, and so I don't know when to start it because I will probably only want to play it once, but also want it to be feature complete by which time it will probably be to daunting to start.

If it helps, I think my 1000 hours in BG3 is divided over 4 different runs in the game. It is probably possible to complete it in under 200 hours, and that should enable you to see everything outside different story choices. According to howlongtobeat.com BG3 should take you around 180 hours if you do both mains and sides, though different choices can change the game pretty drastically...

@Fiendish-Beaver Strangely I have less concerns over something like AC: Valhalla because although it's long I know I would get a bit bored and can put it down. It's unlikely to grip me in the same way.

The problem is games I fall completely in love with and I end up staying up till the birds are tweeting, or trying to fit a few hours play into the work day.

For me it's Elden Ring, BG3, Cyberpunk, FF7 Rebirth, Persona, KCD, Hades, Monster Hunter, Death Stranding, MGSV, Metaphor re:F, Xenoblades... plenty of lengthy RPGs in fact. I'm pretty certain these will all pull me under for a while. Can't do it when I have big projects on, which is most of the time.

@themightyant I'd say Hades is quite a bit shorter than most on that list, I got to the 'true ending' in less than 50 runs and I did about half those runs in around the 20 mins mark. The platinum does extend it quite considerably though and can be a bit of a grind (if you're an achievement hunter). I would also thoroughly recommend the game (one of my personal all time favourites).

@Llamageddon You are right if they have a 30 FPS tax…. GTA6 might be low 90’s

@AlwaysPlaying also giving gta6 an 8 out of 10 (when most are giving it 10s) would drive a lot of traffic to that review even if it was pure rage baiting. I like to think all reviewers have the integrity to not do that but I'm not naive enough to believe that's the case.

Those times when you are up until ridiculous hours are some of the best gaming moments we have, @themightyant, albeit I know they are usually to be avoided.

One of my favourite memories in gaming is playing Horde in Gears 3 with 4 of my mates, with the game finally ending at 4 a.m., and whilst I know that is not particularly late (in terms of what we are talking about) the host had to be up at 5 a.m. in order to go to work! We still wax lyrical about that to this day, and that was well over 10 years ago now.

I've lost count of the days in which I started gaming in an evening only to suddenly realise there is daylight outside! I don't do it very often these days, but when it happens it does usually mean you are playing something worthwhile...

@Fiendish-Beaver They certainly are, but gaming is a privilege and life has to come first. I'll get there one day!

@Llamageddon Appreciate that. I was basing it off the HLTB times which is around 100+ hours for Hades, and I am always slower than what they say. When I love a game I usually try and complete it. Will get to it soon no doubt. I've played and loved all their other games from Bastion to Pyre and Transistor.

@themightyant absolutely, supergiant is one of my favourite small Devs, great consistency and variety. Look forward to what they cook up next (as much as I love the Hades games, they have too much talent to be stuck making one series).

#4102. Final Fantasy 14: Evercold sets itself a release date at the tail end of winter, alongside offering a look at its second, avian-inclined new job

Let's start with the bad news: Final Fantasy 14: Evercold has been delayed. The good news, that doesn't matter all that much, as it's only a delay of roughly a month, and a release date has been set in stone too: February 23rd, 2027. It's cutting it a bit close to the seasons shifting towards spring, making the game seasonally inappropriate, but hey ho, February is still winter!

That release date was revealed during this week's Final Fantasy 14 Fest Fest held in Tokyo. It was paired with a big ole cinematic that'll open up the expansion when you do actually get to play it. You can watch that down below if you fancy, that'll just depend on whether you want to go into the expansion knowing as little as possible. Looks pretty at least! I like the big dragony ship we've seen previously.

The expansion's second new job has been revealed too. It's called Zephyr, a physical ranged DPS that uses a crossbow and comes with its own avian familiar to assist you in battle. Seems like a pretty good option for folks afraid of getting in close but want to get some damage in. The bird friend you get is neat too. I hereby request that every other job gets a bird friend! I don't care if it doesn't make sense!

Most annoyingly, for me personally as someone that's only managed to play A Realm Reborn and doesn't really have time to go through a ridiculous number of hours and expansions just to get to this one, a preview for the Evangelion collab alliance raid was shown off rendered in the style of the original anime's post-credits, next episode teaser reels. I love those dang big robots and feelings of depression, don't make me go through all those expansions just to let my Viera dress up as Asuka or whatever loot you end up getting.

Anyway, don't forget to mark your calendars, February 23rd! Be there or be, uh, anywhere else I guess. I'm not your boss.

#4101. New TMNT: Splintered Fate Update Adds Even More Reasons To Play In Co-Op

Super Evil Megacorp has been steadily pumping out new content for its TMNT Hades-like, Splintered Fate, ever since launch, and today, the team has added a bunch of new reasons to embark on your roguelike runs in co-op.

The new Shell Squad Co-Op Update goes live today, and as its name suggests, it's all about the multiplayer fun. This free patch adds 24 new co-op powers, eight new co-op tools and eight new co-op masteries, so you can bring the heat to Shredder and the Rat King with even more skills when playing with friends.

The update also includes improved flame visuals, options for character swapping when playing co-op online or locally, and improved Lucky Dice communication.

Here are a few examples of the new powers and tools added in the update:

24x new co-op powers (3 per power tree). Examples: - Passing the Torch - The first player you touch while affected by Rapid Fire also gains its effects, for as long as you have Rapid Fire active. - Shared Warmth - When a player consumes a Splinter's Revive, heal all players. - Chain Reaction - Players' Specials have a chance to trigger a Chain Lightning, dealing Utrom damage per link.

8x new co-op tools (1 per power tree). Examples: - Bubble Trouble - Spawn a bubble on you and the farthest player. The bubble deals Water damage and Freezes enemies, and grants bonus Water damage to players. - Tether Beam - Tether to the closest player. Enemies caught in the beam will take Utrom damage every second. - Shadow Pact - Grant yourself and the closest player a Dark Shell. Each enemy defeated extends it.

8x new co-op masteries (1 per character). Examples: - Donatello - When using your Tool, the closest player becomes invulnerable. - Raphael - When any player lands a critical hit, they have a chance to Multi-crit instead. - Michelangelo - When using your Special, you and the closest player gain a Torrent Strike stack. - Leonardo - When activating your Special, the closest player gains Light Shell.

That's not all the news on the Splintered Fate front, either. The dev also announced its next paid cosmetics DLC: the Trench Coat Pack. Once again, it's another pretty self-explanatory one here, with all the Turtles (and the additional DLC characters) donning the team's iconic trench coats. This one is also available today, so there's no waiting around here, either!

#4100. Forza Horizon 6 explodes on Steam even before it's officially out

Forza Horizon 6 looks to have easily delivered the most successful launch for any game in the series on PC, with record-breaking player numbers.

Steam is abuzz this week with a couple of long-anticipated launches, but in Forza Horizon 6’s case, at least, the game isn’t even out for what will be most of its players. The anticipated sequel in the open-world driving game series doesn’t officially launch until May 19, but owners of its most expensive version - the Premium Edition - can play it right now.

That version of the game includes more than just a few days of early access, of course, but you’d think the $120 price tag would’ve only been palatable to a small group of players. Not the case with this game.

Forza Horizon 6, which has spent 16 weeks in Steam’s global top sellers list, currently occupies the number two spot, having jumped up three spots this week in anticipation of the launch. The game has also naturally been popular with players, so popular in fact that it has already overtaken the player counts of all other Horizon games on the platform.

At the time of writing, the game has peaked at 128,157 concurrent players on Steam alone (via SteamDB). The figure has already climbed several times during the writing of this story, so you can only imagine how much higher it’s going to get deeper into the weekend.

All of that, of course, days before the official launch on Tuesday, when, theoretically, the majority of the game’s audience will be able to start playing. In just a few short hours, Horizon 6 has already gone well above Forza Horizon 5’s peak concurrent of 81,096, as well as Forza Horizon 4’s peak 75,689 players.

Steam is the only platform that publishes player numbers, of course, but it’s easy to see how similar the enthusiasm is going to be on Xbox. Though the game is not yet part of the Game Pass line-up, those who don’t want to wait could buy the Premium Edition Upgrade to get the included content, and play it right now.

Game Pass, and Xbox / Windows Store numbers don’t factor into Steam’s, which is another thing to consider when viewing the numbers holistically. Indeed, given how successful Forza Horizon 5 has been on PlayStation 5, Horizon 6’s upcoming release on Sony's console is bound to be even bigger.

Forza Horizon 5 has been off to a similarly flying start in the first few days of its own advanced access launch, so it’s obviously not surprising to see Horizon 6 do better there. In case you missed it, check out our review of Forza Horizon 6. In short, we really liked it, even if we expected more.

The greatest compliment I can give the Legend of Zelda-inspired Twilight Sword RPG is "I have no idea how they weren't sued while making this." It distills everything that makes Ocarina of Time, Wind Waker, and the rest so beloved before lacing that knowledge into a D&D-style game.

I was able to get my hands on a physical copy early, and as a lifelong Legend of Zelda fan who also happens to adore the best tabletop RPGs, believe me when I say that Twilight Sword is entirely my jam. It may be the closest we'll ever get to riding across Hyrule at our tables, and it's immediately gone onto my to-do list once I've finished my current D&D campaign.

Twilight Sword has just hit shelves. You can either pick it up straight from publisher Free League or, if you're based in the UK, grab it for a discount via Wayland Games (which tends to be a good source of reduced tabletop RPGs or bargains on the best board games).

Twilight Sword wears its heart on its sleeve. Between a Breath of the Wild-esque cover and monsters that feel as though they've been plucked from Hyrule field, this RPG isn't ashamed of its roots. It's a love-letter celebrating all things Legend of Zelda (up to and including the recent Ocarina of Time remake), from a world map using the classic wheel and spoke structure to formatting that wouldn't look out of place in Tears of the Kingdom. There's even a corrupted castle at the center of everything, covered in a familiar red glow reminiscent of Calamity Ganon.

In other words, this game wants to be the Legend of Zelda RPG – and after spending some time digging through it, I think the development team at Two Little Mice deserves their flowers. Its muse may be obvious, but the result isn't usually slavish; even though some references fly incredibly close to the sun (more than one enemy looks like their Nintendo equivalent with the serial number filed off), Twilight Sword skillfully identifies and leverages the tropes that make Zelda so beloved. Whether that's noble kingdoms fallen into ruin or cheerful woodland spirits who always seem to be getting themselves into bother, it understands what makes the franchise tick.

Despite being close enough that they feel drawn from a lost Zelda game, I'd argue this extends to the RPG's take on monsters like Moblins or Lizfalos. They're an iconic part of the franchise, so removing them from this tribute would strip away something crucial.

You could modify Twilight Sword to set it in Hyrule, of course, but its bespoke world of Radia does have a lot to offer. Besides proving some truly whimsical and novel locations, there's a sense of discovery – of plunging into the unknown – that you couldn't get with a true Zelda tie-in, or the best Legend Zelda merch. There's also joy to be had in exploring a world that's new yet strangely familiar.

Twilight Sword shares a lot of DNA with D&D but is simpler on the whole. You still have numbered stats like Strength or Charisma that vary based on how good you are at that particular ability, but your aim here is to roll less than your score with a d12 to succeed. (As an example, rolling a 1 is the best possible result here.) Resources like Stamina points play a big role too, and they can be used to activate certain abilities such as the 'Feats' that differentiate your class – here called a 'Way.'

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

When you factor in your health by measured by hearts, Twilight Sword feels a lot more arcade-y than many tabletop RPGs… and considering its video game roots, that's nothing if not appropriate.

With any luck, this game will go from strength to strength just like its inspiration. And considering how it just launched a new crowdfunding campaign for a Monster Book on Backerit (which has already hit €306,254 in funding after just a few hours, well over the €30K goal), that seems more than possible.

This game feels like Zelda with a dash of Final Fantasy. If you'd prefer one that emphasizes Final Fantasy instead, try the excellent Break!! (currently available via the official store, or on Amazon UK if you're based across the pond).

I've been writing about games in one form or another since 2012, but these days you'll find me managing GamesRadar+'s tabletop gaming and toy coverage (I spend my time here handling everything from board game reviews to the latest Lego news). I've also been obsessed with Warhammer since the 1990s, and love nothing more than running tabletop RPGs like D&D as a Dungeon Master.

#4098. What remains of canned Portal prequel white whale F-Stop is now fully playable thanks to modders and some big leaks

If you're something of a Portal or Half-Life head, you'll probably already be familiar with F-Stop, an unreleased Portal prequel that remained quite mysterious for many years. Back in 2020, a much deeper look was revealed in a semi-official capacity, revealing a pretty neat concept (that isn't so dissimilar to that of Superliminal). Now, all these years later, assets and source code for the game has leaked, and what exists of F-Stop is fully playable.

As spotted by Kotaku, the Valve Cut Content team and a number of leakers have been able to put together a playable version of F-Stop so that you can try it out for yourself. Mechanically, it works like so: you take a picture of an object, and said object disappears, turning it into a photo. You can then use this photo to rematerialise the object, sometimes changing the scale of it to help you navigate particular puzzles. It's cool! Just not something Valve thought was worth going all in on, evidently.

So the story goes, Valve overlord Gabe Newell did actually quite like the early version of the game that never was, it's just it didn't test all that well. I do kind of think that this is a lesson in not always listening to test audiences; the aforementioned Superliminal really is quite similar in execution, even tonally it's on the same kind of wavelength, and it ended up being quite a tight little experience that ended up being received quite positively, generally. In the end, bits of F-Stop were Frankensteined into Portal 2, so, at least we got that out of it!

The reason for the delay in being able to play F-Stop in this unofficial capacity is because of the crucial source code and map data. Back in August about 12TB of Steam data leaked, but that only contained the assets for F-Stop. Mods in the Valve Cut Content Discord server said that the person who leaked the F-Stop mapsrc asked for $1000 before just handing over the data in any case. Glad they did, $1000 bucks is a lot, I wouldn't pay it myself. Cool little bit of history to be found here, shame it never materialised in the way it was meant to.

#4097. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.3 will take us deeper into the World in Canvas and make Mortenax Blade playable

Honkai: Star Rail's next big outing will see the continuation of the Planarcadia story, and it's going to be with us soon.

HoYoverse has today delivered full details on the next major update for Honkai: Star Rail. Version 4.3, dubbed The Lethe Below the Living, will be available for all players on June 1. The upcoming update adds a new chapter to the Planarcadia arc, and introduce a new playable character.

The new narrative chapter will also unveil more about Mortenax Blade, the Trailblazer themselves, and the husk of the Aeon.

Mortenax Blade is the hero of this chapter, and he’s going to step into the World in Canvas. The goal is to - by borrowing the power of Voracity - excise Shuhu from his body and end the curse.

The Trailblazer goes on a trip of their own in Version 4.3, this time to Inkford Hermitage, right on the edge between the World in Canvas and the real world. They’re going to undertake this journey to warn Graphia of the Asat Pramad threat.

In case you hadn’t already guessed, Mortenax Blade is this version’s new playable character. The 5-Star Fire-Type swordsman is on the Path of Nihility. Blade’s Ultimate allows him to enter an enhanced state by deploying a special Bounded Field.

While the field is active, all enemies receive more DMG. Entering this state is also how Blade unlocks his skill, which uses a Sword Formation to deal more damage. This is then used to essentially unlock a second, more powerful Ultimate for him.

The benefits of Mortenax Blade’s kit extend to his teammates, too. Any ally who attacks an enemy with him on the team, they inflict a debuff on them. This also builds up a special Charge that Blade can later use with his Skill.

Version 4.3’s launch arrives alongside the Gift of Tempered Blade event. Through it, you can claim a new Trailblazer Outfit piece for free, but only after getting Mortenax Blade from Warping. The first phase’s rerun will be Yao Guang, and the second phase will bring back both Cyrene and Phainon.

You can also expect the Wispae Amusement Park to arrive within the World in Canvas, which you’ll get to design. You can plan where the rides will go, pick the different themes, set visitor routes and more.

Starward Mode is another new addition, which can be found in Memory of Chaos, Pure Fiction, and Apocalyptic Shadow. Starward will see you take on three different stages, which you’ll need three teams for. Clearing each challenge with full stars will reward you 100 Stellar Jades extra per chase.

There’s more coming down the line, too. A new Fate/Stay Night [Unlimited Blade Works] collaboration will arrive in a content up this summer. The event will give players a chance to earn Gilgamesh or Archer for free by logging in.

For players who demand complete customization, the REVO MAX offers advanced adjustment options to adapt the controller to their playstyle; these options are in addition to all the REVO features detailed above.

#4094. Dune: Awakening's seasonally appropriate Blood and Ice expansion gets a December release date, and in a plus for preservation, an offline mode this month

December is certainly going to be the month of Dune. The biggest Dune of Dunecember will obviously go to Dune: Part 3, which is Duen out December 18th. A little bit before that, however, is a well-timed free expansion coming to Dune: Awakening. It's called Blood and Ice, which sounds gross, but hey, I guess free blood and ice isn't entirely a bad thing?

"The expansion introduces the Polar Sink, an entirely new survival map where everything you've learned about surviving in the desert will be put to the test," explains a Steam blog post. "Instead of protecting yourself from extreme heat, you'll need to find ways to stay warm. The technology you've developed to survive the desert won't be enough here, and you'll need to upgrade your equipment, gather new resources, and adapt your strategies to survive the cold."

You'll find two biomes in the Polar Sink, the tundra and the ice cap, the former being where you'll kick off your time in this expansion. "While conditions here are more manageable than on the ice cap itself, these families won't welcome anyone interfering with their operations," the blog notes. Your main goal is to get the ice cap and gather up all of its valuable resources, namely, ice! Said ice can then be used to "cool your base equipment and speed up production."

Apparently you'll get about 35 more hours of "new progression, along with new vehicle modules, augments, and specialization traits," out of the expansion, and there are plans for future updates that'll give you reason to come back to the Polar Sink in Duen time. Beyond that, there is also a new cosmetic store, which lets you purchase "optional cosmetic items, including outfits, vehicle variants, and additional ways to customize your bases." I'm sure this will go down well.

Perhaps most importantly, this November will see the arrival of offline mode, meaning you don't need an internet connection to play it. Hopefully if (probably when (sorry to be a pessimist (realist))) the servers go down, this means it'll still be playable. Character copying so that you can copy your character from multiplayer servers to single-player will be coming in January, alongside full cross-play. Lots coming essentially!

#4093. Monopoly Go x The Simpsons crossover is almost here

After a long wait and exhaustive leaks, the highly-anticipated Simpsons event will finally arrive in Monopoly Go very soon, alongside new content.

Monopoly Go players have been looking forward to a major crossover event for what felt like months, and though most of the details ended up leaking, nothing actually beats official information.

The world of The Simpsons has officially arrived in Monopoly Go, and there's a whole lot for players to dive into. The show's creative team even produced a new animated short, featuring Mr. Monopoly, and Mr. Burns.

Available June 3 through July 29, the new event allows Monopoly Go players to jump in the world of The Simpsons. You'll be able to build, and explore all around multiple iconic locations from the show.

Along the way, you'll run into Simpsons characters like Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and of course, Mr. Burns. Developer Scopely teamed up with the show's creative team to create many references, and Easter Eggs for you to discover. You'll find some of those on chance cards, but most of the world has been changed to be part of The Simpsons, including getting to bribe Chief Wiggum to escape jail.

The developer promises a deeply connected world with Simpsons narratives and characters that alter seasonal maps, and offer unique sticker sets and animated sequences to dive in. Incidentally, this is The Simpsons' first appearance in a mobile-exclusive game in 13 years.

Here's a breakdown of everything you can expect, straight from Scopely:

Episodes: Narrative-driven encounters that create stories inspired by The Simpsons. Episodes play out across seasonal boards, sticker sets, and minigames, all capped off with an animated short.

Sticker sets: Every Episode comes with its own limited-time sticker set, taking cues from the latest Simpsons story. Collectible artwork, character journeys and other rewards are yours to claim for the duration of each Episode.

The Simpsons Run: Every two weeks, a new Springfield character will take over the Free Parking tile, kicking off character-driven runs.

Simpsons-themed Shutdowns and Heists: Monopoly Go's shutdowns and heists get a Simpsons makeover, with Springfield-inspired chaos and disasters.

Bribe Wiggum: This changes Go to Jail to allow players to bribe Chief Wiggum, giving you a chance to earn a bigger reward, but not without introducing an element of unpredictability.

Simpsons chance cards: The chance card collection grows with over 50 Simpsons-themed cards full of memes, references and one-liners from the show.

If you're excited to jump in tomorrow, be sure to check out these Free Monopoly Go Dice Links before you dive into the new content.

The Rings of Power season 3 has debuted to a respectable Rotten Tomatoes score

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Rings of Power season 3 is finally here – and it has debuted to a Rotten Tomatoes score that is solid, but lower than the previous two installments.

This season of the Lord of the Rings TV show revolves around Sauron and his quest for the One Ring, while the Elves continue to struggle against him.

The show has debuted to a score of 79% on Rotten Tomatoes, which, while very decent, is lower than season 2's 85% and season 1's 84%. But, season 3 so far only has 29 reviews counted on the site compared to season 2's 173 and season 1's 487.

Our own The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 review awarded the show 3.5 stars, with our verdict reading: "With Sauron's terrible might threatening Middle-earth and the forging of the One Ring at hand, The Rings of Power season 3 is a dark, thrilling installment – but one still mired in dense, dragging subplots."

The Rings of Power is set to run for five seasons on Prime Video, which means there are still two seasons remaining. The show is set in the Second Age, long before the events of the Peter Jackson movies, and will take us up to the events of the Fellowship of the Ring prologue.

You can stream four episodes on Prime Video now, and keep up to date with the rest with our The Rings of Power season 3 release schedule. For more, see our roundup of all the other most exciting upcoming TV shows.

#4091. Gag Order is a co-op, SCP-ish horror shooter about surviving as best you can against some nasty, tentacle covered cephalopod creatures

Don't let it touch me, please and thank you

What makes Carrion interesting obviously lies in playing as the monster in a horror game rather than being the one chased down by it. The game's nasty tentacle monster still gives me the heebie jeebies, so I really would hate to be hunted by one. This is where I point you towards Gag Order, a shooter where you are in fact hunted by a disgusting cephalopod creature all while tracking down a distress signal.

Gag Order is not designed to be played solo, it feels wrong to call it friendslop given how unfriendly it is in vibes, but it does feel like it fits into a similar lineage as Lethal Company at the very least. In it, you are a research lab's Guardian Unit member, and you get a distress call "from one of the core parts of the complex." Upon arrival, the atmosphere is rotten, and you quickly come to understand that you are not equipped for what you have to deal with.

The solution, then, is to take care of those nightmare-inducing cephalopod creatures. Except during the first phase of a run, it sounds like they're invincible. Your guns do seem to be able to fend them off at the very least, but it's the second phase, which is geared around a "fast paced team-bossight" where it sounds like you'll be trying to take these things down. I'm not quite sure what the process is to get between those two phases, but I'm quite fond of the vibes on display.

It feels a touch reminiscent of 2000s shooters with some slightly contemporary mechanical sensibilities. I'm fond of the light SCP vibes it has going on, alongside the faint surrealness of certain elements like a bunch of crows hanging out in an abandoned office building. Creepy! Good looking stuff. Gag Order is apparently due out by the end of 2026, though we're obviously getting close there, so it's worth keeping an eye on it by throwing it a wishlist on Steam, if it takes your fancy.

#4090. Gallery: Hollow Knight & Silksong's Switch 2 Physicals Are A Delight For Map Fans

Fangamer announced earlier this year that it had two swanky new Switch 2 physical releases in the works for both Hollow Knight and Silksong, each complete with a couple of bonus goodies inside the box.

With the release date finally upon us, the good folks over at Fangamer have sent us a copy of each, and let it be known, they are both really rather sexy.

Both boxes boast wrap-around cover art (for some particularly detailed spines) and reversible sleeves so you can opt for a design without all of the Switch 2 T&C text down at the bottom.

All of the DLC for the first game is included on the cart, too, and while Silksong's Sea of Sorrow expansion obviously isn't on there at the moment (we're still waiting for a firm release date on that one), it will come as a free download to all those with a copy when it eventually drops.

Inside, both copies contain some bonus booklet goodies, too. Each has its own instruction booklet, containing introductions for everything from both the Knight and Hornet's movesets and upgrade abilities, to points of interest in the world. Gosh, we didn't realise how much we had missed physical manuals.

A physical copy of each game's map is included in the box as well, which folds up into a little wax-stamped envelope — a very neat touch, if we've ever seen one. This gives you a detailed rundown of each location for both games, and could prove as a valuable route tracker for those still trying to uncover Hallownest/Pharloom's secrets.

Both the Hollow Knight and Silksong Switch 2 physicals are now available on the Fangamer website.

#4089. Here's What Xbox Owners Need To Know About 'Moving To New Zealand' For GTA 6

So, it's finally almost time for GTA 6. You've probably preloaded the game on your Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S already, and now you're eagerly awaiting the official launch that takes place on November 19th.

However, there are more than a few whispers going around about the "New Zealand" trick — something we've seen time and time again over the past decade-plus on Xbox — and it looks set to have a big influence again with GTA 6.

But what is it, and most importantly could it get you banned? Let's take a look at the facts:

On this page: Here's What Xbox Owners Need To Know About 'Moving To New Zealand' For GTA 6

A game like GTA 6 obviously has a set release date of November 19th, but it lands at "midnight local time" depending on the region you're in. That means New Zealand ends up being the first region to get access, and their "midnight" corresponds to 3am PT / 6am ET / 11am GMT on November 18th.

Therefore, if people want to play the game as early as possible, they'll need to be in New Zealand - and the "New Zealand Trick" refers to changing your region in your console's settings, providing slightly early access to GTA 6.

There's always been a lot of chatter online about how Xbox doesn't really care about you "moving to New Zealand" to get around release times, but that's technically not the case. Xbox's terms and conditions specifically state that trying to "circumvent regional content restrictions" is prohibited, and this is mentioned a few times in documentation:

The official answer is yes - Xbox could take whatever kind of actions they wanted against an account that was found breaking the rules to play GTA 6 early on Xbox Series X and S. It could result in a warning, a suspension, a ban, or anything else they see fit.

You might also get away with it, as have the majority of people with many other games in the past, but it's still something you should only do at your own risk. We don't recommend breaking the rules just to play a game a few hours early, but we're also not naive enough to think that people won't be trying it come November 18th!

Something to also keep in mind with this is that spoilers will likely begin hitting the web from the New Zealand release time on November 18th (if not earlier). At that point, we expect all kinds of footage and screenshots to begin flooding social media, so you may want to have a bit of a digital detox until the 19th if you don't want to see anything.

Anyway, we know this is a hot topic, and feel free to share your thoughts about it in the comments below. The decision is up to you - but just know that you are running a risk by "moving to New Zealand", however small it might appear to be.

#4088. As if the injury descriptions weren't already ghastly enough in Dwarf Fortress, the legendary outpost builder is getting a "meat biome"

"Lots of meat terrain - muscle, bone, vertebral walls, sinew, sphincters."

Legendary outpost builder Dwarf Fortress is getting a meat biome. A terrible netherworld of bone and artery. A sunken redoubt of gristle and gizzard. An appalling labyrinth of squirt and squelch. Honestly, the biggest shock here is that Dwarf Fortress doesn't appear to have a meat biome already. It certainly has plenty of florid descriptions of fatal injuries.

These foul omens arrive care of a massive "Future of the Fortress" thread on the Bay 12 forums, in which studio co-founder (and prominent genAI disliker) Tarn "Toady One" Adams fields questions about the on-going development. As a forum thread, it's not a formal news source, so please season these tales of gutsy geology with whatever Condiment of Scepticism you consider appropriate.

There's no date for when the new biome might arrive, but Adams says it'll likely exist underground, and will be revolting. "Lots of meat terrain - muscle, bone, vertebral walls, sinew, sphincters," he promised. "We would have rivers of blood/fluids if we ever get to the fluid update, but no new fluids as it stands. We had thrown out the idea for maple syrup style taps on the vertebral walls for cosmic spinal fluid but alas, this is not in the game." At the very least, there won't be any meat trees, but you can mine the meat for resources.

Adams doesn't discuss the origins of the meat biome in the thread – is it more of a headless, fungal phenomenon, or is there some kind of huge mammalian cadaver down there? If it's the latter, one consolation is that the meat biome can't be resurrected. "Ha ha, I don't think regular meat can be animated currently?" Adams remarked in response to a question about biomes of squirming, zombified meat. "So probably not."

The bulk of the conversation around Dwarf Fortress at present concerns forthcoming changes to the magic system, together with how arcane knowledge is categorised, transmitted, preserved and lost throughout each procedurally generated world. There's a lot of speculative chat about that in the Future of the Fortress thread, too much to cleanly summarise. It's saying something about the density and stature of Dwarf Fortress that the addition of flesh caves feels like an afterthought.

Developer Bay 12's current plans for the game also include a crystal biome, which I would say is the nicer option, but then I remembered that this is Dwarf Fortress, the game in which you might end up getting besieged by the ghosts of the very children you callously sent to hunt down a wild elephant. There is absolutely going to be something in the crystal biome that gives you nightmares. Dazzling, prismatic nightmares.

Allowing more people to play your game leads to more sales, who'd have thought?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Square Enix's financial results are looking healthier right now than they have done for some time, as it seems its multi-platform strategy with the likes of Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth coming to Xbox and Switch 2, as well as other great JRPG releases like The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales, are all paying off.

In its latest financial results, covering the six-month period ending on September 30 (the first half of FY2027/3), Square Enix reports a year-on-year increase in both its net sales and operating income "driven by higher sales in the Digital Entertainment segment" – y'know, games. Net sales reached 163.1 billion yen (around $1.03 billion), a 21.9% increase on the 133.8 billion yen ($840.6 million) during the same period last year, and 157.5 billion yen ($989.6 million) the year before.

Looking at the numbers within the Digital Entertainment segment specifically, net sales for the period are actually down slightly compared to this time two years ago (still up massively compared to last year, though), but operating income is trending upward, seeing a huge increase this time around at 32.8 billion yen ($206.07 million) compared to 16.8 billion yen ($105.5 million) for the first half of FY2025/3.

Square Enix says this has been "driven by stronger sales of new titles and catalog titles," pointing to the likes of Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth, The Adventures of Elliot, and Final Fantasy Resonance – though the latter launched after the window for these financial results closed, so its full sales won't be reflected here. The announcement of Final Fantasy 14's next expansion, Evercold, has "improved player activity" and therefore boosted net sales for the MMO, it adds.

Rebirth, of course, launched on Switch 2 and Xbox Series X|S back in June, and Square Enix says it's seen "solid performance" from it since, along with "growth in sales of catalog titles." This once again proves its plan to take its big games multi-platform is working – not that anyone could really doubt that making games available to more players would have a positive effect – and bodes well for Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, which will be arriving on PS5, Xbox Series X|S, PC, and Switch 2 simultaneously next year.

After Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, series lead says Square Enix is "more likely to invest in new titles and new games" than more JRPG remakes.
