#4086. GTA 6 Will Be Playable On Xbox One Through Xbox Cloud Gaming

Rockstar also confirms GTA 6 will run at 30FPS

Update [Tue 10th Nov 2026, 4:03pm]: According to The Verge's Tom Warren, he believes GTA 6 will only be playable on Xbox Cloud Gaming on consoles, with PC and mobile excluded. Xbox Wire recently posted the three ways to play GTA 6 on Xbox. We've updated the article to reflect this.

Original Story: Buying current-gen Xbox hardware isn't cheap these days, and with GTA 6 is now confirmed to be running 30FPS on Xbox Series X|S, what chance would an Xbox One have of running the game, even if it had launched for previous generation tech?

Well, thanks to Rockstar's pre-load notes, we now know GTA 6 will be playable on Xbox One through Xbox Cloud Gaming at Xbox Series S graphics settings. This means those of you who can't upgrade to Xbox Series can still play GTA 6 on November 18th November 19th!

"The game will also be available via XBOX Cloud Gaming on XBOX Series X|S and XBOX One consoles, utilizing XBOX Series S graphics settings. And as with all cloud streaming, connection speeds and other technical factors may influence game performance in ways that would not impact local gameplay. GTAVI will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and XBOX."

You'll of course be at the mercy of Xbox's fresh Cloud Gaming time caps, limiting how long you can stream games depending on your Xbox Game Pass subscription. You can purchase additional time beyond your allotted amount, and if you're still stuck on Xbox One, topping up your cloud gaming hours could work out cheaper than buying an Xbox Series console. A free ad-supported version of Xbox Cloud Gaming is also currently in testing.

However, there may be a catch. According to Tom Warren, it appears that playing GTA 6 via Xbox Cloud Gaming will be restricted to Xbox consoles. If you were planning on streaming the game on PC or mobile, you may need to think again.

"I also incorrectly assumed it would be like every other Xbox Cloud Gaming title and support phone, PC, web, and TV streaming too. GTA 6 is unlike any other game, so clearly an exception has been made here to restrict to just Xbox consoles"

In a recent Xbox Wire post, Microsoft adds weight to Warren's claims, stating the three ways you can play GTA 6 on Xbox:

But back to Rockstar's notes, the Scotland-based dev did indeed confirm that both Xbox and PlayStation devices will target 30FPS whilst pushing the hardware "to their absolute limits" to play GTA 6. My advice would be to give your Xbox a good clean before release. You don't want your console overheating just when the game finally comes out!

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants."

Pre-loading GTA 6 is live now, even if you don't officially own the game yet. If you'd like to know how, then be sure to check out our preload guide featured at the bottom of this article.

#4085. Skyblivion modders reveal a former volunteer is "threatening to sue for damages upwards of €30,000" over work on the unofficial Oblivion remake project

"I just hope that we can get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with the planned release"

The team behind Oblivion remake mod Skyblivion are being threatened with legal action by a former volunteer on the project, according a video posted by current lead Kyle 'Rebelzize' Rebel. The situation looks like it'll need resolving before the mod, which was originally set to release last year, can finally make its way out of the Imperial City sewers.

"Recently, a former volunteer who contributed to Skyblivion’s development departed the project," the Skyblivion team outlined in a written statement and a YouTube video presented by Rebel. "We want to be completely transparent with the community about what has happened since their departure. After they left the project, we had several discussions regarding the continued use and maintenance of his work. The main disagreement centered on their objection to our decompilation of parts of their work — a necessary step our team took to maintain functionality and fix issues in systems already built into the project after access to the original source code repository was revoked."

"To protect ourselves from more stress and try and ensure a clean break, we decided to take the high road," Rebel explained in the video. "We have removed that work entirely. Thankfully due to some of our volunteers stepping up and simply learning new skill sets, as well as help from prominent Skyrim modders and permissions to use and integrate existing Skyrim mods, we've been able to implement replacements that we think fit Skyblivion's needs, in some cases even better than what we had before."

However, Rebel and co claim that despite them making it "clear multiple times to this former volunteer that we have removed their contributions", the ex-Skyblivion dev is "threatening to sue for damages upwards of €30,000". They claim that the ex-volunteer's legal threats "demand personal information of multiple volunteers [on Skyblivion] including full names and addresses". Rebel noted that the team see these demands as "something that we are simply not willing to share with someone that we don't even know" and feel are "just completely disproportionate for what's really going on".

The modders say they've consulted with legal counsel already and have a lawyer on standby if necessary. Though, since said lawyer's services will - the Skyblivion team claim - cost €2,500, they've put out a call for anyone with "a background in IP law or GDPR law" willing to offer them pro bono legal aid to get in touch via the mod's website.

"Please don't turn this into any kind of witch hunt, despite this very unfortunate situation," Rebel said in closing. "We don't wish ill on a former volunteer over all this and I just hope that we can get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with the planned release, which is really what we're working towards. You will hear more from us soon on the actual release."

This situation makes it two years running that Skyblivion's found itself engulfed in drama during the final months of what's supposed to be its release year. In 2025, former volunteer Dee Keyes had a public disagreement with the project's leads over whether releasing the mod that year was a reasonable or achievable goal. Skyblivion was subsequently delayed into 2026.

This past weekend, Keyes tweeted a response to the Skyblivion team's statement on the alleged legal threats. "I've had my issues with the project and left because of it, but I left knowing that my work would remain with [Skyblivion] (happily so) and didn't want to hurt the project's progress," he wrote. "I understand [the former volunteer] being upset, but I really don't see why they'd go so far as to demand their work ripped out."

Here's hoping the Skyblivion team and the ex-volunteer can resolve things without all the expense and effort that'd inevitably be necessary if the dispute ends up in court. Given there are now less than two months left of 2026, and Skyblivion's modders have this on their plates on top of any remaining work needed to finish their creation, I'd personally be very surprised if its release doesn't end up being pushed into next year.

#4084. Talking Point: With Big Walk, The AI-In-Game-Dev Debate Just Got A Lot Murkier

"The line must be drawn here! This far, no further!"

Please forgive the Captain Picard First Contact quote (it's been a couple of weeks since Patrick Stewart's death and only now can I mention his most famous character without welling up) - I promise it's relevant as an illustration of an admirable, principled stance.

In the Borg, good ol' Jean-Luc had a well-defined enemy to engage, with the threat of humanity's assimilation providing a pretty clear line between good and bad. There are larger philosophical questions about the hive mind and our aversion to Star Trek's cube-riding automatons, but for the purposes of this article, let's assume we're all in agreement: Borg=baaad.

Back in the real world, though, that line between right and wrong often isn't so easy to define. Today there'll be a lot of commentators in the video game space, players and developers alike, longing for a better understanding of another encroaching, all-consuming entity.

House House's belated disclosure that LLMs were used during the development of indie hit Big Walk pours fuel on an already raging debate and brings questions over permissible AI use in game dev right back into the discourse - specifically the differences between generative AI for player-facing audio-visual assets and writing versus coding and other less obvious uses.

News Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage

This latest flashpoint followed a statement released by a subset of IGF Award jurors explaining why they won't be voting for games developed using any form of generative AI.

Last year, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — which swept The Game Awards with nine wins from 13 nominations — raised similar questions after the Indie Game Awards disqualified Sandfall Interactive's game upon discovering AI had been used in the development pipeline.

I've voiced my distaste for GenAI, and it remains a massive no-no - professionally and personally. I'm fortunate to not have corporate overlords mandating its use around these parts, which certainly isn't the case for some other outlets, nor for many creatives in the gaming space. The gulf in quality between the human-written word and generated bilge is still enormous and easily identifiable, and for now, the same is broadly true of GenAI visual artwork, too.

What this Big Walk situation highlights, however, is how difficult it can be to discern in other places, and the increasing pull it has on even the most principled developers.

Talking Point Does It Bother You That Big Games Companies Are Using GenAI?

The phrase gets bandied around a lot, but it's fair to call Big Walk a proper 'critical darling'. It garnered "Universal Acclaim" back in August, with an impressive 91 Metascore. Alex gave it a "Great" 8/10 after reviewing the Switch 2 version for us - technical hiccups took the shine off it for him, but he still loved the co-op experience. And by September it was already Nile's GOTY.

As someone who didn't play Big Walk at launch, its place in my GOTY-catch-up priorities may have shifted, but wherever you land on the GenAI spectrum, the consensus among critics and players is as unanimous as it gets: Big Walk is an excellent video game.

There are many issues to consider — not least where AI use crosses from tool to theft — but an important one relates to how this game in particular has had a profound effect on many players. Rejecting something flagged as 'suspicious' on principle is easy, especially with so many brilliant games releasing each week. But something you've played already and internalised and loved? From a dev team you respect?

For some, this revelation will feel like when a beloved artist/actor/writer/musician is revealed to be problematic, but we're not talking about illegal behaviour or allegations here.

If House House's statement is to be taken at face value, the team used a chatbot to find a solution to a coding issue with Unity, the third-party engine the game is built on. People online with real chops have already investigated the specifics of House House's single example:

took me 3 hours but I figured out the “URP culling shadowcasters behind the camera” issue House House cites in their disclosure. This culls immediately when the object is off-camera, but modifying the culling params with a custom frustrum is straightforward

this needs cleaning up but is basically the gist

This was a terrible use of 3 hours, but I know just a bit more about how to do something cool. I’m sympathetic to them wanting to ship something good but AI rots your damn brain

That's the one example the devs offer in their statement, and the language around further usage feels vague. The impression it gives is of a team searching for a solution to a specific problem using common tools, as opposed to vibe-coding huge swathes of the game.

Now, I've never programmed anything in my life, but I can appreciate that efficient code must be an art in itself. Is it any less of an art because that code is invisible to players? Then again, to me, generating great chunks of game code feels very different from using an LLM to squash a bug or find a solution when third-party documentation fails. Is one usage as 'bad' as the other, or is this slippery slope, gateway-drug territory?

(Perhaps if any programmers are reading, they'd like to share thoughts in the comments - as the headline says, this is very much a talking point and I'm keen to explore with as much nuance as the internet will permit.)

My point is that seeing exactly where to draw that line is increasingly difficult when AI tools of all types become ubiquitous. A blanket rejection of anything inevitably now means excluding not just an increasing number of games, but also artistically significant, important ones.

And with executives like former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser advocating the use of AI for indie teams to improve workflow, it's also easy to understand how a developer might turn to the tech. The whole topic is getting greyer by the day, much to the pleasure of evangelists, I'm sure.

Like it or not, this situation forces AI sceptics to reconcile their positive feelings for the game. House House estimates "well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code" has any trace of generative AI, but to paraphrase a certain Starfleet captain again, "How much does it take before it becomes wrong, hmm?" That is the question.

For some players who simply don't care, it's a non-issue. Some may reluctantly cut the game from their lives and GOTY lists. I suspect that others, though, disappointed or otherwise, will start reconsidering where they personally draw the AI line.

And if House House hadn't disclosed this, would anyone have ever known? I'd guess not. And if a celebrated indie team turned to AI as a problem-solver, how many other devs aren't disclosing similar usage? And how many sure-as-hell won't do so after this?

Lots of questions, no clear answers, just murk. How unsatisfying. I've heard 'ends-justify-means' sentiments online — 'hey, if the game is good, does it matter?' — which feel unsavoury given the documented, quantifiable damage AI is doing to the games industry and the wider world. It's that damage which has IGF jurors abstaining from voting for Big Walk this year: an understandable, admirable stance.

Which leads us to one final question: What would Captain Picard do?

Naturally, he'd call everyone into the Observation Lounge for a big old meeting in a calm, civilised manner, that's what. Conference.

Let us know below if this revelation changes your relationship with the game or where you draw the line when it comes to generative AI in its various forms.

I’m not a game dev but a software engineer with over 15 years of end-to-end more than just full stack software development experience who helped build up 2 successful startups with my own hand written code, no matter the coding language, backend, front end, infrastructure as code.

I’ve started to increasingly use AI because in today’s world it would burn you out to do anything without AI with all the pressure coming from needing to survive as a business.

My own rule is simply to use AI only to the capacity that ensures you have full control and AI doesn’t take over, and not in a way that replaces Human Resources but improves efficiency. In art this is difficult to achieve, but for coding it is simple.

1) If it’s some quick one-time tedious type of work (e.g. migrating to a new system), AI can be immensely helpful, you only need to review the end-result/output. I find the use of AI okay if you are capable of ensuring quality output and review it.

I had AI write scripts to do several types of migration work where it would take me weeks to learn all the tiny bits and unknowns, then write all the code. I used to do it all by hand and it is thankless work where you learn a lot of things you will never apply again in your life. Perfect scenario for AI to just do it. It can research everything needed and think of unknowns you couldn’t think of. Once the work is done, throw the scripts away because migration is done. Weeks of work reduced to a mere few hours. Instead I can focus on more fun parts of my job.

2) if its production level code that impacts user experience, I feel you should only use AI for assistance to improve and not to build. You need full control. We had an instance in the company somebody wrote the entire microservice via AI in a way he was incapable of debugging without AI. One part of it I had to rewrite completely by hand to fix it. They had no clue what they were doing and it could have been a disaster.

Unfortunately, I personally have come across too many lazy developers that make me prefer AI written code over their code, because AI simply codes better, more structured, can follow design patterns properly.

If you are unable to clearly envision the expected logic you intend to write, the expected design patterns used, don’t use AI. Learn first.

This brings me to 3) using AI to improve your skills is an extremely powerful tool. I told a friend to have AI teach him design patterns since I have no time for doing that, but he can always cross check with me. He has never improved so fast in his own hand-written creations before AI.

— Now I’ve tried using AI in various ways for coding and one thing for sure is that you need to be extremely good in giving boundaries and directions. Basically the correct “prompt”, and you can only do that if you have enough experience and skills yourself to control AI in that way. And you can never get there if you just let AI do all the work. It makes a lot of mistakes.

Now if I had to not worry about money, I would use AI far less and only for code reviews or learning, basically jsut as “feedback”, not a producer. But that’s not something I can afford, especially in a world where all employers now expect you to use AI to improve cost-efficiency.

Maybe not a common take, or a popular one, but I'm not a developer, yet I've been able to do amazing things with AI that I never could have without it. I have always had ideas and never been able to do anything with them because I lack the skill to code, and the time/desire to learn.

Since picking up Claude Code less than a year ago I've made several small games for myself that were terrible and I abandoned, but I've also been able to make some great stuff:

All of these projects are open source, on my github, and I will never charge for them, so I have the luxury of saying if you don't like it, don't use it. But I can sympathize with people who CAN code and are being forced to work faster not smarter on commercial projects, or losing their jobs altogether because 1 developer can do the work of 3, with the quality of none.

At work I've been able to (with my CEO's blessing) teach an AI agent how to fix 80% of the issues we see regularly to the point where over half of my daily work is done now with fully deterministic code, written by an AI agent, and the rest is triaged and investigated before I ever see it. Our time to resolution has gone down, and customer satisfaction has gone up, and we still send every communication by hand. None of the code is user facing, and none is supported by our dev team, so it's only to benefit our support staff.

I'm absolutely against using AI to replace people, whether it's in development, design, art, writing, communication, or anywhere else, but I'm a huge proponent of using it to enable your team to hand-off the time consuming, repetitive tasks to agents and focus on the things that the love about their job instead.

One of the most common defenses of AI is that it's just a tool. This is, technically, true.

A hammer is also a tool. You can use a hammer to make a beautiful birdhouse. You can use it to make an ugly birdhouse. Or you can use it to bash in the brains of someone who criticized your birdhouse.

The difference is that there are already well established rules/laws in place about ethical hammer usage. With AI, we're really only getting started, and it's probably going to take a long time to figure out all the nuances, especially with a technology that will only continue to evolve.

Y'know, I've struggled with my own thoughts on AI, a thing that describes the ultimate plagiarism machine approved by the dumbest and worst people in the entertainment industry but also completely normal shortcuts used in various aspects of tech that were fine to good before renamed the same thing as the plagiarism machine as a marketing tool.

And my main thought is to think of how people will bring up the most logical extreme to try to get a less extreme thing to happen. This is a compromise in many places, but the one that comes to mind is when the creator of a family friendly show wants to do anything that isn't just the safest, made for 6 year olds only story possible. So they'll put something with zero chance of making it past the censors, so that they can sneak in something more reasonable because its less extreme.

I think that's my stance. I am as anti-AI as reasonably possible, because I only want the reasonable examples of AI (much of which we did not call AI 10 years ago, always keep that in mind) to exist. And the only way to do that is to push against AI entirely, because that is likely, the only way to prevent the bad parts of AI to happen.

Though part of it is also that the bad parts of AI are so obviously terrible that this is the level of nuance you need to present for any of it to be remotely tolerable. Which is admittedly, unfair. But in that case, the blame for that is on the people that (sometimes quite literally) poisoned the water. If this is just a new tool, it is a new tool. But when you make it AI vs. artists, the only correct opinion when you are forced into an all or nothing choice is to burn it all down to save artists. And at the end of the day, this is maybe the most obviously, corporate approved, forced trend of my lifetime. Being anti-AI is just being against the extreme of corporate destruction and replacement of art, because there's not much of a choice otherwise.

I feel bad for people stuck in the middle, and I hope someday we can have a more nuanced look at all this. But while I wouldn't say people should or need to or that even necessarily I would refuse to buy a game for this exact scenario (I'm almost certainly gonna buy E33 someday and that had its own weird AI controversy), if someone did, I would not blame them. It is not difficult, even in this scenario, just be like "no thanks", and move on to the many games where you don't have to even think about this nonsense.

Also for me personally, sometimes I'd just rather not waste my time thinking about such things at all. Being annoyingly controversial and nuanced is not something that makes me want to buy a game, sounds like a pain. I think way too much about way too much bad stuff, I don't need to spend my time on being conflicted about a game choice when I could play countless other games.

@dartmonkey I'm an embedded software engineer who has dabbled a bit in AI-assistent use in the context of my work. I'd say at the moment I have a "middle of the road" stance on AI usage in this form. I've seen the advantages and disadvantages of using AI for code generation/fix/support and I acknowledge both the opportunities and threats that AI present.

In my experience, the code that an engineer writes is a means to an end, a way to implement a certain logic concept into something that actually works. As such, I consider my core work to be the conceptual logic I think of, whereas the actual coding part is merely a necessary task to fulfil that logic. It's no surprise then that code generation has been used for decades already in software engineering, be it model-based or low-code or whatever that I'm not even aware of. Though most of those solutions were not very smart, the generation works based on a very strict logic and it's the engineer task to make sure that logic translates into correct code. In this context, using AI to generate code seems merely a new iteration of the same concept, but now it's smarter. It uses the experience of thousands of software engineers to try and generate the correct code based on the prompt. A different way to achieve the same result.

Now, some would say that writing the most optimized, efficiently running and easily maintainable code is also an art in itself. That may be true, but history has also shown that humans engineers are phenomenally bad at achieving that result consistently (which explains why code generation is even a thing). We're reliant on other, more experienced engineers to show us how to achieve those code quality goals, the best design patterns and the best practices. And that in turn makes the code we write only as good as the teachers that taught us. Now compare that with using AI, which will eventually (MAJOR caveat there, "eventually" is doing a lot of heavy lifting) be trained on the best quality code, best design patterns and best practices of hundreds of thousands software engineers. That's a huge win. It's a good result, especially in the context of "just writing the code". If the engineer creates the correct design, the AI only needs to generate the best possible code to make that design a reality. Based on this view, I do not consider AI use to generate, fix or optimize code an issue.

@dartmonkey But I'd like to reframe the concept to something you as a writer can better relate to. How do you feel about the following scenario. A writer is struggling with a paragraph in a certain text, even after multiple drafts they are not satisfied. Eventually, they contact a fellow writer and ask the very simple question "how would you write this part"? Perfectly normal, right? But how about that writer uses an AI to ask the same question. Instead of getting one suggestion from a known source, they get the combined response of over thousands of writers. Sure, these are anonymous sources and might not have given this response explicitly, but the end result is much the same, I think.

This is similar to the coding scenario, I believe. The question becomes, what is your core output as a writer. The message you want to convey, or the way you present that message. Now, I can see how for writing that presentation is much more important that the coding is for achieve a logic result; calling the actual writing of a text "a means to an end" for a message is going too far. But, I think considering this view has merit.

And so, with the use of AI in any context, I think the way AI is utilized is very important in determining the "morality" of its use. There's a huge difference between asking an AI to "write a positive review about this game" and "reword this paragraph to make it sound more neutral". Same as there's a huge different between asking an AI to "make a game where an electrician jumps on platforms" and "make the physics of this jump routine more natural".

#4083. Beloved Co-Op Adventure Big Walk in Hot Water After Failing to Disclose AI Usage

Big Walk, one of the most highly-rated games of 2026, has suddenly found itself in a spot of bother, and it's all thanks to those controversial AI tools.

This story stems from the Independent Games Festival Awards (IGF); some of the jurors have taken a hard stance against usage of generative AI or LLM technology.

These jurors recently put out a statement in which they condemn the tech, and in the aftermath of this, it's come out that developer House House did in fact use gen AI, albeit in a minor capacity, when making Big Walk.

On the game's official website, this is now addressed directly in a new FAQ page.

In the statement, House House says LLMs were used "sparingly" near the end of the game's production "to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs."

"In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

The statement goes on to provide an example of how and why the tech was used.

Ultimately, it seems the team has utilised AI very minimally, but that its use was not previously disclosed has rubbed people the wrong way.

Usually, generative AI usage is declared on a game's Steam page, but House House says it didn't do so because "the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage" but has made it public information in light of IGF's actions.

It opens up the debate about gen AI once again. Whether you like it or not, more and more games are being built with the tech to varying degrees, and I expect the number will only grow bigger over time.

However, its ubiquity doesn't safeguard it from criticism, especially when it comes to generating in-game assets, writing, or other creative aspects.

In Big Walk's case, an LLM was used to help with specific technical issues, which I think is relatively harmless, but others may still feel any gen AI is too much.

@nessisonett Technically, "gen AI" describes AI systems capable of producing new content based on patterns learned during training. That content can take many forms:

What you call (modern) "AI assisted debugging" is as "gen AI" as generating art assets. The underlying technology may differ (LLMs, Diffusion models, etc.), but most AI models these days are multimodal in nature, combining multiple technologies to achieve the desired results.

You could refine that distinction and say you're against using AI to generate content trained on protected IP. But even then, you'd be in muddy waters somewhat, because source code is as copyrighted as art.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has praised The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake amid chatter that it's competing with GTA 6.

November 2026 has been pretty barren as far as major AAA releases are concerned, with publishers flooding the September and October 2026 markets, as well as February 2027, to avoid the monolith that is GTA 6.

Nintendo, however, is unbothered, moisturized, happy, in its lane, focused, and flourishing, as it released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake regardless.

This led many to position the two as rivals, even going so far as a viral SNL sketch about the two November releases. There was even a comment from an Activision exec saying Nintendo's remake doesn't stack up against Modern Warfare 4 and GTA 6, which certainly has aged well, given that nobody is talking about the former anymore.

Speaking to GamesBeat, Zelnick was asked if he viewed Ocarina of Time as a competitor following its release last week and its status as the highest-rated game of 2026. He acknowledged GTA 6's November competitor, saying, "It's terrific, and they should be very proud of the title."

Zelnick adds, "In the entertainment business, you compete against everything and nothing." Why? "Because there are so many ways consumers can spend their time, and nothing, because if there’s nothing good out there, people don’t need to consume any of it."

He finishes off by saying that entertainment is not a "must-have" the way food is. Rather, it's a "want to have." That's why "it's our job to make the best entertainment on earth. When we do that, people will show up for it."

#4081. Delve into "a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors" in the latest Fallout 4 quest mod from the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project

A mysterious bunker with out of this world contents

After adding a whole new town to Fallout 4 last month, a group of modders have released another in their long string of extra quests for the RPG. This latest mission revolves around a dungeon delve in the Glowing Sea, where a mysterious bunker's just been unearthed.

"The harsh radioactive winds of the Glowing Sea have uncovered a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors," the group behind the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project (CSEP) declared the description of this latest work, Under The Stars.

A fresh dungeon with a quest attached, the mod tasks you with donning your hazmat suit for a trip to a sunken bunker in the region of post-apocalyptic Boston with the least chill weather. Inside await voiced holotapes and puzzles offering clues as to what went down in this cosy corner of the Commonwealth, plus some new gear to make braving whatever lurks within worth it.

Spoilers: Judging by the screenshots, it looks like the place is an Area 51-esque hidey-hole for evidence of aliens and other cryptic oddities.

If you're unfamiliar, the CSEP lot are responsible for a bunch of popular Fallout 4 quest mods based around the likes of deadly cults, underground wars, post-apocalyptic detective work, and Brotherhood of Steel drama. While Under The Stars doesn't look have been as big an undertaking as those, that previous form points to it being an expertly-crafted addition that'll slot seamlessly into the game.

The modders have put Under The Stars together as part of a community-hosted modding jam called Fallout Flood, with this latest one based around the theme of being underground. Among the other works to have come out of it thus far are another Fallout 4 quest mod dubbed Stranded - The Oasis, a dungeon full of funky rats called the S'Laven, and a new robot enemy you can wear as a hat. It's also produced a New Vegas quest mod about exploring an abandoned NCR railway, so seems to have been very productive gathering of modding minds.

To give Under The Stars a go, your copy of Fallout 4 will need to have the Automatron and Vault-Tec Workshop DLCs.

#4080. Xbox Vs. PS5: GTA 6 Specs Revealed, And These Are The Biggest Differences

"Pushing both platforms to their absolute limits"

Rockstar Games has today lifted the lid on a bunch of specs for both the Xbox and PS5 versions of GTA 6, revealing some of the biggest differences (and similarities) between playing the game on each platform.

The most notable bit of information is that every single console runs the game at 30FPS. Regardless of whether you're playing on Xbox Series S, Xbox Series X, PS5 or even PS5 Pro, the max you're getting is 30 frames per-second.

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants."

There will obviously be resolution differences between each platform, but Rockstar has yet to reveal these details. Expect the Series S to fare the worst, the PS5 Pro to fare the best, and the Series X and PS5 to be pretty much equal.

Rockstar does say that GTA 6 "plays best" on PS5 though (and let's not forget that Sony appears to have a marketing deal in place with Rockstar Games for this release), highlighting the differences between the PS5 and Xbox versions as being "high-fidelity haptic feedback" for the PS5 DualSense controllers, improved spatial audio rendering, and bizarrely, improved load times. That last one is surely just a minimal advantage at best!

Grand Theft Auto VI for PS5 includes high-fidelity haptic feedback fully integrated across the game on DualSense controllers and adjustable via accessibility settings, improved spatial audio rendering so all in-game sounds take full advantage of Tempest 3D Audio, and improved load times, making Grand Theft Auto VI play best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

Beyond that, the PS5 Pro version will benefit from improved clarity via PSSR along with ray-traced shadows.

However, the Xbox version has one massive benefit in the form of Xbox Cloud Gaming. It seems Xbox will be the only platform offering cloud streaming for GTA 6 at launch, making it an exclusive of sorts - at least for now. The bizarre bit is that it only appears to be for consoles, rather than other devices like PCs and mobiles.

The Xbox and PS5 versions will also support Remote Play (allowing you to cast your game to another device from your console). Nothing has been said about Quick Resume yet on Xbox, but we assume it'll be supported as well.

Ultimately, GTA 6 is bound to run great regardless of whether you buy it on Xbox or PlayStation, and the "plays best on PS5" differences mentioned by Rockstar Games appear to be minor advantages rather than major ones.

We can't wait for footage to start appearing online next week — especially for the Xbox Series S version — and here's hoping it's going to live up to the ridiculous hype that's been fueling the past decade. Not long to wait at all now!

#4077. Mouse Work, The Switch 2 Game Using Joy-Con Mouse Controls, Arrives This December

Prepare for your shift by pre-ordering today

Update [Tue 10th Nov 2026, 11:35pm]: Nitrome has now officially announced Mouse Work will be arriving for Switch 2 on 7th December 2026.

It's described as the ultimate showcase for the system's mouse controls, and will include a "massive 8-10 hour campaign solo" or you can bring a crew with you for a co-op experience. This includes 1-4 players locally and online via GameShare.

"In Mouse Work, players take on the role of adorable mice that are just trying to earn some cheddar. Fortunately for them, the local Job Centre has a wealth of offerings available, each testing our mice with new and innovative cursor-based gameplay."

This title will set you back $19.99 / £15.99 and pre-orders are now live on the eShop. Nitrome has also shared a new trailer, which you can check out above.

Original Story: Remember Mouse Work? It was announced by developer Nitrome for the Switch 2 just a few months before the system's launch and requires you to use mouse controls to complete all sorts of fun and challenging jobs.

We've not got an update about this title since last year, but it looks like it's finally on the way. According to a listing that has recently appeared on the Japanese Nintendo Store and eShop, it will be arriving this holiday season on 7th December 2026 for 2,200 yen.

The translated description notes how the campaign is 10 hours across more than 50 unique stages. You'll also be able to participate in local and online multiplayer, including GameShare support. When we hear more about the local release, we'll provide an update.

Nitrome has previously released games such as Bomb Chicken and Shovel Knight Dig on the original Switch. Are you excited for its new game on Switch 2? Let us know in the comments.

#4076. The Voidjoy Elite Extender only makes sense for Pro Controller purists

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Voidjoy Elite Extender is aimed at anyone not ready to give up the Nintendo-specific features of their Pro Controller while dodging that pricey new-generation gamepad. Ultimately, its back button feel and placement don't live up to the quality offered by sometimes cheaper, third-party controllers, though its analog triggers make for a compelling prospect as long as you're buying for a split PC / Switch setup with a strong racing theme on the former platform.

Solid, durable connection and build quality

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

The Voidjoy Elite Extender answers a commonly asked question with a complicated answer. Is it worth buying a new Nintendo Switch 2 controller solely for its back buttons? If you're still rocking the original Switch Pro Controller, the JSAUX brand's add-on back button attachment stands to save you around $50 on the price of the Switch 2 Pro gamepad. But it's not quite that easy in the grand scheme of the wider market.

The $39.99 accessory slots into the USB-C port on the top of the OG controller, providing two additional back buttons underneath as well as two Hall effect triggers up top (note that these flippers only work on PC). If you're sticking with old faithful for its rumble, NFC, and motion controls, it's a worthwhile endeavor even if it's far from a seamless integration. With the price of Ninty's next-gen hardware seemingly always on the rise, I'll take any shortcuts that manage to evade extra costs.

If you're simply looking to add back button controls to your Switch or Switch 2 gameplay without funding the full $89 Pro 2 Controller price, though, I'd recommend heading in a different direction.

Does the Voidjoy Elite Extender fulfil its primary aim? Absolutely. Is it the best way to bring back buttons to Switch 2? No - and I'd argue it's not even the most cost-efficient either.

With third-party gamepads offering back buttons and additional features like TMR thumbsticks and charging docks, for as little as $29.99 in some cases, the Voidjoy Elite Extender's appeal is going to be limited to those who really can't leave their existing Pro Controller behind.

The Voidjoy Elite Extender is still new to the market and is available via Amazon and the brand's own site. Note that it's not currently on the shelves in the UK or EU.

Nintendo Switch Pro Controller (unconfirmed third party suitability)

The Void Joy Elite Extender doesn't exactly hide itself away on your Pro Controller. The chunky plastic casing curves neatly around the top panel of the controller itself in two panels. A wider base sits flush with the back of the gamepad, while another raised platform houses the P1 and P2 back buttons, swooping up to provide access to additional triggers on the top of the controller. This is also where you'll find USB-C passthrough as well as five tiny little flush buttons for power, Bluetooth connection, on-the-fly button mapping, and platform switching.

Placing the back buttons on this second raised platform quickly became one of the first downsides I noticed as I made my way through the first few hours of Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time Remake. Many of the best PC controllers already using back buttons will place their clackers on the grips themselves. This means a quick action becomes more of a squeeze on the controller's leg than a specific button push. It's also how the Switch 2 Pro Controller places its own back buttons.

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

Raising the P1 and P2 clackers above the main base of the grip, however, means I'm having to hold my fingers a good distance from the actual back of the controller to keep them in position. It's not exactly a natural position, and one that worked itself into fatigue fairly quickly. If I ever returned my fingers to their natural resting spot on the back of the grip itself, I would often find myself missing inputs - mistaking the first ledge of the attachment for the buttons themselves during the heat of the moment.

Combine that with the fact that the Elite Extender itself top-loads the weight of the original Pro Controller, leaving my natural grip slanted more forwards than usual, and my time in Hyrule was a little more strained than I expected.

Aesthetically, the Voidjoy Elite Extender matches the black of the Pro Controller well, with a glossy accent around the main base and back buttons themselves and a matte finish on the upper platform. Branding is kept to the rear of the device, with a simple light gray logo printed on the plastic, and functional buttons along the top are clearly designated.

The little flipper trigger add-ons are fully removable, slotting comfortably into the device with two sturdy prongs, and can be reversed for flat storage as well, which is a pretty nifty trick. That physical USB-C connection to the Pro Controller is also rock-solid, with no wiggling or undue pressure on the port itself.

Of course, there are the headlines: those two additional P1 and P2 back buttons - but the Elite Extender has a few more handy tricks in its arsenal. While I was disappointed to find out the analog triggers are reserved for PC use only, they provide a nicely tensioned 1,280-step optical response for racing titles and can be easily stowed away when not in use.

It's not just PC either; the Elite Extender works alongside your Switch Controller on both iOS and Android, with Touch Mapping available for the latter as well. This is done through the KeyLinker App, though, and I have mixed feelings.

The app itself has enough scope to provide a robust selection of controls, even if the interface runs a little on the jankier side. You've got deadzone settings for both the regular Pro Controller sticks and those additional triggers here, with a simple menu of key assignments to play around with.

Unfortunately, even after updating both the app and device firmware to their latest setting, there's no designation for the P1 and P2 buttons in here. Thankfully, setting up keybindings directly on the pad itself is pretty simple with the Fn key - just keep in mind that your settings won't be saved across games like the official Switch 2 Pro Controller.

The KeyLinker software also opens you up to 42-step macros as well as turbo with adjustable speed as well.

The Voidjoy Elite Extender feels like a stopgap, rather than a set of well-crafted back buttons ready and waiting for your original Switch Pro Controller. The clackers themselves are positioned a little too awkwardly, and actuate with a little too high a tension to truly be reliable in faster-paced games and comfortable in more relaxed settings.

After a little re-learning, I was still able to hit the jump and roll/sprint settings I had assigned to P1 and P2 in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but I was often missing inputs after relaxing my grip or by simply forgetting the pressure required to actuate each clacker.

Switching over to PC, my first playthrough of Control: Resonant has been saved by the super-speedy back buttons on the Razer Wolverine V3 Pro. Here, I had to measure my expectations. It's fair enough - a set of $39.99 buttons isn't going to beat one of the best Xbox Series X controllers (with a $199.99 MSRP, no less), and it shouldn't have to to be worth its price of admission. The Voidjoy Elite Extender is no miracle worker, though.

Control: Resonant requires fast spamming of those back buttons in my current control setup for smooth getaways and faster secondary attacks. These tappers are just too awkwardly positioned when set this far away from the palm, and too heavy to actuate for that to be truly workable. These switches were not made for repeat inputs.

While my PC was warm, though, it was time to give those triggers a test in Forza Horizon 6, and I was pleased with how these worked. While the start of each actuation can feel a little stiff, there's a smooth glide downward that makes fine-tuned acceleration and braking all the more immersive. It's a pity these haven't been carried over to the Switch 2, though perhaps the software isn't quite there to take advantage of them, because they're one of my favorite things about this gadget.

It's easy to see the $89 price tag of the Switch 2 Pro Controller and feel priced out of back buttons on the new handheld. If you're moving from the OG Switch to a brand new Switch 2, the Voidjoy Elite Extender represents a compelling budget-friendly alternative to going all out on Nintendo's second-generation gamepad. The placement and feel of its back buttons, as well as the extra front-loaded weight added to your controller, however, would have me recommending a new third-party gamepad instead.

The GameSir Super Nova, for example, is regularly on sale for $29.99 at Best Buy, despite its $49.99 MSRP. Side-by-side, back button handling between the Extender and this whole second controller is night and day, and you're getting a spare gamepad with Hall effect sticks, trigger stops, and a charging dock for $10 less than Voidjoy's price tag.

While it's nearly double the price, the 8BitDo Ultimate 2 will also net you a far better back-button experience with boosted TMR sticks and a range of extra features for $69.99.

There is someone I'd recommend the Voidjoy Elite Extender to, however. Anyone determined to bring the Nintendo-specific features of the original Pro Controller (easy connection, NFC, HD Rumble) to their Switch 2 upgrade, or anyone looking to keep those Ninty features on the original handheld will be interested here. If it's official or bust, the Voidjoy Elite Extender can offer a set of additional inputs that can see you through slower endeavors with a little muscle re-learning at a fraction of the price of a brand-new official kit.

I used the Voidjoy Elite Extender in a Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake marathon, taking me from Link's first moments in Kokiri Village all the way through to the end of the Fire Temple (with plenty of Skulltula hunting in between). I also connected to PC to continue Control: Resonant and test the triggers in Forza Horizon 6. For more information on how we test controllers, check out the full GamesRadar+ Hardware Policy.

We're also rounding up the best Nintendo Switch 2 accessories on the market as well as the best PS5 controllers available now.

Managing Editor of Hardware at GamesRadar+, I originally landed in hardware at our sister site TechRadar before moving over to GamesRadar. In between, I've written for Tom’s Guide, Wireframe, The Indie Game Website and That Video Game Blog, covering everything from the PS5 launch to the Apple Pencil. Now, i'm focused on Nintendo Switch, gaming laptops (and the keyboards, headsets and mice that come with them), PS5, and trying to find the perfect projector.

The game is also now the most pre-ordered Microsoft Store title ever

We're getting a whole ton of GTA 6 details coming out today, and Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has taken to social media to issue a statement about the game's pre-orders, as well as a new 10-year partnership with its publisher Take-Two.

Sharma didn't share any specific details about the partnership in her post, but we did cover the deal at the beginning of October, which allows Take-Two to develop and sell Xbox-compatible products across all Xbox devices. The Xbox boss did also highlight that GTA 6 has now set a record for the most pre-orders of any Microsoft Store / Xbox Store game in history.

It's no surprise that the most anticipated game of all time is picking up its fair share of pre-orders ahead of launch. The numbers were looking good as early as August, when Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick described GTA 6's pre-orders as "unprecedented and astonishing".

Of course, Zelnick wasn't talking solely about Xbox's pre-order total, but it's great to see Sharma commenting on Microsoft's numbers specifically.

Beyond handling Rockstar's GTA and Red Dead Redemption IPs, Take-Two Interactive also manages 2K and Zynga titles. If Sharma intends to entertain more than a billion players every day, striking up a cloud streaming deal with Take-Two is a great place to start.

#4074. Fewer genAI clones of "someone else's specific game" should flood the net going forwards, as Anthropic tell Claude to stop messing with some stuff other people own

It will still let people generate "original" games using the tech

Anthropic have told their genAI tool Claude to start ducking requests from users to recreate or clone existing games, following a flood of folks using the tech to generate six-fingered remakes. Instead of risking infringing on the intellectual property of series or titles that companies which aren't Anthropic own, Claude will instead restrict itself to only generating "original" games slopped together based on whatever data it's drawing on.

"We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Anthropic staffer Addy Osmani wrote on not Twitter in response to a rando with a cat profile picture having spotted the change.

"Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working," Osmani continued. "We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way." Game Developer reached out to Anthropic for confirmation and were pointed to Osmani's post.

The change should make it harder to add to the horde of genAI-powered decomps, recomps, and ports which have hit the net recently. It's hardly a surprising one, given studios like Bethesda have seemingly had to take matters into their own lawyers' hands to get the likes of an AI-generated Fallout game taken offline, with games that've just been ripped wholesale or barely tweaked likely on even more perilous ground. That said, not every corp's responded to the DIY decompilation craze by immediately taking legal action.

There's a serious degree of irony to Anthropic slapping Claude and telling it stealing is bad. One of the ways the company develop and train their genAI models is by scraping publicly available data from the internet via a web crawler.

So, some nicking of stuff is bad, little bot people keep asking to regurgitate stuff into slop they can then try to pass off as something they've created. But not all nicking of stuff, lest our whole business be on rather shaky ground.

It's unlikely this move from Anthropic does much to convince actual developers of original games they're safe to put demos of their games out prior to release, without risking dickheads using genAI to clone said demo and potentially release a slop version in rapid fashion, but one can dream of that genie being put back in the bottle someday.

#4072. PSA: Nintendo Ending Google And Apple Sign-Ins On Nintendo Accounts In 2027

You'll need a Nintendo Account from here on out

If you currently use a Google or Apple account to sign in to your Nintendo Account, Nintendo has got some news. In an official notice, it's announced the discontinuation of Google and Apple account sign-ins on Nintendo Accounts.

This will take place on 26th January 2027, so we're just a few months out. "As of" this date, it will no longer be possible to link a Google or Apple account. Nintendo notes this exact end time "may be delayed depending on the progress of the system change work".

Nintendo: "We apologise for any inconvenience to those who used a Google or Apple account to sign in to their Nintendo Account."

Here's what this means when it does come into effect:

And "if you are already logged into your Nintendo Account on a device, you may not have to sign in again". If the sign-in page does appear, you'll need to sign in using the email address or sign-in ID and your password for your Nintendo Account, or a Passkey.

If we hear any updates about this, we'll let you know. What are your thoughts about this announcement? Let us know in the comments.

Liam is a news writer and reviewer on Nintendo Life. He's been writing about games for more than 15 years and is a lifelong fan of many iconic video game characters.

#4071. Fix up towering robots while battle rages outside in Bay 12: Mech Repair, a first-person job sim with some handsome heavy duty analog tech

The most important thing to know about Bay 12: Mech Repair is that these are mechs of the MechWarrior or possibly Patlabor school – that is, basically WW2 tanks on hydraulic legs, with cockpits full of switches and wireframe displays. Their bodies are assemblages of pistons and reactors. They are not biomechs like the ones in Evangelion. An Evangelion Repair game would be… different. Less industrial, more Oedipal. You would dread removing the smallest piece of housing.

Which isn't to say that Bay 12: Mech Repair represents life on Easy Street, exactly. There's a big war happening outside, its fortunes palpable in the minced leg joints and pocked torsos of the war-bots lowered into your hangar. You're also fed details about the lives of pilots when you accept a work order. Lieutenant Iona Vale of the 3rd Recon Company says there's "left leg hesitation after extended operation", especially at higher temperatures. That sure sounds like a thing that could get Lieutenant Iona Vale killed.

It's not clear whether you can diagnose faults incorrectly, and shape the progress of the conflict, but the context brings extra emotional charge to what might otherwise be a cosy process of glueing together very expensive Air-Fix models, for all the sense of scale.

Bay 12: Mech Repair follows a familiar flow, as job sims go. Banged-up Iron Giants arrive in a steady procession. You figure out what's wrong with them based on scans, pilot reports, and so forth. Then you get out there with a welder, drill and spanner to make it right. Busted parts can be salvaged for scrap for custom components. Completed work orders net you credits that must be divided between restocking your inventory and buying new tools.

You also have the option of clearing away rust and applying a new paintjob. I'm fascinated to know if this has any real impact on either the story or your fortunes, because I guarantee that I am going to spend far more time obsessing over dazzle camouflage than giving the ol' actuators a haircut.

Read more on Steam. The devs, Crimson Herring Studios, are them wot did Sovereign Syndicate, an apparently decent Victorian fantasy RPG that we never found time to review. Look, I am not made of thumbs and eyeballs. As for the daunting possibility of an Evangelion Fixing Sim, the recently announced Valkyrie Iteration gets into some of the squirming detail, there.

#4070. Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks live, where to buy the 40th Anniversary handheld

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks have been filtering onto the shelves in the last week, following the Ocarina of Time remake's release date on November 5. With a number of stores bringing 40th Anniversary edition consoles to the party during midnight releases, or well-timed online drops, many lucky stock hunters managed to snag their handheld in time to face Ganondorf.

Right now, there's no Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock live on the shelves, and even finding that Pro Controller or carry case is proving difficult. There's a ray of hope to be had here, though.

In the last week, Target and Nintendo have both dropped new Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks, while Walmart's had the special edition gamepad on the shelves. GameStop is prioritizing in-store orders only, so your best bet is to head down to your local store to check on their inventory.

In the UK, Amazon has been rolling out its restocks in smaller waves, running through last week, over the weekend, and once again on Monday.

Here's hoping we'll see more Legend of Zelda Switch restock action in the coming days - we'll be covering all of it live right here.

I've been tracking hard-to-find stock for over six years now, starting with the incredibly limited releases of the PS5 and Xbox Series X. I've been reporting on how retailers operate with high-demand products, from anniversary releases to brand new consoles, ever since then - including the Nintendo Switch 2 itself.

Amazon has been quieter for restocks since it dropped its first round of handhelds at launch. Still, there's been a good amount of time since release day - enough for the online retailer to potentially re-fill its warehouses?

Walmart's had a bit of a time of it. The retailer cancelled a number of pre-orders just the day before launch, and has been catching up on its backlog ever since. While new stock might be already allocated to those burned by pre-order mishandling, it's worth keeping an eye on any movement here.

Target has been the most active of US retailers in the last week, running scheduled in-store and online restocks around November 5-6 last week. While that inventory might take some time to re-emerge, it's worth keeping an eye for accessories here as well.

Best Buy kept its most recent allocation of Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock for its midnight Ocarina of Time launch event. Since then, the online side of this retailer has been pretty quiet.

Nintendo itself has held its own online Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks pretty regularly since launch. This is always one to keep an eye on.

GameStop is only running Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 restocks in stores, so you won't find any online stock here. That goes not just for the console, but for the Pro Controller and carry case as well.

Amazon UK has been dropping Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks in smaller waves over the last week, so it's always worth keeping that tab open and regularly checking back.

EE has offered Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks twice since launch, and has also been offering additional discounts on Ocarina of Time and Pokemon Pokopia bundles as well.

Smyths Toys was one of the first retailers to drop its original wave of Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock when the handheld was announced, so we're expecting more action here in the near future. It's also one of the only UK retailers I'm seeing with listing pages up for the Pro Controller and carry case.

Here's the thing with Very. It often bundles up difficult-to-find stock with extra accessories or games to keep resellers at bay. That means you'll be paying a little more here (though still only RRP for everything you're getting) but stock often holds out a lot longer.

Argos was previously offering Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock ahead of launch, but things look to have run dry now. The store organises its inventory by postcode, though, so it's always worth checking your local area's delivery and collection options.

Currys previously had a listing page up for the Legend of Zelda Switch 2, but it seems to have disappeared now, instead sending us to a generic consoles search page.

Nintendo has also stated more stock is on the way, so you'd expect its own store to be one of the first with fresh handhelds up for grabs.

There's not been much movement today at all, not even the whisper of a carry case. While retailers may be recuperating their supplies after a heavy week last week, we're holding out hope for more drops later in the week.

We've seen retailers like Amazon and Nintendo dropping Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock in dribs and drabs over the last few days, but that could ramp up to a bigger wave next week. That's giving stores a good two weeks to restock after last week's Ocarina of Time launch, and retailers - like Walmart - who are yet to see major online drops plenty of time to catch up.

Nintendo itself has been securing additional Zelda Switch 2 handhelds after it initially underestimated demand. The brand has been hosting its own very short, but far more regular, drops over the last few days so it's worth staying in touch here and checking back regularly.

It's well worth signing up to as many notification systems as possible while your Zelda Switch 2 stock hunt continues, Nintendo's offering its own and Target has also now launched its own email registry as well.

Had you asked me at the start of this stock hunt, I probably would have guessed that the special edition Pro Controller would be easier to find in stock than the handheld itself. That doesn't seem to have been the case, though.

The Legend of Zelda Switch 2 might be difficult to find reliably on the shelves, but it has been flitting in and out of stock at different retailers since launch. I can pinpoint maybe two or three times I've seen the Pro Controller file back onto the shelves - and it was gone just as quickly if not faster than the console.

While still currently out of stock, EE has been offering Nintendo Switch 2 bundles with the special edition handheld and discounted games. Nestled between Pokemon Pokopia and Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream, you'll find the Ocarina of Time remake with £10 off its regular price. Once stock returns to these shelves, we're hoping the bundles will once again become active.

The UK has also seen its own restocks over the past week, primarily from Amazon with a few from EE earlier in the handheld's life. While those Amazon restocks are fleeting, I haven't spotted any dropping so far today. It's well worth keeping in touch there, though, as the retailer seems to be adopting a 'little and often' approach.

From what I can see over the course of our restock tracking so far, Walmart has never publicly offered online restocks of the Legend of Zelda Switch 2 itself. Accessories have been spotted, but with the retailer reportedly fumbling its pre-order phase (and having to catch up as a result), things have been particularly quiet here. That could mean big things once those inventories are reset, though.

Nintendo's listing page states that "more inventory is on the way," undoubtedly a good sign for future Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks. However, it's worth remembering you can also add the special edition handheld to your Nintendo Store app wishlist and get notifications on your phone when stock does return.

Nintendo Switch 2 Legend of Zelda Edition | Check stock at Nintendo

Here we go again, another week of tracking all the latest Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks. We're keeping a close eye on all things Walmart right now, but Nintendo, Amazon, Target, and Best Buy all represent solid online restock opportunities as well.

#4069. You can make a vampire hunter who's afraid of the dark, disease and small spaces in Hunter: The Reckoning - Deathwish, and that's surely the best way to play

A month or two back I penned a 1500 word whine about feeling too powerful in Blood of Dawnwalker. "Gimme a vampire sim in which I'm a pathetic vein-nibbling goblin," I wrote, using many more adjectives than that. Well, never let it be said that I'm biased against vampires, for I am equally keen to play an RPG in which I am the least capable vampire hunter in the universe. A vampire hunter who screams when he wakes up with his hair over his face. A vampire hunter who has to spray the vampires with antibac before staking them.

An RPG like Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish, perhaps, which presents you with a choice of Advantages and Flaws when creating a character. You have to balance these out on a gnarly weighing scale, before they'll let you through the game's front door. Here is a video showing all that off, together with a lot of sixpacks.

The Advantage/Flaw system looks familiar on the surface. Advantages include Warrior, which gives you +15% chance of a critical hit, or Charmer, which gives you a +1 to Persuasion skill checks. Flaws include clumsy, bad reputation, fear of darkness, hypochondriac, and claustrophobia.

I don't know much about the tabletop game on which Deathwish is based, and the video skims the detail here, but I suspect the last three Flaws will boil down to something like "-1 Constitution in Unlit Closets". Still, I really enjoy the idiocy of going up against crypt-dwelling undead while being unable to tolerate shadows, small spaces, and disease. In general, I'd love it if Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish steered well away from any possibility of simply overpowering the vamps, to say nothing of the werewolves and other creatures of the night.

This appears to be the idea: devs Teyon have stressed their desire to make something more story and investigation-driven, after the stomping gibfest that was RoboCop: Rogue City. As narrative designer Mateusz Działowski put it in a previous dev diary, they've "switched from action with RPG elements into RPG with action elements". Amongst other things, you'll need to put together a team of fellow would-be slayers, each with secrets and traumas, and gather clues about best tactics while roaming the game's condensed and shiny New York City. You can read more about it all on Steam.

#4068. 'Generally Favourable' Review Scores For Trio Of Xbox Game Pass Launch Titles

Decent scores for Warhammer Survivors, Tanuki: Pon's Summer, and Football Manager 27

Three games from November's Xbox Game Pass lineup are launching today, and they're already picking up some pretty decent review scores.

Warhammer Survivors, Tanuki: Pon's Summer, and Football Manager 27 Console are available for Ultimate and PC Game Pass members today. It's a pretty busy day for the service, especially if you're interested in playing all three, so we decided to do quick review roundup of them all.

This way you can see what the critics are saying and maybe decide which game you fancy playing first. So, here's what reviews are saying about the three new Xbox Game Pass titles:

"You’ll find yourself smiling as you log dozens and dozens of hours in this installment of Football Manager, which takes a leap forward from last year’s revolutionary release, offering a more polished, streamlined game with even faster processing speeds. The loss of official team name licenses is becoming a serious problem, but once you get past that hurdle, Football Manager 27 offers a well-rounded managerial experience that’s increasingly optimized and satisfying." - Google Translate

"Football Manager 2027 marks a strong return to previous highs, following the stumbles last year, with the standout feature being the impressive and engaging changes to the tactics system, enhanced by greater control and noticeable feedback. Fans of the series should, and will, enjoy it, and it will make a good move forward for those who have been sticking with FM24."

"Football Manager 27 has finally regained its appeal with improved controls and greater tactical depth. Unfortunately, AI glitches and missing features continue to be a nuisance."

"We have not yet returned to the levels of Football Manager 2024: the interface needs to strike a more convincing balance between accessibility and efficiency, while the game engine remains the primary obstacle to the project’s full success. It is difficult to overlook certain player behaviors when the rest of the game encourages an ever-greater focus on tactical preparation."

"Tanuki: Pon's Summer is a charming, nostalgia-filled adventure that captures the magic of childhood summers through BMX exploration, quirky characters, and an impressive variety of mini-games. Its vibrant rural Japanese setting and fantastic soundtrack make every delivery feel like a new discovery. While limited BMX tricks and underdeveloped shrine customization leave room for improvement, Pon's summer adventure is a heartfelt experience that's easy to get lost in."

"This adorable adventure has clearly been made with a lot of care and attention, and that shines through in the engaging cycling gameplay and the endearing characters. Its mini-games do their best to hide the fact that the game's mainly a series of fetch quests, but the love that's gone into making it is contagious."

"Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is the rare cosy game that truly lives up to its premise, balancing both whimsical and snarky humour, alongside gameplay that manages to keep you moving just enough to hide its more shallow mechanics. Combined with a surprisingly generous array of content and impressive presentation, this is a Game Pass launch well worth checking out, even if a few wobbly wheels may disrupt your journey."

"TANUKI: Pon’s Summer is seriously charming, and that goes a long way to papering over some of the issues I had with it. If you loved Pon as much as I did then you'll definitely enjoy your summer with him."

"Warhammer Survivors is as addictive as Vampire Survivors, but has some unique twists that keep the experience interesting. It's also nearly flawless on the Steam Deck."

"All in all, Warhammer Survivors perfectly melds Games Workshop's property with poncle's timeless formula, resulting in another exceptional roguelike experience."

Mini Review Warhammer Survivors (PS5) - Absurdly Addictive Crossover Is a Match Made in Bullet Hell

"If you’re looking for the next twist on the Vampire Survivors formula and the idea of a Warhammer spin-off excites you, absolutely do not skip Warhammer Survivors – it’s on virtually every platform, it isn’t demanding on the system and and it’s quite cheap. It’s full or Warhammer goodness from two universes, and it introduces various twists the make the combat more varied and engaging. A slow start and the game being a lot less varied and content-filled than Poncle‘s masterpiece do limit the game’s long-term potential, but Warhammer‘s survivors-like romp is a blast, one that will keep me glued to the screen for quite some time even after this review."

"Considering these examples, Warhammer Survivors is a few days late and dollars short, albeit at a budget price. For those of you who’ve fully rinsed Vampire Survivors… Well, first off, that’s simply an impressive feat; well done. But secondly, here are another 40 heroes to max out, with hundreds of objectives to clear. Consider your bullet heaven buffet fully restocked."

There you have it, folks! Decent scores all around for today's Xbox Game Pass launch titles. Of the three, Football Manager 27 appears to have impressed the most, but only time will tell if that remains the case. Warhammer Survivors is pulling in mixed scores, although there's still a chance its score could climb a smidge.

Sony has begun advertising PS5 hardware and accessories directly through the console's PS Store via a new Hardware tab at the end of its horizontal scroller.

The new page promotes PS5 consoles, controllers, the PS Portal, headsets, PSVR2, and PS5 Covers. There's then a part below it that details the sort of benefits you get by ordering through PlayStation Direct.

From there, you can buy PS5 systems and accessories.

I suppose this works well as an advertisement for the more casual gamers who may not be aware of the latest PS5 accessories, controllers, and console covers. However, the more tuned-in fans will already know to simply head to PlayStation Direct for those peripherals.

#4066. Unknown 'Mega Man Legends' Project Surfaces Online

As Capcom gears up for Mega Man's 40th anniversary next year, more findings related to the long-running IP are surfacing online.

As reported by Mega Man fan site Rockman Corner, a production titled 'Mega Man Legends' has appeared on ACTRA Toronto's "What's Shooting" database (a public listing of production registered with the Canadian performers' union) this week.

It's filed under "new media" and the production start date was in September, with it scheduled to wrap up by December. Casting is apparently in house, but that's all that's known about the mysterious project.

As the source notes, "new media" could be everything from "video games to television and film". It's also mentions how Capcom "could be looking to Canadian voice talent as an alternative to SAG-AFRA Actors" after "Mega Man: Dual Override became the subject of a SAG-AFTRA 'Do Not Work' order" earlier this year.

Mega Man Legends was originally released as a 3D video game in 1997 and was followed by a second game in 2000. There was also a prequel spin-off in 1999, and a cancelled third entry for the 3DS.

This latest finding also follows a rating board classification in Korea at the end of last month. It featured various classic Capcom console titles, including multiple Mega Man games.

News Multiple Capcom Console Classics Have Been Rated In Korea

If we hear anything else about this listing, we'll provide an update.

Liam is a news writer and reviewer on Nintendo Life. He's been writing about games for more than 15 years and is a lifelong fan of many iconic video game characters.
