#4039. Play as water and rain on wildfires in Atuel, a short, free game about the power and vulnerability of nature

Well, have you played Atuel? If not, you can do so within the next hour - it's a tiny, free, 25-minute walking sim, albeit one with little actual walking on account of you playing most of it as a river. More of a running sim, really.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Technically, Atuel calls itself a "documentary game", and not without justification. While its sweeping Patagonian landscapes are rendered with a dreamy otherworldliness, and certain moments are downright mystic, the whole watery journey is based directly on the Atuel River that runs through western Argentina. As you drift downhill, taking control of water, clouds, and the local wildlife, you'll hear real-life scientists and historians monologuing on the Atuel and its relationship with the human cultures it's nourished. Mercifully, these are delivered with thoughtfulness as well as earnestness, maintaining the game's contemplative atmosphere without making it sound like the audio guide to a museum of Birmingham canals.

A few bends in, Atuel also takes on the climate crisis, directing you away from the soothing freshwater and into wildfires and parched riverbeds. I'd say this was preaching to the choir, at least for anyone who a) desires a functioning planet and b) learned about the water cycle in primary school, but then it isn't really preaching. Rather, developers Matajuegos weave between the beauty of the Earth and the need to protect it quite gracefully, and end their river tour on a more hopeful note than its darker moments may have intimated.

There's plenty else to leave an outsized impression in your memory matter: the understated, naturally-textured soundtrack, for instance, or the patiently gradual zoom-outs that slowly unveil the Andes' wild splendour. For me, and without wanting to undermine the importance or the accuracy of Atuel's environmental point, it was mainly just nice – therapeutic, even – to float through its gorgeous, surreal scenery like a cloud. And sometimes, as one. You can download it for free from Steam and Itch, with a pay-what-you-want option on the latter.

#4038. It's Official, Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Has Sold Over 5 Million Copies In 4 Days

Nintendo has announced that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has sold a total of 5.2 million units in just four days.

This number includes 810,000 copies sold in Japan alone, and makes Ocarina of Time the fastest-selling Nintendo-published Switch 2 game since the console's launch. For added context, the N64 original sold an overall total of 7.6 million units, according to Video Game Sales wiki.

This also makes it the second highest-selling Switch 2 game, with initial sales putting it above Donkey Kong Bananza's lifetime sales at 5.05 million (as of 30th September 2026). The best-selling Switch 2 game remains Mario Kart World at 16.48 million.

It's not clear what the digital/physical split is at the time of writing, though we should have a slightly better picture of this once Famitsu releases the Japanese boxed charts later this week.

Nintendo Co., Ltd. (HQ: Kyoto, Minami-ku, Japan; President and Representative Director: Shuntaro Furukawa, “Nintendo” hereafter) announced that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 sold over 5.2 million units worldwide (including 810,000 units sold in Japan) in the first four days following its launch on November 5, 2026.

This is the highest global sales for any Nintendo-published Nintendo Switch 2 game in its first four days.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2, released worldwide on November 5, is a full remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, originally released for Nintendo 64 in 1998. Link travels between two time periods, as Young Link and Adult Link, making use of different abilities and items available in each period to progress through his adventure. Developed for Nintendo Switch 2, the game features reimagined visuals and enhanced playability, while preserving the experience of the original game.

The game also supports ZELDA NOTES, a service available within the Nintendo Switch App for compatible smart devices. By using ZELDA NOTES, players can access a variety of features that support gameplay.

In the UK, it was confirmed that Ocarina of Time was the second biggest physical launch in series history, coming in just behind Tears of the Kingdom. It stormed to the top of the charts to become the biggest physical video game launch of 2026 (so far – hi, GTA).

As for our review, we awarded Ocarina of Time a 9/10, stating it to be "the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time":

"Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is a stellar reimagining of the original, one that completely revamps the experience with stunning visuals, modernised gameplay, and vastly improved audio. Despite some minor blemishes, this is comfortably the most visually stunning work Nintendo has ever put out, and it’s unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time."

What we need is for elements of both older and newer gameplay mechanics to evolve the franchise. This idea was somewhat close in concept with Echoes of Wisdom.

Nintendo have already said they aren’t abandoning the open air exploration element in future games, so it’s just going to be really important that they find a way to bring back in some of the more classic elements (Dungeons, specific items to unlock that manage progression, and turn down the survival element a tad) to marriage a really good mix and innovate.

TOTK was getting there in terms of it’s Dungeons and Temples, but they still weren’t on the same level of intricate design as past games. I don’t know the answer to this however, so hopefully Nintendo will find a solution with whatever comes next.

#4037. Silica, an FPS and RTS hybrid that mixes a smidge of Dune and Helldivers together, has left early access and entered 1.0

The concept of fusing an RTS and an FPS always sounds like a fun one, and since 2023 Martin Melichárek has been trying to make a new take on the combination under the watchful eye of DayZ devs Bohemia Interactive through Silica. Today marks the day that Silica leaves early access and enters 1.0, fully fleshing out its hybrid and mish mash of Dune's Arrakis and Helldivers' Terminids.

Digging into Silica a touch more deeply, it is a sci-fi shooter set on a planet where there's a fancy resource you're trying to mine that definitely isn't the spice. There are two warring factions competing for said resource, when, uh oh! Some bug-ish, giant aliens aren't very happy you're doing all that. So, you can either join the fray on the ground with some classic first-person shooting alongside your friends, or you can take the role of commander and dictate your artillery from above.

The 1.0 update obviously comes with a few additions, namely the Centauri Campaign, a "story-driven single-player experience set in the war for Baltarus. It opens with a cinematic intro and features fully voiced mission briefings and in-game dialogue. Between missions, a 3D planetary globe tracks the war as territory changes hands." Commanding your army should be a better experience now too, with the ability to "arrange units into formations, issue more precise movement and attack orders, and quickly select all units of the same type. Improved AI targeting and vehicle movement also help your armies operate more effectively in large-scale battles."

Beyond that, 1v1 matchmaking has been added in, where you can fight against another commander. The Steam Workshop sandbox tools have been expanded for building your own scenarios and sharing them with others. And there are a whole bunch of bug fixes, quality-of-life improvements and additions, and more. You can read about some of those in more detail in this handy little blog post. If you like what Silica is putting down, then you can pick it up on Steam.

#4036. Shrek 2 Remastered Has No Official Reviews Yet, But The User Reviews Are Quite Bizarre

It has a high score on Xbox right now, but a Mixed one on Steam

Yesterday marked the launch of Shrek 2 Remastered on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S (along with other platforms), and if you're wondering why nobody seems to be talking about it, it's because there are no official reviews yet.

It seems codes were only sent out at launch for this one, which means it's going to take a while for the critics to catch up and share their thoughts on this remaster of an original Xbox cult classic.

We can at least see what the initial user reviews are saying about it though, and if you look at the Xbox Store, everything seems to be pretty rosy. Shrek 2 Remastered has a 4.3/5 rating on the US Xbox Store as things stand, with 76% of people giving it a 5-star review, while most of the (minimal) grumbles are focused on bugs and crashes.

The Steam reviews for Shrek 2 Remastered are quite bizarre though. Over there, the game currently has a "Mixed" average rating based on over 350 user reviews, with 46% of people rating it "Positive" overall.

If you look at the "Most Helpful" reviews that appear first, there are multiple people suggesting it's not a great port, highlighting issues with bugged cutscenes, a lack of settings options, and even claims that the CPUs are less intelligent than they were in the original game (although others debate that it plays "exactly the same" as it used to!). There are also multiple accusations that the remaster might have been partially put together using generative AI, although this is just speculation and not confirmation by any means.

Some people are totally put off by all these issues, while others are still really enjoying their time with the game.

Satan Claus on Steam: "Shrek 2 was one of my favourite games growing up, and I honestly can't explain how happy I am to have the chance to play it again after all these years. It's just as special as I remember, and seeing it brought back with changes that do the original justice is wonderful. Even better, being able to enjoy it on modern hardware, especially the Steam Deck, feels like a dream come true. Some childhood memories are worth revisiting, and this is absolutely one of them."

Mikey on Steam: "I was really hyped for this remaster since this game is a game I grew up playing with my sister, but I am sort of disappointed with the state it is in right now. Lots of camera bugs, cutscenes ending aprubtly, missing skybox textures, characters looking woody and uncanny and lots more. It's like they just threw a paint bucket on it and called it a day. I'll wait for patches, since there still is hope."

As mentioned, Shrek 2 Remastered is getting a much better reception on Xbox than Steam right now, so perhaps we ended up getting the better version (or Xbox fans are more lenient), and you can check it out for yourself at the price of £22.49 / $26.99 for Series X and Series S if you're interested.

We do actually have a review copy of the game that we'll hopefully be able to check out soon, so stay tuned for our impressions in the near future. We'll also keep an eye out for raw Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S footage comparisons so you can get an idea of how it plays across both consoles.

For now though, we'll leave you with some basic gameplay from Shrek 2 Remastered down below.

#4035. Sony Cancels Fairgames After Years of Work on PS5 Live Service Shooter

PlayStation has officially cancelled Fairgames, the PS5 and PC live service shooter it had in production at Haven Studio.

The news comes from Bloomberg journalist Jason Schreier, though it's been sourced from an internal email distributed to PlayStation employees, and a company spokesperson has commented on the story.

That spokesperson told the outlet that Haven Studio will remain open following the cancellation, and it won't suffer any job losses. The developer, originally headed by Jade Raymond of Assassin's Creed fame — who left about a year and a half ago — will now become a support team within PlayStation Studios.

In the email to PlayStation employees, it's said a recent test of Fairgames didn't deliver the results the company wanted.

It said: "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set. Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

Announced more than three years ago, Fairgames was one of the headline announcements from the infamous PlayStation Showcase that properly pushed Sony's live service efforts — it was also where Concord and Helldivers 2 debuted.

Since then, absolutely nothing official from the game has been made public except for studio departures.

The game has reportedly done poorly during pre-launch and private tests, which has now been confirmed in the email to employees this week. There were rumours Fairgames would be brought back with a new name, Break In, around the summer season of games conferences earlier this year, but it never materialised.

It's yet another failure from PlayStation's first-party efforts during the PS5 era, which has seen many cancellations to the likes of The Last of Us Online, Payback from Bungie, live service titles from Sony Bend and Bluepoint Games, and Twisted Metal. You might as well throw Concord in there too, because while it did actually release, it was taken offline permanently after just two weeks.

Let's hope the PS6 generation doesn't follow in these footsteps.

#4034. The Citadel Project is a Thief-inspired dark fantasy, survival-horror lite stealth-em-up with some lovely shadows set in a medieval megastructure

You know, given the whole stealthy element of Thief-like immersive sims, I'm surprised there haven't been more of them with horror elements. There's Gloomwood, sure, but it's not as common as I'd like. That in turn then makes me curious about The Citadel Project, an immersive sim with some survival-horror elements set in a nasty, parasite-infected dark fantasy world, all apparently made by just one person.

In The Citadel Project, "the last line of defense built by the Ancient Kings in an attempt to preserve what remains of humanity in the face of the Great Storm." Some kind of evil force is ruining it from the inside, and you have to make your way through a medieval megastructure to figure out what happened. You aren't anyone special, "just a simple prisoner who manages to escape from a cell deep within the Citadel." Truthfully, the story sounds fine enough, I'm more smitten with the vibes put on display.

The shadows are what sells me, for the most part. They're dark and moody, looking plenty ripe for hiding in. And look, if you hand me a megastructure to explore, I'm going to do so. I'm also a fan of your main weapon, a crossbow. Not enough games with crossbows if you ask me! There's all sorts of bolts you can use with it, like a fire bolt that, obviously, sets things or enemies alight, a rope bolt to help you quickly climb or swing out of danger, a decoy bolt that makes a lot of sound to distract with, or a moss bolt; I'm not sure what that one does, my guess would be to dampen your footsteps and make it easier to sneak up on unsuspecting baddies.

Said baddies also appear to be infected with some kind of parasite, the severing of which appears to come in handy when trying to take them down. Overall, The Citadel Project likes a neat little im sim with just enough going on to make me curious to explore further. Which I might do, when I get the chance, as there is a demo available on Steam. Alternatively, I could just wait a week, as the game is out in early access November 11th, just over a week away. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

#4033. What Happens When Two Games Have The Same Title? Indie Publisher Reveals Heartwarming Answer

"I signed their game and now we're launching both"

With so many games releasing these days, it must be so difficult to come up with a completely unique title without encroaching on another developer's work.

Case in point, an indie game by the name of Piece by Piece from publisher No More Robots launched earlier this year on Steam, but in an amusing twist of fate, another game called Piece by Piece came out in the same week.

Now, this isn't the case of a washed up dev blatantly copying another for easy money – both titles here are radically different to one another, but they just happen to share the same name.

If this were a big publisher like EA, Ubisoft, or even Nintendo, you could easily imagine that it would be taking action to force a name change. That is if it doesn't work to remove the duplicate game from sale altogether.

However, as highlighted by Mike Rose from No More Robots, the developer of the other Piece by Piece game couldn't afford to bring it to Switch. So, in what is no doubt a remarkably kind gesture, No More Robots did it for them.

I have some 🌟feel-good news🌟 to share today! Earlier this year we launched a game called Piece by Piece. In the same week, *another* game called Piece by Piece came out I heard from the dev that they couldn't afford to bring their game to Switch. So I signed their game and now we're launching both

"I have some feel-good news to share today!

"Earlier this year we launched a game called Piece by Piece. In the same week, *another* game called Piece by Piece came out.

"I heard from the dev that they couldn't afford to bring their game to Switch. So I signed their game and now we're launching both."

Both titles are available for pre-order via the Switch eShop ahead of their release on 25th November, and you can also opt for a bundle if you're keen to try out both.

Rose states that Nintendo "absolutely hated this", questioning why both games have the same title during the certification process. We totally understand Nintendo's position on this, but it's wonderful to see that it approved everything in the end. Rose ended his announcement to say "Anyway, mega happy to be helping them out with such a fun thing. Not all publishers are evil, I promise!!".

#4032. "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games

You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.

In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.

The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.

And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!

Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."

They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.

#4031. 'We Will Put In Our Best Efforts To Develop For It' - Stellar Blade CTO Wants Xbox Helix Dev Kit

"Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox"

Shift Up CTO DongKi Lee, best known for his work on Stellar Blade and the studio's mobile games, recently spoke at a developer panel about his excitement to get hands-on with Xbox Project Helix development kits. All whilst in front of a senior official of team Xbox.

As Inven Global puts it, Lee was one of five panellists, comprised of execs from other development studios, and answered questions on what it's like developing games for console in the Korean gaming industry.

When asked about what advantages the console platforms have compared to PC, fellow panellist and former Tekken CEO Katsuhiro Harada took the opportunity to throw some shade at the Xbox Series S, jesting "I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released", attributing additional development resources to optimising games for the lower spec console.

In response to this, the Shift Up CTO spoke about his excitement to work alongside Xbox and his eagerness to see Project Helix developer kits in Korea:

"Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox 'Helix'. From an engineer's standpoint, if you provide us with a dev kit first in Korea as early as possible, we will put in our best efforts to develop for it."

Xbox players have been asking for a Stellar Blade port for quite some time, regularly mocking up fake Xbox Series box art and posting it to socials, and usually asking when Shift Up will bring the game to Microsoft hardware. It's certainly a possibility, and DongKi Lee's enthusiasm for working with Project Helix is encouraging. That, and this tweet from Edo, Shift Up's 'publishing guy':

During the panel, Lee was asked about the recent Switch 2 version of Stellar Blade and the effort involved in porting the game from PS5 to NS2. The Shift Up CTO shared a chuckle with the panel moderator and CEO Harada whilst discussing what could and couldn't be compromised during the port. Specifically, how reducing the polygon count on protagonist Eve's 'rear' was "never an option".

@themightyant If they release a Helix S or something similar, it would be very different from the Series S from a developer's perspective. If I've understood things correctly, the Xbox Helix OS will be much closer to a Windows PC environment. That would mean developers wouldn't need to create a specific port for the Helix S, just like PC developers don't make a separate version of a game for every possible hardware configuration.

It would basically come down to a different settings profile that's optimized for the hardware. That's essentially how games work on devices like the Xbox ROG Ally. Developers don't make a special version for it, it's the exact same PC version, with only the configuration and performance settings changing.

I don't know exactly what the Helix OS will look like in the end, but there will almost certainly be a greater level of standardization between PC and Xbox games. The differences between the two platforms should end up being pretty minimal which would greatly reduce the amount of work developers have to do. That's pretty much the message Xbox has been pushing so far, especially in its talks and presentations aimed at game developers.

Yes, it's interesting how Series S made developers optimise games and how those optimisations would later be used on weaker hardware like Switch 2 and Steam Deck. If Xbox games become just Windows games like any PC game, that would benefit Helix massively, and it could still run them with specific settings and optimisations added with that purpose.

However, why not just release several Helix models with different internal storage, e.g., 512GB, 1TB, 2TB? Memory is the most expensive component. RAM as well, but is it worth sacrificing RAM on a home console when there will be handheld devices?

#4030. Ubisoft are reportedly tapped as one potential company that could acquire Arkane, though the Dishonored studio's own management may be in the running too

I'd really like it if it weren't Ubisoft though

Things are potentially looking up for Arkane, depending on how you feel about Ubisoft (and depending on who actually ends up acquiring them). I mention the Assassin's Creed developer because, reportedly, they're interested in buying the studio from Microsoft, having even made a bid for it. I'll go out on a limb here and say it's the whole being French thing, but uh, I'd really rather someone else bought Arkane.

This comes from, you guessed it, Bloomberg, who say that sources they've spoken with claim two other gaming companies have also made a bit. There is even the potential that Arkane would be sold to their own management, as Xbox are considering such a move. But overall, it doesn't yet sound like anything is leaning any particular way, as Xbox haven't formalised a deal with any of the potential buyers. Bloomberg also note that if a deal is made, this should then allow Arkane to finish their work on their Blade game, which is expected to release within the next couple of years.

Apparently an Xbox spokesperson told Bloomberg that the gaming company is exploring their options ahead of their December deadline, but didn't comment any further. Ubisoft reportedly did not have a comment to make on the matter. For some context on that December deadline, because of French labour laws, companies that have over 1000 staff members are required to search for a buyer for three months before they can just completely shut down. That makes December 13th the final date that such a deal has to be made by, meaning there's about a month and a half left to go.

Arkane's sale comes as part of a sweeping range of cuts, sales and closures being made by Microsoft at the moment. In July, it was announced that studios like Double Fine, Undead Labs and Compulsion would no longer be a part of Xbox, with all three going indie; Ninja Theory was also announced as part of these cuts, but unfortunately it's looking like they'll be shutting their doors. Thousands of Xbox staff were also laid off at this time, with more laid off in September, and even more coming this month and January reportedly. As always, solidarity with all workers affected by Microsoft's heartless and money hungry cuts.

#4029. Sony's 10 Most Profitable PS5 Games Reported in New Estimates

Sony's received a lot of criticism for its first party output this console generation. It's no secret that the company has chased live service trends at the cost of single player experiences — the kind of games that solidified the PS4 as a fan favourite machine.

And so it's interesting to see which Sony-published titles have actually made the most money across the last six years or thereabouts.

Now, I should stress that the numbers I'm about to relay are not official. They're estimates based on Alinea Analytics' data-tracking methods — but by and large, the outfit does end up providing fairly accurate numbers.

The team's put together a list it claims are the top ten Sony-published games of the PS5 generation, ranked by premium gross revenue.

Revenue is primarily driven by sales — and so it makes sense for Ragnarok and Spider-Man 2 to be up there at the top, given that they're Sony's two best-selling releases of the generation.

The former has sold roughly 21 million copies, while the latter is closing in on 20 million. The report states that both are evergreen titles, meaning that they're continually selling a decent number of copies despite their age.

Meanwhile, Helldivers 2 is the real outlier on this list. The live service shooter has made Sony a fortune, but most of that money's come from the game's success on PC platform Steam.

The report estimates that just over 66% of copies were sold via Steam, while PS5 accounts for just 26%. The other 8% belongs to Xbox.

Stellar Blade is interesting, too. It's a roughly 50-50 split between PS5 and Steam, with PS5 just edging it.

Are you at all surprised by this top ten? Are there any games on there that have done better than you thought? Tell me about your favourite Sony-published PS5 title in the comments section below.

#4028. Opinion: A Pokémon Rave Just Might Have Been The Strangest Night Of My Life

It's a strange feeling, finding yourself in a dark room with thousands of Pokémon fans while a DJ blasts EDM so loud you can feel it in your chest.

Yet that's how I found myself yesterday evening, bobbing my head along to tunes far from my usual playlist and cheering whenever a Pokémon appeared on the giant screen that encompassed the performer. To add to the fever dream, a glance at my watch informed me that it wasn't even 8pm yet.

This was the Pokémon Night Out, a live Electronic Dance Music event organised by The Pokémon Company that came to London's O2 Arena last night after an LA show in October. Artists Marshmellow (the guy from Fortnite) and Alison Wonderland (not from Fortnite) headlined, and I can honestly say that it was unlike anything I have ever experienced before.

Not being a particular fan of either large crowds or loud music, it may come as a surprise to hear that I'm not a natural raver. I am, however, a big old Pokémon fan.

So armed with my finest earplugs and the most outrageously expensive beverage money can buy, I made my way to the seated area just in time for the first set.

The above images do a pretty good job of illustrating the experience, but let me paint you a picture anyway. Alison Wonderland stood behind her decks on the main stage, with one of the largest screens I've ever seen extending up behind her. Throughout the set, this screen would be adorned with all manner of flashes and alternating colours, occasionally with a Pokémon popping into view.

And yes, I use 'occasionally' on purpose there. There were a lot of Pokémon visuals, no doubt, but I was surprised at the number of times the screen was 'mon-less.

This was doubly true of the music, which was hardly packed with tunes from the series. There was a particularly jarring EDM mix of the Lavender Town theme at one point, but I struggle to remember many other motifs entering the setlist.

Giant DJ-ing Pikachu and Mimikyu helped keep everything suitably Poké-themed, mind you, both receiving a huge cheer when they wobbled on stage and 'played' a track of their own.

Marshmellow's set was more of the same, though his elevated position in the backing screen meant that the visuals could really sing. As out of my depth as I was, I fully cheered watching a giant battle between Groudon and Kyogre play out behind Mr. Mellow, sat with a cheesy grin as huge Greninja and Lucario animations showcased their kung fu moves, and I'll even admit to shedding a little tear at seeing the OG starters round a grassy knoll as Lana Del Rey's Summertime Sadness blared in the background.

The finale featured giant Eevees, confetti, and those light-up wristbands you see at a Coldplay gig. I still wasn't fully convinced that the worlds of Pokémon and EDM are a match made in heaven, but I was kind of swept up in the strangeness of it all. 'The first in my bloodline to see this,' and all that.

It will take a massive change of heart (and perhaps a blow to the head) to convert me into a full-bodied raver, but as I looked out into the crowd of those standing and witnessed three Ash Ketchums dancing with a Pikachu and a rather sweaty Bulbasaur, I knew that I had just experienced a night out unlike any other.

Does a Pokémon rave sound up your street? Let us know in the comments.

Jim came to Nintendo Life in 2022 and, despite his insistence that The Minish Cap is the best Zelda game and his unwavering love for the Star Wars prequels (yes, really), he has continued to write news and features on the site ever since.

#4027. "An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process," Nexus Mods say as they rule out barring generated creations from their site

"We drew the line where the real argument is"

The owners of Nexus Mods have ruled out instituting an outright ban on AI-generated works being uploaded the site, instead opting to expand their current rules on modders disclosing how they've used AI in making their mods. This latest move to address the waves of AI-created or AI-thumbnailed mods now hitting Nexus Mods on a daily basis follows Nexus' modus operandi up to this point, which has been simply to try and ensure AI usage is clearly labelled so prospective downloaders can make informed decisions.

"We won't introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods," Nexus Mods owner and CEO Victor 'Foledinho' Folmann wrote in a news post. "You may ask me why, since that is not the solution some of you were looking for. The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process, but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.

"This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct. Mod Authors should have a chance to decide about the further use of their work, and you should be able to decide for yourselves how much AI-based content you want to see, whether more, less, or no content at all.

"As for our own position: Nexus Mods will not use your mods to train AI and will not sell or license them to anyone doing so. We refused to do that in the past, and we will refuse to do so in the future. Given such a variety of opinions within our community, not everyone will agree with any decision taken. These are the ones we believe are right for Nexus Mods today, and we’ll keep adjusting them as the tools evolve and as we see how these changes work in practice, with your feedback guiding that."

In terms of the changes which are being brought in to toughen up the site's current three tag system design to make mods containing AI-generated content, AI media, or made with AI assistance easier to spot, Nexus are making AI disclosures mandatory for those uploading new mods. "What this means is that for mods tagged as AI-assisted, we’re also introducing a requirement for a public explanation of how and where AI was used, which should give you a better understanding of what you’re downloading, rather than leaving you to make assumptions on a tag alone," Folmann wrote. "We’re also going to make AI tags on mod pages more prominent, displaying them immediately after adult-content tags so they’re easier to spot."

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that’s not going to happen," he continued. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules." New "permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods" are also being worked on, with the hopes of giving modders more control over how their works can be reused. Finally, Folmann noted that the site are "investing in security tooling and specialised staff" to address concerns over generative AI making "bespoke malicious code hidden inside mods" more prevalent.

Mod makers are being given a 60 day grace period to make sure their existing works meet the new rules, which'll run until January 2nd.

As you can imagine, the comments section of this Nexus Mods announcement is lively. Over on LinkedIn, Folmann patted himself on the back a bit about the mixed reception being an indicator the site are going about this the right way. "Some wanted a full ban. Some think we went too far. That tells me we drew the line where the real argument is," he declared, adding that "transparency beats prohibition". He also reiterated that his vision is of "modding that's Spotify-easy to play and GitHub-powerful to create, with humans in charge".

I reckon that with or without these changes, in the absence of its owners taking a strong stand browsing Nexus Mods is going to carry on be more of an exercise in ducking dodgy stuff than it was prior to most games' pages being splattered with the likes of icky AI-baked Geralt clones standing where decent screenshots of the actual game would've been more than adequate.

The silence is over. The servers for Dark Souls 2 and 3 have been reactivated after they were suddenly turned off at the end of October due to apparent security issues, with FromSoftware saying the problems have been resolved.

The studio announced that normality has resumed today, November 11. "Regarding the temporary suspension of the game server for Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3, the investigation has been completed and the fix has been applied," the company writes. "The game server and online features are now restored."

Whether you enjoy invading other players and trolling them or helping people out in particularly hefty encounters, all is now well once again across the planes of Drangleic and Lothric. As much as can be anyway, they're still perpetual hellscapes scarred by centuries of brutality and tyrants. But nowhere's perfect.

A relief as is, the quick comeback for the servers this time around is even more so because we've seen the online aspects of these games turned off for much longer before. Both installments of the series went quiet on the server side on PC in 2022 for weeks, leaving the community completely in the lurch.

The circumstances were similar too, because it was another potential security concern. Whatever was going on, FromSoftware took a lot longer to figure out what's what and put in appropriate safeguards.

This turnaround was mercifully short, though we still don't know the ins and outs. But then, we don't need to. The important part is that the games are back and players can enjoy them to their heart's content again. Hopefully, any potentially harmful characters keep their invasions to their characters and other players.

#4025. Smash hit cyberpunk storekeeper Probably Stolen was originally a different, non-cyberpunk game that seemed destined to sink without trace

Publisher tinyBuild celebrates turnaround after very underwhelming demo numbers

Space station trading game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim has been doing rather well on Steam, attracting over 162,000 concurrent players last night. I've been feeling the urge to fire it up again myself, after my brief launch-day trawl through its quagmire of black market economics and factional rivalries.

The game's big numbers come as a shock given that it began life as another, non-cyberpunk kiosk job sim called Deepspace Emporium, which still has a Steam page as of writing. Deepspace Emporium seemed doomed to fizzle out in obscurity. But publisher tinyBuild got behind it regardless, working with developers Questing Goose to overhaul the art direction and lay on extra brainchips. The gamble paid off.

"Probably Stolen was initially a game under a different name with a released demo," summarises tinyBuild CEO Alex Nichiporchik on Twitter. "That demo peaked at 28 concurrent players. We loved the concept and gameplay, and worked with the dev to reinvent the visuals and focus on what works design wise. This is the result."

The original Deepspace Emporium seems very similar to Probably Stolen in broad strokes. The core of the game is haggling with strung-out ne'er-do-wells, buying or selling goods of varying quality and legality in order to surf a fluctuating market and pay the rent. It's Papers, Please, but you're searching for fake watermarks on cigarette packets, and wondering whether you dare stock contraband weaponry. You also have to appease or outmanouevre factions with competing interests, from station security to underworld barons.

From what I've played, Probably Stolen essentially takes all that and pumps up the Netrunner parallels with posher visuals. Not having played the now-unavailable Deepspace demo, I can't say how much intrigue it adds to all the shady transactions going on beneath the hood.

I'm not blown away by Probably Stolen's pixelart – I find it quite flavourless, as depictions of cyberpunk space stations go – but it has pleasing texture. I am disproportionately fond of the rolled-up sleeping mat beneath my counter. Looks nicely padded! Still, the meat of this game is undoubtedly the vast collection of items you can get your greasy fingers on, with a choice of retail lines and vocational pathways such as gunsmith and chemist. You can sell rat corpses, tins of caviar, robotic hands, scavenged shotguns, and purple tubers of uncertain origin. I am Commander Silverhand, and this is my favourite store on the Citadel.

It's lovely to think of a developer transforming a probable write-off into a chart-topper by means of some canny plumping and reorganising. The situation is almost certainly more complicated than Nichiporchik makes it sound. Still, let's take the opportunity to reminisce moist-eyed about a few other games that underwent a dramatic visual transformation during development.

The obvious one is Team Fortress 2, which once upon a time looked like a prototype Silent Hill environment with some khaki toy soldiers. Gearbox worked similar sorcery upon Borderlands, which once looked like a hungover Fallout 3. The prevailing wisdom is that piping in some colour and whimsy propelled these games to greatness, but who knows, perhaps if they'd clung to the old "football stadium toilet bowl" vibe, they'd have made an extra billion apiece. Any other precedents come to your mind?

#4024. Two Major Developers Explain Why They Like And Dislike Making Games For Xbox Series S

"I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released (laughs)"

Over the years, we've heard all kinds of stories from all kinds of developers about whether they either like or dislike making games for the Xbox Series S, and former Tekken boss Katsuhiro Harada falls into the "dislike" category.

In a recent panel discussion that was transcribed by the folks at InvenGlobal, Harada noticed that a senior Xbox official was in the audience, and joked that he wanted to let them know how much he isn't a fan of the Xbox Series S.

"Since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released (laughs)."

He then went on to explain that although the low memory is "an issue" of the Xbox Series S, the hardest part is that it's actually so similar to the Series X, but with "awkwardly lower performance". Harada also pointed out that players direct their complaints to the developers rather than Microsoft if they don't like the visuals and/or performance.

"Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance [...] Furthermore, in markets like the US, there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners. Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking "Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?"

Finally, he also noted that developing for the Nintendo Switch 2 is actually easier in some ways because it's a "distinct device for Nintendo fans", whereas the Xbox Series S is akin to "having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child" compared to putting in your "absolute best output" for the Xbox Series X.

Despite what it might seem like, a lot of this conversation seemed to be very lighthearted and full of laughs, and when Cyberpunk 2077's Paweł Sasko stepped in to highlight the benefits of the Xbox Series S including its affordable price and the ability to better optimise for low-spec platforms, Harada admitted that he made it sound a lot more attractive.

In fact, it was so convincing that Harada jokingly worried that it might lead to a similar Project Helix alternative!

Director Paweł: "Harada speaks a lot of truth. Players don't fully understand the technical context behind why fewer characters appear on screen or why visuals are downgraded. However, intensely optimizing for lower-spec platforms definitely brings the benefit of making the game run significantly better across all platforms—including PS5, high-end PCs, and handhelds like Steam Deck and ROG Ally.

And the biggest advantage of Series S is that its affordable price makes it accessible. Not every gamer can buy expensive high-end hardware, so from a developer's perspective, even if the strict constraints are painful, there is a silver lining in expanding market penetration to deliver the game to more players."

CEO Harada: "Director Paweł packaged Series S so gracefully that the Microsoft representative in the audience keeps nodding along. I'm worried they'll feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well (laughs)."

It's best not to take any of this too seriously, but it does at least highlight the differing opinions throughout the industry about whether the Xbox Series S was a good or bad idea in hindsight.

From a consumer perspective at least, we reckon it was a fantastic idea. The Xbox Series S has continually managed to deliver incredible-looking games over the past six years, and in a time where console prices are constantly on the up, the Series S at least provides a somewhat affordable current-gen hardware option - at least if you find a good deal.

#4023. 'It Felt Like a PowerPoint Deck of Executive Ideas': Beta Testers Share Thoughts on PS5's Cancelled Fairgames

Haven’s heist shooter Fairgames – first announced more than three years ago – has been cancelled, rounding out a rough generation for Sony’s live service ambitions.

While we saw very little of the game publicly, a trailer for a title named Project Espresso emerged in September, giving us our first proper look at the title in years.

This video was used to promote a playtest, which ultimately got the game cancelled today. Sony executives said it failed to meet the “goals” it had set for the game.

To be fair, this is an example of the platform holder learning lessons from Concord, as it’s now abundantly clear Fairgames was never going to find an audience. Exactly why it took so long for the company to recognise that is up for debate.

While the abovementioned playtest was under NDA, some users are now starting to share their experiences online.

Writing on the ResetEra forum, user RedBullCola wrote: “I was in the late stage testing group and it wasn't very good. The feedback in matches was also not good. It felt like a PowerPoint deck of executive ideas, same thing with Horizon Hunters Gathering.”

Horizon Hunters Gathering could be the next game to get cancelled, as Dutch dev Guerrilla has been given until December to retool it. We’ll probably get word on the status of that project soon.

Over on Reddit, user Darkdhalias echoed the negative sentiment on Fairgames: “As someone who participated in said playtest, cancelling it was 100% the right move. [The] game was still years away from being compelling, and was one of the most unpleasant alpha/beta experiences I’ve ever had.”

Back on the ResetEra forum, user srrai was a bit more positive: “I played it and yeah just wasn’t for mainstream people. They weren't gonna buy and/or play this enough to keep it going. Though it was fun [in my opinion]. Would I have bought it? Maybe at $40.”

Still, this is the kind of feedback that PlayStation would have been receiving from the playtest, and the reason the game was ultimately cancelled.

Sony had bold ambitions for live service this generation, and while Helldivers 2 has admittedly been a big hit, virtually all of its other bets have ended up being blunders.

The good news, at least, in this instance is that Haven Studios staff will keep their jobs, and will be reassigned support work on other PS Studios titles for now.

#4022. Square Enix's Big Reset Is Working As It Increases Its Full-Year Forecast

Publisher reports "solid performance" for FF7 Rebirth

Square Enix has released its latest financial data for the six-month period ending 30th September 2026.

In short, it looks like the company's efforts to reset its business is working. It reported increased sales compared to the same period in 2025 and has therefore increased its overall forecast for the remainder of the fiscal year.

Net sales for the period totalled ¥163,179 million, an increase of 21.9%, while operating income totalled ¥38,793 million, an increase of 41.3%. Square Enix has cited strong sales of games, including Final Fantasy VII Rebirth on Switch 2 and Xbox Series X|S along with The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales.

The company now forecasts total net sales of ¥310,000 million over its previous estimate of ¥298,000 million, with total operating income now forecast at ¥59,000 million over its previous estimate of ¥49,000 million.

It also provided a fresh breakdown of physical sales vs. digital in the entertainment sector. The figures in the west are particularly telling, with physical sales down year-on-year from 1.09 million to 1.01 million. Digital sales, however, increased substantially from 5.83 million to 8.19 million.

Overall across all regions, digital sales made up just over 89% of Square Enix's total sales.

Looking ahead, Square Enix will release Final Fantasy VII Revelation on 8th April 2027. Unlike the previous two entries, the Switch 2 version will launch day-and-date alongside all other platforms.

The Lenses of Truth allow you to see through illusions in OoT, at the cost of magic power

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Lenses of Truth in Zelda Ocarina of Time are an essential item used to reveal hidden objects, illusions, and secrets that Link might have otherwise missed. In the original OoT these were actually called the Lens of Truth, presented as a flamboyant magnifying glass, but in the Remake they're recreated into a pair of equally flashy glasses. Either way, the effect and their location in Kakariko Village remains the same, so I'll explain where to find them in the Remake below.

To get the Lenses of Truth in OoT, you need to have progressed to the point where you can travel between eras in the Temple of Time. Once you've done that, however, you can obtain the Lenses with the followng steps:

Lenses of Truth can be equipped like any of the masks from the Happy Mask Shop. However, while being worn, they drain your magic constantly.

The benefit is that while wearing them, you can see through illusions and other optical effects. These include:

#4019. "Keep talking about it": Raw Power Games call for Wishlist aid as they, and their historical strategy sandbox Chronicles: Medieval, lose funding

Raw Power Games, an independent studio comprising veteran developers of The Witcher 3, Total War: Three Kingdoms, and Crusader Kings III (among others), have called on players for support after losing their funding - an existential threat to both the organisation and to their debut, the still-in-development historical strategy game Chronicles: Medieval.

In a statement posted last week, Raw Power announced that "the necessary funding" behind the studio was no longer in place, despite Chronicles: Medieval – which was unveiled last year with an expensive-looking, Tom Hardy-narrated trailer – apparently being within touching distance of its planned early access launch. Hardy or no Hardy, however, the statement declared that they aren't "going down without a fight", hinting at talks with what could be possible new investors, asking interested would-be fans to "keep talking about" the game, and encouraging its inclusion on Steam Wishlists.

A few days on, the impact of this rallying call remains unclear. Raw Power Games have made no further statements, and Chronicles: Medieval does not seem to appear on Steam's own list of Top Wishlisted games. SteamDB have it at #26 in their desire-o-rankings, representing no change from its position immediately before the funding announcement was made, and while the game's Steam follower count has increased by over 1,000 week-on-week – significantly more so than surrounding games in the list – that doesn't feel like the kind of wild grassroots support that might save a dozens-strong studio.

Still, as my childhood television used to say, every little helps, and I'm inclined to hope for Raw Power's survival if only as an antidote to the enthusiasm-poisining dread of seeing so many other developers being laid off and shut down. Chronicles: Medieval looks promisingly ambitious too, mashing up sprawling Mount & Blade-style battles with an RPG-flavoured strategy layer that involves the player's custom-created character ascending the snooty social hierarchy of 14th century England. Best of luck to everyone trying to get it over the early access line.

#4018. Xbox Brings Its Free Tier Of Cloud Gaming To Loads More Players Today

You may recall that back in July, Xbox announced a new free version of Xbox Cloud Gaming that would allow you to play games at no charge, but you'd be forced to deal with ads as a compromise.

That tier of Xbox Cloud Gaming was in testing for months, but as of today (November 11th), it's rolled out publicly - meaning the vast majority of Xbox users around the world should now have access to it.

Xbox has been very quiet about it today so far, but based on what we've seen around the web, the free tier of Xbox Cloud Gaming will provide you with a 30-minute slot to stream "select games from your library" as well as select free-to-play games, after which time you'll be kicked off and will have to start a new session.

You'll see ads before the session begins, and seemingly never again throughout your 30-minute playtime.

"You can stream select games for free by watching ads before each gaming session. Session time limits apply. After a session ends, you can watch another set of ads to start a new session."

News Xbox Introduces Free Game Streaming With Ads, Outlines Five Principles They'll Adhere To

Rolling out now as a "test" for Xbox Insiders

Despite the rapid session length, this could prove a popular option for anyone who wants to play GTA 6 on Xbox One (for example) without being forced to pay anything for Xbox Cloud Gaming. We'd urge some caution for now though, as Xbox has yet to confirm whether GTA 6 will be one of the "select" games that supports this feature.

Meanwhile, the cloud playtime limits that were announced a while ago for Xbox Game Pass members have now started kicking in, which also means you can now purchase "Cloud Playtime" to top it up if you run out.

The prices for this here in the UK are as follows:

Curiously though, I've checked the new "Cloud Playtime" option in the Settings menu on my Xbox Series X and I'm being informed that I've still got "Unlimited" access to Xbox Cloud Gaming with my Ultimate membership, so it might be worth checking the same thing on your end and seeing what it says for you.

I'm not the only person who's spotted something similar:

Anyway, we've thrown Xbox's official tweet up above, and you can hit the link in it to find out even more details.

#4017. EU 'Digital Fairness Act' Could Have A Huge Impact On Loot Boxes And Virtual Currency

After being leaked earlier this week, the European Commission has today presented its proposal for the 'Digital Fairness Act' — a rule update that aims to offer "better protection for consumers and fairer competition for businesses" in the games industry.

To be clear, the proposal has not been adopted by the EU Commission just yet, but if it does go through, it could have a huge impact on several hot-topic game mechanics like loot boxes, virtual currencies, pay-to-win options and more. What's more, the act would apply to all EU member states without the need for individual approval.

So, what does the act set out to fix? The big notes that stand out to us appear in Article 15, which would require all companies offering "variable reward schemes" (or loot boxes, as you might know them) to be upfront about the items' contents and the probabilities of unlocking them. It calls for a requirement to toggle these options off in an "easily accessible manner," and no such items should appear in games designed for those under 18.

Likewise, Article 13 of the act prohibits personalised pricing based on user profiling — whether that profiling uncovers that the user is a minor, or if they are vulnerable to pricing practices in other ways due to their "age, credulity, disability, or any specific misfortune or circumstance of such gravity as to impair the consumer’s judgment".

Article 14 is all about virtual currencies, and it stipulates that companies must disclose "their estimated monetary value in the currency" to all customers. Any virtual-currency-related purchases must be turned off by default for minors, it continues, and can only be switched back on by a parent or guardian.

The Digital Fairness Act also proposes clampdowns on pay-to-win mechanics in games played by those under 18, and disabling toggles for any mechanics based on "[encouraging] compulsive or excessive use," like log-in bonuses and daily rewards.

Mechanics that fall under the umbrella of all the no-nos outlined above are subject to change, and the proposal states that the EU Commission will be able to add to the list at any time.

It's a rather dense read, and we struggle to see how many of the proposed changes would actually work in practice — how can you turn off pay-to-win strategies for under-18s and still keep things fair when playing against adults? — but it would certainly pose quite a change to the games industry as we know it.

With the soaring popularity of the likes of Fortnite and Roblox, it's only a matter of time before stronger unified regulations come into play. Whether those regulations end up looking like the Digital Fairness Act, and whether they actually protect customers, is another question entirely.

News PEGI Targets Loot Boxes With Its New Overhauled Ratings System

#4016. Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.

It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.

While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.

It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.

This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

#4015. PS5 Has Officially Crossed 100 Million Sales, Sony Confirms

The PS5 has now officially surpassed the 100 million sales milestone.

This news comes via Sony itself, which has just released newly updated figures for the current-gen console.

On the Sony Interactive Entertainment website, it states PS5 has sold "more than 100 million" units as of 10th November, 2026.

This means that, since the end of the last financial quarter (30th September 2026), Sony has shifted another 2.1 million machines.

It's taken slightly longer for PS5 to reach 100 million than its predecessor, the PS4, which was reportedly the fastest ever console to hit the milestone.

Given the many hurdles PS5 has contended with during its lifespan — launching amid the COVID-19 pandemic, shortages, hardware prices skyrocketing, etc. — it's quite remarkable it's managed to maintain such a healthy momentum.

It's possible this recent surge in PS5 sales is related to the imminent arrival of GTA 6, as well as the usual bump due to the approaching holiday season.

In any case, PS5 joins the list of consoles that have surpassed the milestone, and it's the fourth Sony home console to achieve it.

Sony also reports that PS5 is its most profitable generation ever, so all-in-all, it's been a very good generation for business.

The console still has a bit of time left before the inevitable PS6, which is expected to arrive within the next couple of years; whether Sony can keep the momentum going into the new generation remains to be seen.

Stephen has been part of the Push Square team for over six years, bringing boundless enthusiasm and a deep knowledge of video games to his role as Assistant Editor. Having grown up playing every PlayStation console to date, he's developed an eclectic taste, with particular passion for indie games, arcade racers, and puzzlers. He's also our go-to guy for Sonic-related matters, much to his delight/chagrin.

#4014. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#4013. Oblivion and Skyrim’s gap was bridged by forward-looking books about a murderous floating island, so why is The Elder Scrolls 6 stuck reanimating a world that’s stood still since 2011

Why the Umbri-hell has time stopped in Tamriel?

Long waits between mainline entries in a series aren’t a new phenomenon, if perhaps a bit more common nowadays due to big games' ballooning development cycles. It took about 23 years for BioWare’s Baldur's Gate 2 to be followed up by Larian’s Baldur’s Gate 3, though there were a decent amount of spin-offs and remasters peppered between the two.

The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel hasn’t stretched on that long quite yet, but as Bethesda finally revealed concrete details about it just in time for Skyrim's 15th birthday, it really hit home for me that TES VI will be tasked with restoring motion to a world where calendars have been stuck in the 201st year of the 4th era since 2011. Perhaps it’s because I’m still in my twenties and haven’t lived long enough to see that many things I like pause their forward march for this long before returning. There’s also a good chance my expectations of timelines rolling forward on a regular basis without the need for a whole new entry are coloured by the constant stream of new stuff fed into most games via updates and live service passes these days.

However, when I look back at the interregnum between the last two Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion and Skyrim, I can’t help but feel that what Bethesda and ZeniMax have packed into the gap between Skyrim and Sentinel might have done the latter no favours. Sure, The Elder Scrolls Online has arguably meant that there’s been far more for series fans to sink their teeth into between mainline games than ever before, but because the MMO's a prequel, none of its tales and lore push the Elder Scrolls' timeline forwards. Meanwhile mobile and card game spin-offs like The Elder Scrolls: Blades, The Elder Scrolls: Legends, and The Elder Scrolls: Castles have all either slotted in before Skyrim or not been tied to a specific point in time.

On one hand, that leaves the devs a nice clean slate to take the sixth entry wherever they like narratively upon the conclusion of the Dragonborn’s adventures. On the other, Bethesda has missed the opportunity to paint out the world and further set up the stakes for Sentinel in the interim. Back when we were waiting for Skyrim's original release, the developers were pumping out spin-off books that daubed some fresh adventures onto the Elder Scrolls' canvas.

I bought these books - 2009’s The Infernal City and 2011’s Lord of Souls - ages ago upon hearing their tales referenced in the sorts of Elder Scrolls lore videos which appeal to sad nerds of my ilk, but have only gotten around to reading past the opening chapters in recent months.

In hindsight, I think I bounced off them that first time because it just felt a bit weird to be reading about set characters getting up to adventures in Tamriel rather than setting off on them in the boots of my own custom created protagonist. I didn’t run into the same with The Witcher, as you’re seeing that world through Gerry from the River’s eyes no matter where you turn. Anyway, the two Elder Scrolls novels by American author Greg Keyes tell the tale of the Umbriel crisis which took place 48 years after the Oblivion crisis and about 153 years before Skyrim’s dragon crisis (Tamriel does love a crisis). The Umbriel crisis saw a floating island powered by souls and formed via some Daedric drama, carve a path of destruction from Black Marsh to the Imperial City. Yep, the empire’s not-Roman soldiers had to fight a flying hunk of land. At one point some mages had to float a legion up in the sky so they could get their bottoms kicked by Umbriel’s defenders.

As you might’ve gathered, the books take the opportunity to tell a story which - especially in terms of where tech was in 2009 - wouldn’t necessarily fit an Elder Scrolls game. Or, at least, not one of the more straight-laced variety Bethesda have made in their post-Morrowind days. A lot of time’s spent looking through the eyes of two characters who’ve snuck aboard Umbriel, the floating island, after it destroyed their hometown and have to adjust to the strange customs of its inhabitant lords and their underlings before finding ways to help take it down. On the ground, things take a more familiar form, as a very serious Dark Elf named Sul and a nepo baby Imperial prince trek across bits of Cyrodiil, Morrowind, and Elsweyr on a quest to do their bit in vanquishing the threat. Then, there’s a Penitus Oculatus spy named Colin trying to figure out if the Umbriel Crisis is an inside job of some sort and a few tales of regular Imperial troops working to evacuate citizens living in the floating island’s path. In an Elder Scrolls game, you’d get some of that, but not be able to hop from person to person chapter by chapter in the fashion the books do.

Umbriel slowly floats across Black Marsh, southern Morrowind and Cyrodiil with an army of zombies in tow, much like this article’s about to float into mildly spoilery territory for the two books. You see, The Infernal City and Lord of Souls outline what happened to cause the red year, a volcanic eruption which took the land of the Dark Elves from the beautifully alien place it was at the time of The Elder Scrolls 3 and reduced it to the ash-covered wasteland it’s outlined to be at the time of Skyrim. As the latter game’s lore books would subsequently set in stone, Baar Dau - the meteor suspended in the air above Vivec City at the time of Morrowind - fell and destroyed the city following the disappearance of the metropolis’ namesake ex-Tribunal god-king. The books reveal that the big rock didn’t fall the moment Vivec vanished, but was kept afloat by a device called the Ingenium, which is essentially a magic box powered by regular soul sacrifices. Two Dunmer, Vuhon and the aforementioned Sul, ended up having a fight rooted in the tech’s murderous nature and that’s actually what led Baar Dau to finally hit the ground.

Either way, the meteor falls, but that's not an insubstantial bit of backstory for a source outside of the games to add to the Elder Scrolls’ canon. Also wound into the tale of how Umbriel came to be is a bunch of extra flesh on the bone of the relationship between Daedric prince Clavicus Vile and Umbra. In the games, the latter’s always just been a powerful sword which imprints a new personality onto its wielder, but in the books it’s portrayed as a being capable of nicking some of Vile’s godly power and plotting to escape the prince’s realm of Oblivion via the building of Umbriel. Beyond those, the books also offer a chance to get to know emperor Titus Mede I, the warlord who took over the Empire following a post-Oblivion crisis interregnum and whose offspring you murder during Skyrim’s Dark Brotherhood questline.

None of this is anything close to required knowledge for playing Skyrim. No characters from the books pop up to say hello, likely because enough time’s passed for most to perish of natural causes. The sole reference I can recall comes via a chat about a location called Sleeping Tree Camp, which isn’t tied to any of the main questlines. You can, and I did for a long time, totally ignore these time-bridging tomes. That said, I do feel that having now taken the time to read them has helped me see the history of Tamriel as something not as strictly limited to the specific snapshots in time presented by each of the games.

Tales like these, which aren’t conveyed with as much natural emotional detachment as I tend to feel when reading much-condensed accounts of historical events or far off places on the pages of in-game lore books, really help in creating the illusion that The Elder Scrolls’ world is growing and evolving as our own does. It’s not just a snow globe that only shifts whenever some prophesied hero piloted by a controller or keyboard rocks up to shake it.

I do think, in large part due to the size of the real world gap between it and Skyrim, The Elder Scrolls 6 would have and still could benefit from having spin-offs like these to keep gently nudging the timeline forwards. A complicating factor is that judging by this week’s teaser, Sentinel seems like it could be set in the 206th year of the fourth era, a mere five years after the events of Skyrim. That’d mean no 200-ish years of wiggle room in which to slot some spin-off stories without serious risk of influencing things that’d have to be reflected in the new game. Unless Bethesda wanted to either put serious barriers up around where the spin-off could tread or get into a game of arbitrarily deciding what is or isn’t canon. With some collaboration, it could certainly be done, but it could also be a headache the studio wouldn’t want.

It’s likely too late to start the ball rolling now anyway, but that doesn’t stop it being worth asking why Bethesda and their famously adaptation-loving corporate bosses at Microsoft didn’t make sure they had something akin to these books in the works when Sentinel was punted down the road in favour of Starfield.

You did this well once, why haven’t you managed to pull it off again this time? I’m hoping that isn’t the inquiry which’ll come to define The Elder Scrolls 6 as much as questions about where a chunk of the old Bethesda magic had gone did with the studio’s trip to space. Lest the next long wait for a game from them be packed with even more uncomfortable silence.
